A borrowing of French aile, wing, so a plane has wings inside; its silent S was added to match [[see:isle]].
Metathesis of ask in London and American dialects; Rob says it is not a survival of Old English axian but the same phenomenon recurring.
German for current, leading Euro English speakers to use [[see:actual]] that way.
The Arabic definite article; a word starting with al- of unclear origin is probably Arabic.
The Arabic definite article, still found at the start of many English loanwords such as [[see:alcove]], [[see:algebra]], [[see:alcohol]] and [[see:acton]].
The Arabic definite article, often seen at the start of Spanish place names such as [[see:Almería]], [[see:Alicante]] and [[see:Algeciras]], legacies of Arab rule.
American gangster arguably the first [[see:public enemy number one]], since a newspaper dubbed him that.
Arab television station whose name, the island or peninsula, is the same Arabic word as in [[same-root:Algiers]].
Persian mathematician who wrote the book behind [[see:algebra]] in Baghdad around 820; his name means 'from Khwarezm', like da Vinci, and gave [[gave:algorithm]].
Mathematician of the 9th and 10th centuries, rediscovered in medieval Europe; his name means 'the person from' a place, like Da Vinci, and gave [[gave:algorithm]].
The longer name of [[see:Madinah]], meaning the enlightened city.
The first fake name considered, rejected as too common, before [[see:Alan Smithee]].
Recorded as a magic word in the early 1900s; earlier a placeholder for incomprehensible foreign speech, probably mocking Arabs saying Allah.
A DJ credited with taking the music to white audiences in the 1950s by calling it [[see:rock and roll]].
The Directors Guild's sanctioned pseudonym for disowning directors, from [[see:Death of a Gunfighter]]; [[see:Al Smith]] was rejected as too common.
The fake film director's name put in the credits when someone doesn't want to be credited; discussed in an earlier episode.
From an Italian cry, 'to arms', one of several terms from Italian warfare.
Dating from the 3rd century, combining a water clock with a mechanism that dropped pebbles onto a gong at set times.
Another name for Britain, from the Latin for white, probably after the White Cliffs of Dover; possibly linked to [[same-root?:elf]].
Listed among English words that still carry the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Once much closer to [[from:alcatraz]], but probably reshaped by Latin [[from:albus]], white, because the birds are big and white.
The flying machine in [[see:Clipper of the Clouds]], a multi-rotor gyrodyne or compound helicopter lifted by vertical air screws.
Golf score named after a bird, following [[see:birdie]], with bigger birds for bigger feats.
Changed in English from [[from:alcatraz]], perhaps under the influence of Latin [[see:alba]], white; the reverse of what happened with [[see:alpaca]].
Means noble bright, with the same -bert ending as [[same-root:Robert]].
Means noble bright.
Associated with [[see:absurdism]], meaning, very reductively, that everything we try to do is relatively pointless.
Like [[see:Winston Churchill]], someone who has hoovered up many misquotations.
Albert the Great, said in legend to have made a talking bronze human or head offering advice; Naudé's description of it gave [[gave:android]].
Possibly related to [[same-root?:elf]] through a root meaning white.
A word for Britain, used as a grand, patriotic name for clubs like West Bromwich Albion.
Latin name for Britain, thought to come from albus, white, maybe for the white cliffs; nearly the name of [[see:Sydney]].
Means noble bright, like [[see:Albert]].
The German [[equivalent:nightmare]], literally elf dream.
German word for a nightmare, essentially an elf dream, discussed in an earlier episode.
The name means white bumblebee, making it possibly related to [[same-root?:elf]].
French poet who proposed the [[see:point d'ironie]].
Portuguese for pelican, presumably naming the prison rock; from Arabic [[from:al-ghattas]], sea eagle, and the source of [[gave:albatross]].
Iberian Spanish word for a pelican, from Arabic [[from?:al-qadus]], the jar (the pouch), or possibly [[from?:al-ghattas]], the diver; it gave [[gave:albatross]].
An Arabic adaptation referring to the research done in [[from:Kemet]], the land of black earth; [[same-root:chemistry]] is related.
Arabic adaptation of a Greek word probably meaning land of black earth, Egypt; the science of turning base metals into gold, which later became [[gave:chemistry]].
At least partly Arabic-derived; its truly separable part is the Arabic article [[see:al]].
From Arabic [[from:al-kuhl]], 'the kohl' eye makeup, seen as the essence or spirit of a mineral; alchemists used it for fine powders; general drinks sense from the 1600s.
From Arabic al-kuhl, the [[from:kohl]], a fine eyelid powder; it came to mean any distilled substance, then strong liquor, then any alcoholic drink.
Rebracketed so -holic is tacked onto words like [[see:workaholic]], though in [[from:alcohol]] the detachable part is Arabic [[see:al]].
One of many English words that still begin with the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Came via Spanish from an Arabic word for a dome or vault.
From Old English ealdorman, the Anglo-Saxon counterpart of Norse-origin [[see:earl]]; now a local judicial post, it is the same word as elderman.
From Albrecht Discounts; feuding brothers both kept the name, creating [[see:Aldi Nord]] and [[see:Aldi Süd]].
Short for Albrecht Discount, formed from the opening letters of each element.
One brother's half of [[see:Aldi]], found in northern Germany including Berlin.
The other half of [[see:Aldi]], in southern Germany and also the Aldi found in the US and Britain.
The original name for [[see:italics]] type, after [[see:Aldus Manutius]].
Author of Brave New World, recipient of the letter first using [[see:psychedelic]]; took mescaline under Osmond's observation, inspiring [[see:The Doors of Perception]].
Introduced [[see:italics]] type in Venice in 1501.
Scandinavian languages use variants of it for beer; its root may mean bitter; historically unhopped and English, versus hopped continental [[see:beer]], per Peter Mathias.
Hired by local authorities or courts to test a district's beer strength; conner is from an Old English word meaning tester, unrelated to [[unrelated:con man]].
Covered in the weird jobs episode; an inspector of beer purity, whose post Johnson called a sinecure for decayed citizens.
English occultist who popularised [[see:magick]]; a colourful character who inspired fictional characters and much symbolism.
The letter meaning ox, whose ox's head was rotated to give A; also the first letter of the old Arabic order behind [[gave:abjad]].
From Italian [[from:all'erta]], a call to go to the watchtower; the 'al' is the preposition 'to', not 'all'.
Inventor of the modern battery, the [[see:pile]], who gave his name to [[gave:volts]].
Local water bailiff and part-time journalist who wrote about the [[see:Loch Ness Monster]] in 1933.
Highly successful Manchester United manager who called the tense end of a match [[gave:squeaky bum time]].
Greek name meaning defender of men, its -ander from [[from:andros]], man, as in [[same-root:androgynous]] and [[same-root:Andrew]].
Took the Gotham Club's rules and founded the [[see:Knickerbocker Base Ball Club]].
Scottish-born American naturalist after whom the [[see:gardenia]] is named, a case of [[see:nominative determinism]].
Wanted [[see:ahoy]] as the telephone greeting but lost out to [[see:Thomas Edison]]'s [[see:hello]].
His Homer translation's 'all the phantom nations of the dead' was turned into [[gave:phantomnation]].
Spelled with an F in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]] partly so Spanish speakers would not say 'alpa'.
Listed among English words that still carry the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Came into English from Spanish but ultimately comes from Arabic.
A Spanish ruler said to foam at the mouth when upset, probably a popular rather than official nickname.
Ultimately means elf council, where [[see:elf]] meant something like genius.
Loved using the [[see:MacGuffin]].
Invented [[see:Scrabble]] in 1938, reportedly setting letter values by counting the letters on a New York Times front page.
Plural of alga, with no English plural algas; algae is often used as a singular too.
From Arabic [[from:al-jabr]], reunion of broken parts or restoration, also used for bone-setting, via the book by [[see:al-Khwarizmi]].
From Arabic [[from:al-jabr]], a reunion of broken parts or restoration, originally used of setting bones.
From [[from:al-Khwarizmi]]'s work, meaning a reunion of broken parts, also used for setting bones; first a way to solve quadratic equations.
Medical term in Italian, Portuguese and Catalan for a bone setter, reflecting the original meaning of [[same-root:algebra]].
Place in southern Spain whose name, like [[same-root:Algiers]], comes from Arabic for the island or peninsula.
Country named after its capital, [[from:Algiers]].
Capital that gave its name to [[gave:Algeria]], from Arabic for the island or peninsula, the word also behind [[same-root:Al Jazeera]] and [[same-root:Algeciras]].
A corruption of the name of [[from:al-Khwarizmi]], which means 'the one from Khwarezm'.
From a Latin rendering of the name of the mathematician [[from:al-Khwarizmi]].
Started on TikTok: creators avoid words like [[see:to die]], [[see:kill]] and [[see:suicide]] for fear the algorithm will suppress their videos.
From Arabic al-Laqant, based on Latin [[from:Lucentum]], from Greek [[from:leukos]], white, as in [[same-root:leukemia]].
Coined the name [[see:Crayola]] in 1903.
Contains the Duchess's line about pigs having the right to fly, an early short [[see:when pigs fly]].
From Arabic [[from:al-qali]], like [[same-root:kalium]].
From Arabic al-qali, the soda or ash; first a salty substance, now a base that dissolves in water; it [[gave:kalium]].
Rhyming slang for a coat.
An 1800s folk song, sung by Rob, that uses [[see:twelvemonth]] in 'for a twelvemonth and a day'.
A [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult read from Rob's mug.
Show many Americans associate with the foolish-person sense of [[see:dingbat]].
An eggcorn for [[from:for all intents and purposes]], which people sometimes use deliberately.
One of several number-one idioms the hosts call self-explanatory.
A Christian festival on 1 November, created when [[see:Pope Gregory III]] expanded the earlier martyrs' day to celebrate all saints.

term: all the Moomins are not in the valley

mentions.note: Finnish for someone not all there, like [[equivalent:the lights are on but no one's home]], built on the [[see:Moomins]].

term: all wool and a yard wide

mentions.note: 1800s idiom for genuine or trustworthy, since cheap cloth of scrap fibres like [[see:shoddy]] was narrower than the standard yard.
Repeated constantly to avoid accusing uncharged people, though it is not the legal cure-all it's thought to be, especially in British law.
An even bigger comparison, a whole story standing for something else, classically [[see:The Pilgrim's Progress]].
Tempo marking meaning fast and lively, literally cheerful.
French name for Germany, from the Latin name for the region.
Basketball term now used outside the sport, from the French acrobatic exclamation [[from:allez-hop]], let's go up.
From Spanish [[from:el lagarto]], the lizard; English briefly used lagarto before adding the article to the start.
Trucker slang for a piece of broken tyre left in the road.
From Spanish [[from:el lagarto]], the lizard, originally lagarto de Indias, lizard of the Indies; the al- is not Arabic.
A folk-etymology name for the [[see:avocado]], prompted by the sound of the original word and its green, scaly, alligator-like skin.
Old English poetry's main device before rhyme arrived from French; ad- plus letter, stressing the repeated letter.
The French telephone greeting, borrowed from English [[equivalent:hello]].
A real person's name used by an author without permission to suggest someone else wrote a work, like signing a bad play as Shakespeare.
A slightly different variant of a sound; flimsy evidence suggests the Greeks used [[see:Q]] for an allophone of k.
Means different lizard because its hollowed vertebrae were unlike other known dinosaurs', not because it looked different; named by [[see:Othniel Charles Marsh]] in 1877.
Days on which official business could be done, listed in the [[see:fasti]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Listed among English words that still carry the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Coastal Spanish city from Arabic for the watchtower, a lookout over the sea, beginning with the article [[from:al]].
From Greek [[from:amygdalos]], with al- added in Spanish on the assumption that it was Arabic, like [[see:alpaca]].
The French word for lark, one of the few words that survive from [[from:Gaulish]].
Possibly related to [[same-root?:elf]] through a root meaning white.
Via Spanish, probably from a Quechua word like [[from?:paqo]], yellowish red, the animal's usual coat colour; al- was added on the mistaken assumption it was Arabic.
Region that repeatedly changed hands between Germany and France, where Alsatian, a form of High German, is spoken.
Name for the [[see:German Shepherd]] adopted because the British avoided saying German in WWI; the dog isn't from [[see:Alsace]].
A later key that gives another key an alternative use.
From Latin [[from:altare]], thought to come not from [[unrelated?:altus]], high, but from [[from?:adolere]], to burn, since sacrifices were burned there.
A high-up heap of clouds.
A high-up spread of clouds.
Pre-Old Norse word for ale inscribed on a [[see:bracteate]], seemingly jewellery honouring a favourite drink.
An example of the Latin -i plural that justifies octopi as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
One of the -us nouns that really does become -i, alumni, in the plural.
In the 1400s a blend of mercury and another metal; an alchemist's term from Arabic al-malgham, a poultice for sores, perhaps influenced by a Greek word.
Red-capped, white-spotted mushrooms that Jess associates with [[see:toadstool]]s, the showbiz mushroom of illustrations.
From Greek [[from:amarantos]], unfading flower; poets love it as the plant of immortality, and many amaranths turn into [[see:tumbleweed]]s.
Means unfading, from [[from:amaranth]]; it appears in [[see:John Milton]]'s work.
Literally means someone who does something for the love of it rather than for money, just like [[see:aficionado]].

Named after the giant river, chosen to start with A for alphabetical web listings and to suggest an everything store; originally [[from:Cadabra]].

Comes not from the fossilised tree resin but from [[from:ambergris]], although the two share an Arabic root.
French for grey amber, a waxy substance the hosts think comes from sperm whales' bile; it gave [[gave:amber]].
A Latin prefix meaning both, related to the amphi- in [[same-root:amphibian]].
Able to use both hands; literally right-handed on both sides, from [[from:ambi-]].
Text readable from multiple directions; coined in the 1980s by [[see:Douglas Hofstadter]], popularised by [[see:Peter Newell]], [[see:John Langdon]] and [[see:Scott Kim]].

A relationship aimed at fixing the partner.
A relatively recent coinage from psychology, one of the few English words for a mixed emotion.

Listed as one of the more fun collective nouns.

Suffragist and women's rights activist ridiculed in the media for promoting [[gave:bloomers]].
Called needlessly Latinate by [[see:George Orwell]].
When a word that implied something bad becomes good; ameliorate comes from French [[from:améliorer]], to improve; the opposite of [[see:pejoration]].

The process by which [[see:terrific]] went from terrifying to great.
A word becoming gentler over time, as [[see:fuck]] has partly done through overuse; the opposite of [[see:pejoration]].

In a different subfamily from the [[see:European badger]] and [[see:honey badger]]; Europeans probably named it for looking like their badger.
A 1950s wave of renaming [[see:french fries]], used for McDonald's-style fries for a while before the French name returned.
Listed among elements named after places.

Named after [[from:André-Marie Ampère]].

[[see:William Barnes]]'s book listing Germanic replacements for classical words, such as [[see:speechcraft]].
[[see:Nathan Bailey]]'s 1721 dictionary of 40,000 words, broader than earlier works but lacking literary depth and consistent structure.
Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next, as in Yoda's fear leads to anger; meaning a doubling back.

Another name for a [[see:heteropalindrome]].
Wordplay dating back to ancient Greece, popular as a witty game in Latin and English; anagrams itself rearranges into [[see:ars magna]].

An example of the different British and American spellings of the [[see:-ize]] ending.
The word most Indo-European languages use for [[see:pineapple]], which English does not; unrelated to [[unrelated:banana]].
What most of the world calls the [[see:pineapple]], used by many Spanish speakers instead of [[see:piña]].
Repeating the same words at the start of consecutive lines, as in [[see:I Have a Dream]]; meaning carrying back.
A form of [[see:hyperbaton]] moving one word, Yoda-style; Greek for turning upside down, remembered via astronomy and Yoda.
Literally fear of ducks, said to mean fear a duck is secretly watching you, from a [[see:The Far Side]] comic; compare [[same-root:anatiferous]].
Producing or bearing ducks, from Latin [[from:anas]], duck, plus -fer, carrying; Johnson's quotation links it to the [[see:barnacle goose]].
Means producing ducks, from their Samuel Johnson episode; it prompts the joke [[see:anatocracy]].
Producing ducks, in Samuel Johnson's dictionary and discussed in their dictionary episode; possibly linked to the belief in [[see:barnacle geese]] born from trees.
Joke coinage for rule by ducks, inspired by [[see:anatiferous]].
Literally a cutting up or dissection, related to [[same-root:atom]].
From Greek [[from:anatomia]], dissection, literally a cutting up: ana means up or into pieces and the second root means to cut.
Borrowed from French, from Vulgar Latin [[from:antianus]], from before, with an unetymological T added in Middle English; it meant the era before Rome's fall from about 1600.

term: and everyone stood up and clapped

mentions.note: The typical ending of [[see:broetry]] posts, often after someone's child says something wise.
Home of most Spaniards who crossed the Atlantic, which is why its [[see:seseo]] travelled to Latin America.
Tempo marking meaning walking, a moderate walking pace.
Confederate prison in the American Civil War where the [[see:deadline]] was drawn.
French physicist and mathematician who coined [[see:cybernétique]] and whose name inspired [[gave:amp]]s and [[gave:amperage]].
Contains the same Greek word for man as [[same-root:Alexander]]; it is Jess's spouse's name.
Had a grey parrot called Poll that reportedly swore loudly at his funeral, helping popularise [[see:Polly]].
The namesake of [[gave:Jacksonville]].
Rule by men, like [[see:phallocracy]]; its opposite is [[see:gynocracy]].
Contains the same andros, man, as [[same-root:Alexander]].
Meaning man-shaped, first used by [[see:Gabriel Naudé]] in the 1600s to dismiss [[see:Albertus Magnus]]'s supposed metal talking head; it [[gave:droid]].
Feels like science fiction, but the word is centuries old.
Named by the Greeks after the daughter of [[see:Cassiopeia]] and [[see:Cepheus]], sacrificed to a sea monster to appease [[see:Poseidon]] and rescued by [[see:Perseus]].
Egyptian sphinxes with male pharaohs' heads and wingless lion bodies, royal or temple guardians unrelated to the Greek [[see:Sphinx]].
Named as related to [[same-root:data]].
The device that measures wind, from a Greek word for wind, [[from:anemos]].
A device for measuring wind, from the same Greek word for wind as [[same-root:anemone]].
Literally daughter of the wind, perhaps for opening in wind or fragile petals; Ovid says it bloomed from [[see:Adonis]]'s blood when [[see:Aphrodite]] sprinkled nectar.
Etymologically a daughter of the wind; the sea anemone is named after the land plant.
A plant-like animal whose name means daughter of the wind, from the Greek for wind, as in [[same-root:anemometer]], which is related to Latin [[same-root:animus]].
One of the Latin words Christian missionaries brought to the Anglo-Saxons.
Used [[see:ay up me duck]] in front of a crowd to welcome [[see:Jack O'Connell]] on stage.
From Old Norse [[from:angra]], to vex or distress; first a verb, a noun a century later meaning ill will or physical pain; related to [[same-root:hangnail]] and [[same-root:angst]].
Related to [[same-root:ankle]].
Would be related to [[same-root?:Ankylosaurus]] if its name meant crooked lizard.
The tribe behind England's name, though people from England aren't called Angles.
Germanic tribe who settled Britain more fully than the [[see:Saxons]], bringing their royals and ruling powerful kingdoms, so [[gave:England]] is named after them.
One of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain from the mid fifth century, bringing West Germanic dialects that became [[see:Old English]].
One of the island names ending in the 'ey' (island) element found in [[see:Eyjafjallajökull]].
Island off Wales whose ending [[from:-ey]] means island; the meaning of the first part is unknown.
A way of speaking that avoids borrowings, especially Romance ones; it uses [[see:fast]] for castle.
A tongue-in-cheek modern movement replacing non-Germanic English words with Germanic equivalents; Rob made a video about it.
Seventeenth-century wars during which English sailors and merchants borrowed many Dutch nautical terms such as [[see:skipper]] and [[see:yacht]].
The Germanic settlers, [[see:Angles]], [[see:Saxons]] and [[see:Jutes]], who introduced [[see:Old English]] to Britain from the fifth century.
Old Norse word meaning sadness or low spirits, related to [[same-root:anger]].
An injury that looks angry may preserve the old physical-pain sense of [[same-root:anger]] rather than being figurative.
Borrowed from the German word for fear and related to [[same-root:anger]].
Simply German for fear, but in English it carries an existential element it lacks in German.
A Latin cognate of [[same-root:eel]], meaning snake or little snake.
Screenwriter who probably coined [[see:MacGuffin]], his name perhaps shaping it.
Meaning life, spirit or breath; Jess first links it to [[see:anemometer]], and Rob says they share a root.
Like [[see:psyche]], means breath, life and spirit; De Anima's principle organising living bodies fed into late 19th-century psychology terms.
A living, breathing thing; its Latin root may specify non-human creatures, though in 14th-century English it could include humans, with [[see:beast]]s set apart.
A guessing-game formula naming three categories of things, reflecting the original sense of [[see:vegetable]] as anything capable of life.
An old word for movies; Jess reckons its coiner was proud of it and annoyed it never caught on.
Related to the Greek for wind behind [[same-root:anemone]]; it's all about movement.
Also from a root meaning joint, and related to [[same-root:angle]].
Means stiff or fused lizard; the root could also mean crooked, which would relate it to [[same-root?:angle]], but that isn't intended.
Once written with a double N, it now uses the [[see:eñe]].

term: anointed sovereign of sighs and groans

mentions.note: A [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult from Rob's mug, which Jess finds incredible.
From archery, not violins: a spare bowstring in case the first snaps, so it originally meant backup options rather than extra skills; Henry VIII's state papers (1524) recommend two strings.
A Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:respond]], which has a slightly different nuance.
The most segmented insect; its name probably goes back to a word meaning cut up, either from its body shape or from biting things off.
Another name for a [[see:contronym]].
Literally opposite the bear, contrasting with [[see:Arctic]]; fittingly, polar bears live only in the north and penguins in the south.
Means without bears, the opposite of [[see:Arctic]]; fittingly there are no polar bears at the South Pole.
The stake in a card game, related to [[same-root:ancient]] through the sense of before.
Literally 'before the war', from [[from:bellum]]; often refers to the American South before the Civil War.
Related to [[same-root:ancient]] through the sense of before.
Under an unsupported theory, from Greek for flower eye, from [[from?:anthos]], after the animals' strange-looking pupils.
From [[from:anthos]], literally a gathering of flowers: a collection of poems or texts seen as a rich bouquet.
An extravagant passion for flowers, from [[from:anthos]]; someone afflicted is an [[see:anthomaniac]].
A person with [[see:anthomania]], such as an orchid thief.
Greek for flower, the source of [[gave:anthology]], [[gave:anthomania]] and perhaps [[gave?:antelope]]; not to be confused with [[unrelated:anthropos]].
Shaping something into human form, from the same Greek word for shape as [[same-root:Morpheus]].
The form Jess has seen more recently, another word for cannibals, related to [[same-root:anthropophaginian]].
A cannibal, used humorously in The Merry Wives of Windsor; from anthropo-, person, and [[from:-phage]], something that eats.
Greek for human or man, not to be confused with [[unrelated:anthos]].
[[see:Michael Halliday]]'s 1970s term for a relexicalised form of a language arising within an [[see:anti-society]]; the hosts find it implies illegitimacy.
A linguistic term for slang or [[see:cant]], implying a language used within a particular circle or for a particular purpose.
A dark twist on a proverb, overlapping a lot with the [[see:malaphor]].
An intentionally separate community of ostracised people or those creating a separate social order, where an [[see:anti-language]] arises.
A 19th-century double negative for opposition to [[see:disestablishmentarianism]]; it became famous as a long word through [[see:Gloria Lockerman]]'s 1955 TV spelling.
Compared with [[see:honorificabilitudinitatibus]] as a long word with a specific usage.
Political term about disestablishing the Church of England, boosted when [[see:Gloria Lockerman]] spelled it on [[see:The $64,000 Question]].
Made famous by [[see:The $64,000 Question]]; Jess covered its origin on her Substack and blog.
An [[see:anagram]] that humorously opposes or changes the original meaning, as with [[see:funeral]] and real fun.
Rhetorical device repeating words in reverse order, common in pithy phrases like [[see:when the going gets tough, the tough get going]].
Means turning about: repeating a phrase in reverse order, as in [[see:ask not what your country can do for you]].
Means not alone because it's found in many compounds, the pro-social element; symbol Sb from Latin [[from:stibium]].
Most likely from Arabic, but mangled beyond recognition in Greek and Latin; powdered antimony was the original [[see:kohl]].
The philosopher the [[see:cynic]]s followed, nicknamed something like the absolute dog; he taught at [[see:Kynosarges]].
His credo that all one needs is virtue and strength of spirit, and that ill repute is good, may explain the dog-like lifestyle behind [[see:cynicism]].
Placing opposite ideas side by side for contrast, as in a line by [[see:Cicero]]; even AI writing picks it up: it's not this, it's that.
Creole apothecary who created [[see:Peychaud's Bitters]] and served mixed drinks like the [[see:Sazerac]] in an egg cup.

term: Antoine Laumet de La Mothe Cadillac

mentions.note: A major figure in 17th- and 18th-century New France who founded [[see:Detroit]], and namesake of [[see:Cadillac]].
Another [[see:DuPont]] fibre name with the -on ending of [[see:nylon]].
Literally just means ring.
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Song Rob sings to illustrate [[see:tile]] meaning a hat.
Jess's example of a comparative phrase that takes 'from', supporting [[see:different from]].
From [[from:Afrikaans]], ultimately Dutch, meaning separateness.
The American word for a [[equivalent:flat]]; Jess prefers it because it literally means a place apart, which Rob finds too long and too general.
Means deceptive lizard, since its vertebrae resembled marine reptiles'; named first, in 1877, so it took precedence over [[see:Brontosaurus]].
A synonym for openly from Coleridge's dictionary, comparable to [[same-root:aperture]].
An opening, cited to explain [[same-root:apertly]].
Example of English p matching a German f sound under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
A short philosophical statement attributable to a specific person, unlike a [[see:proverb]], with a sting in the tail; sometimes criticised as reductive.
Playwright of The False Count, where a character says [[see:as melancholy as a sick parrot]].
From the goddess [[from:Aphrodite]].
A Farmer and Henley synonym for the [[see:monosyllable]], because that's where you play; Jess's new favourite.
Goddess behind [[gave:aphrodisiac]] and part of [[gave:hermaphrodite]].
Sprinkled nectar on her dead lover [[see:Adonis]]'s blood, from which the [[see:anemone]] bloomed.
Sets Psyche tasks such as sorting grains, done by ants, and collecting golden fleece, in the myth of [[see:psyche]].
From Latin [[from:apis]], bee.
The more common modern term for the study of bees, alongside [[equivalent:melittology]].
Latin for bee, related through an ancient root to [[same-root:bee]]; the Romance line has a P where Germanic has a B.
The Greek name for the Book of [[see:revelation]], meaning an unveiling, from apo, off, plus cover. Its end-of-the-world sense came recently through [[see:apocalypticism]].
The belief that the Revelation was near, which gave [[see:apocalypse]] its end-of-the-world sense.
Contains the Greek for hidden, as in [[same-root:cryptocurrency]]. It first meant hidden, then of dubious origin, so an apocryphal tale probably isn't true.
A measurement term for the Moon's farthest point, now used for a climax or high point of any kind.
Someone who defends a stance rather than says sorry, keeping the old defence sense of [[same-root:apology]].
An example of the different British and American spellings of the [[see:-ize]] ending.
Both an admission of error and a formal defence, as in literary apologies like [[see:Plato's Apology]]; the defence sense survives in [[see:apologist]].
With [[see:ataraxia]], one of the highest goals of [[see:Epicureanism]].
The final stage of the [[see:Socratic method]], when the questioning ends in puzzlement.
Greek for turning away, showing an omitted letter; the possessive marks a dropped E from Old and Middle English -es, not a contraction of his.
Borrowed from French, where it marked removed letters, from Greek for 'turned away'; the possessive apostrophe marks a dropped E.
From Greek roots meaning to turn away; in possessives the missing letter is the E of Middle English -es; also a dramatic aside technique.
Archaic in English; from Latin [[from:apotheca]], storehouse, the root of [[same-root:boutique]] and [[same-root:bodega]]; probably dropped because it became tied to dubious 1800s drugs.
The everyday German word for a pharmacy, which recalls the archaic English [[same-root:apothecary]].
Describes a charm meant to turn away disease, danger or evil, like the [[see:abracadabra]] amulet.
Kept some archaic British features, such as [[see:a-prefixing]], that other American varieties lost, but it does not sound like Shakespeare.
Its Latin plural is also apparatus, not apparati; some circles use that plural in English, as apparatuses sounds a bit odd.

term: apparatus for facilitating the birth of a child by centrifugal force

mentions.note: A 1965 patent for a spinning delivery table that flings the baby out of the birth canal into a safety net.

term: apparatus for simulating a high five

mentions.note: A 1994 patent for a mechanical arm on a spring-loaded pivot that slaps your palm back.
John Dennis's 1709 play, a flop, for which he created the new thunder effect behind [[see:steal someone's thunder]].
Related to [[same-root:explode]], to clap outward.
Once simply the word for any fruit, as discussed on an earlier episode, so it turns up in the origins of many fruit names.
Once meant any kind of fruit, as discussed in an earlier episode, which is why the pupil became [[see:the apple of my eye]].
One of Grose's terms for a woman's bosom.
Not technically a [[see:logo]] because it's not a word; the original was elaborate, showing Newton under a tree with words.
Medieval Latin name for the [[see:orange]], perhaps reflecting a folk etymology linking the fruit to the French town of [[see:Orange (town)]].
The French for potato, an example of fruits and vegetables once called apples, like the [[see:orange apple]].
Another background filler phrase like [[equivalent:watermelon]].
Perfect order, first recorded in a British naval officer's 1780s diary; the reason is unknown, one theory being a mishearing of French [[from?:nappe pliée]], folded cloth.
A in the quaint WWI Royal Air Force spelling alphabet, which began 'apples, butter'.
A false comparison of similar-looking things, appearing in late 19th- and early 20th-century writing after replacing [[from:apples to oysters]]; now often used for very different things.
Only compared since the late 19th or early 20th century; before that people compared [[see:apples to oysters]].
[[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for stairs, the pairing Rob first thinks of for comparing apples.
Australian rhyming slang for nice, so someone could be described as 'apples'.
The 17th-century original, recorded by John Ray as 'as like as an apple to an oyster' for things with no resemblance; it gave [[gave:apples and oranges]].
The earlier comparison, recorded from the 1670s in phrases like 'as like an apple to an oyster', before [[see:apples and oranges]].
Used where English lacks approvation; taken wholesale from Latin with its -tion ending, so the v of approval appears as a Latin b.
From Latin praecoquum, early-ripening, via Arabic al-barquq and Catalan; related to [[same-root:precocious]], because the fruit ripens early; appears in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Replaced [[see:Peach]] in the 24-crayon box in the mid-1990s.
Originally a napron, from French; the N moved to the article; related to [[same-root:napkin]] and French [[same-root:nappe]].
Originally 'a napron', which lost its N to the article through [[see:rebracketing]].
A rebracketing example discussed in an earlier episode.
Basically the same word as [[see:ept]].
A name apt for its bearer, like [[see:Usain Bolt]], a tighter term than [[see:nominative determinism]].
Something the Romans had, possibly near-pure alcohol; another water-of-life name like [[see:uisce beatha]].
A [[see:sniglet]] for turning on the bathtub tap with your toes; the hosts note it doesn't hold water etymologically, given [[see:ambidextrous]].
Colour named after the stone.
An example of a [[see:beryl]].
One of the [[see:beryl]] gemstones.
An egregious French borrowing, ironic because the planing comes from a French word for glide.
Scandinavian spirit Rob drank, another spirit named water of life like [[see:uisce beatha]].
Spirit whose name means 'water of life', like [[equivalent:whiskey]].
Water-based phenomena such as rain, snow, hail and dew, one of the four old kinds of [[see:meteor]].
In early meteorology, water-based phenomena such as rain, snow, hail, dew, frost and clouds.
In the 15th-century sense of [[see:meteor]], rain, snow and hail.
A rarer agent ending, seen in [[see:bursar]], which went back to the Latin spelling.
Better called Hindu-Arabic numerals; a positional system that, unlike [[see:Roman numerals]], makes arithmetic easy and requires [[see:zero]] as a placeholder.
Faces backwards because Arabic is read right to left, so it looks like the [[see:percontation point]].
Online said to mean fear of peanut butter sticking to the roof of the mouth, but literally just fear of peanut butter.
From the Greek word for spider; the group also includes scorpions, mites and ticks.
Spiders, scorpions and mites, which are not insects: they have eight legs and two body segments.
The study of all arachnids, not just spiders, unlike [[see:araneology]].
The Lord of the Rings character nicknamed Longshanks, the inspiration for [[see:Ranger]].
The French for spider, compared with English [[same-root:arain]].
An old word for a spider, similar to the French [[same-root:araignée]] and from the same Latin root.
An early English word for a spider, an anglicisation of the Latin word for spider.
The study of spiders specifically, related to the early English word [[same-root:arain]].
A mythical city far to the east whose lord, in the [[see:Enmerkar]] story, was baffled by a cuneiform tablet and forced to submit.
Means old horn face, a one-horned ancestor of [[see:Triceratops]].
Arch- comes from Latin; the Anglo-Saxons earlier said [[see:hēahbiscop]], and a northern variant was [[see:ass bishop]]. It is the top rank, above [[see:bishop]], [[see:priest]] and [[see:deacon]].
Suggested as the term for a [[see:ferroequinologist]] who specifically loves old trains.
A literary term that Jung applied to family figures like the mother and father.
Means rule or leadership, implying rule more than the might of [[see:-ocracy]].
From Greek [[from:arktos]], bear, because [[see:Ursa Major]] is always visible in the northern polar sky.
Means with bears, after a constellation, contrasting with [[see:Antarctic]]; neatly, polar bears live only in the north; discussed before on the show.
The Greek word for bear; Rob half-remembers that these words may relate to honey, which would make them euphemisms like [[see:bear]].
A pejorative, intensifying ending meaning too much, as in [[see:drunkard]], [[see:braggart]], [[see:dullard]], [[see:bastard]], [[see:wizard]] and [[see:mustard]].
An originally intensifying, now pejorative ending for someone who does something too much, as in [[see:braggart]] and [[see:drunkard]].
An intensifying suffix found in [[see:milliard]], [[see:drunkard]], [[see:dotard]], [[see:wizard]] and [[see:bastard]].
Jess's favourite ending, used to make insults and pejoratives, as in [[see:dullard]], [[see:braggart]] and [[see:bastard]].
An intensifying ending, cited for [[see:mustard]]; the hosts joke that it comes up so often it needs its own bell.
Jess's favourite suffix, a pejorative one, which influenced the final D of [[see:hazard]].
Jess's favourite ending, an intensifier that is often but not always insulting, as in [[see:drunkard]], [[see:braggart]], [[see:dullard]] and [[see:wizard]].
Shares a Latin root meaning to burn with [[same-root:arson]].
Colloquial Levantine Arabic remodelling of [[from:artichoke]] used in Syria and Lebanon.
Levantine Arabic borrowing of English [[from:artichoke]], reshaped by folk etymology.
Shares a Latin root meaning to burn with [[same-root:arson]].
Borrowed from the Vikings' Old Norse and related to the Swedish är in [[same-root:jag är hungrig]].
From the Scandinavian languages, replacing Old English [[see:bist]] and [[see:beoth]].
A [[see:rhetorical question]] from the film Gladiator.
Originally a sandy place, of uncertain and possibly Etruscan origin, because Roman amphitheatres were strewn with sand to soak up blood.
Greek war god corresponding to [[see:Mars]].
Sang 'give me my [[see:propers]]', and varied songs each time, making lip-syncing hard in [[see:The Blues Brothers]].
An English word that also comes from Latin [[from:argentum]], like [[same-root:Argentina]].
Named by Spanish colonists who found silver there, after Latin [[from:argentum]] rather than Spanish [[see:plata]].
Place name used for A in the earliest wave of spelling alphabets, before the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]].
From the Latin, not Spanish, word for silver, [[from:argentum]], by way of the [[from:Río de la Plata]], the river of silver.

Shares the root meaning shining or bright with [[same-root:Arges]].
The ship, whose name means quick, unrelated to [[unrelated:argon]].

The mythological sailors of Jason who sailed on the Argo, given as another -naut word.
A coded variety of a language with standard grammar but keywords swapped in a patterned way; narrower than [[see:cant]].
Another term for criminal slang, a French word of unknown origin, sometimes pronounced 'argo'.
Named after the clan in [[from:Argyll]], Scotland.
Daughter of [[see:Minos]] who gave Theseus the ball of twine, a [[see:clue]], then was dumped on an island.
Lost poem by [[see:Aristeas]], surviving in excerpts, about travels in the far north and the [[see:Arimaspi]] battling [[see:griffin]]s.
One-eyed tribe in [[see:Arimaspea]] known for battling gold-guarding [[see:griffin]]s.
Semi-legendary Greek poet and miracle worker whose lost poem [[see:Arimaspea]] contains the first known narrative appearance of a [[see:griffin]].
Rule by the best, which [[see:Plato]] thought the best system, degenerating into [[see:timocracy]].
Scholar at the Library of Alexandria credited with marking texts with three dots for pauses, named periodos, [[see:comma]] and [[see:colon]].
Interpreted [[see:timocracy]] as rule by people with property.

A satisfying state demonym, for someone from Arkansas, that still makes sense to outsiders.
Baroque name for similarly sized instruments, named for where the instrument is held, in contrast with the [[see:viola da gamba]].
Latin for weapons, related to [[same-root:art]] because using weapons takes skill.
A historic Spanish borrowing for a fleet of ships, famously the Spanish Armada, meaning an armed force; etymologically the Spanish equivalent of [[same-root:army]].

Means harp-like and ultimately comes from the Germanic word [[from:harp]].

Rhyming slang for a lodger.

Appointed Chief Secretary for Ireland in 1887 by his uncle, [[see:Robert Gascoigne-Cecil]].
A British man who found hundreds of [[see:Linear B]] inscriptions at [[see:Knossos]] in Crete in 1900, believing they recorded the [[see:Minoans]]' language.
Captain and first governor who named [[see:Sydney]] in 1788 and nearly called it [[see:Albion]].
A music hall comedian who invented or revived the card game that gave us [[gave:spoof]] in the 1880s.

From Italian [[from:articiocco]] and French [[from:artichaut]], perhaps conflated with chaud; sometimes hearty choke, choke perhaps from its choking heart or invasiveness.
Passed from Arabic to Spanish, Italian and English, then was phono-semantically matched back into Levantine Arabic as [[gave:ardi shawki]].
From Arabic via Italian and Spanish, once spelled many ways; a [[see:boomerang word]] borrowed back into Levantine Arabic as [[gave:ardi shawki]].

Its art- comes from [[from:art]], the idea of creating something; originally not negative, compare Latin [[from:artificium]].
The German term for AI, built on [[from:künstlich]], which Rob finds cool because it links back to the word for art.

term: as mad as a wet hen

mentions.note: The last 'mad as' simile Rob gives; hens are 'vicious little dinosaurs'.

Recalled because of [[see:quand les poules auront des dents]]; used in America as well as Britain.

Old English letter written as a and e back to back, used in the old spelling of [[see:grey]].

The native word that French-derived [[see:demand]] sits beside.

An example of a Germanic word with the [[see:a- (prefix)]] prefix.
Once reshaped into [[see:sparrowgrass]] by speakers puzzled by the Latin, before a concerted effort restored the original spelling.
Already discussed in an earlier episode, along with its folk name sparrow grass.
A very old word for several trees, perhaps implying movement from its quaking leaves; Old English called it [[see:quickbeam]].

The US word for the road surface material that Britons call [[see:tarmac]].
The word behind [[gave:daffodil]], now naming a less glamorous plant associated with the [[see:Asphodel Meadows]].
Underworld realm in the Odyssey for ordinary souls, between [[see:Elysium]] and [[see:Tartarus]]; its name might mean fragrant or flowery.
Sounds like it relates to breathing and looks like an opposite of [[unrelated:exasperate]], but isn't one.
A proprietary name formerly owned by [[see:Bayer]], no longer written with a capital, and the subject of a [[see:Xerox]] slogan about getting a headache.

The difference between it and [[from:arse]] comes from early R-dropping before S sounds.
A variant of [[same-root:arse]] that lost its R, like [[see:cuss]].
A northern dialect form of [[see:archbishop]] in Old English. It is just a variation on arch-, but the hosts find it funny.
Given as a good, common, more obvious [[see:compound insult]].
The modern phrase Rob compares with [[equivalent:tit over thumb]].
Older than [[see:assassination]], which is first found in Shakespeare.
Western name for the [[from:Hashishin]] of the [[see:Nizari Ismaili state]]; spread by Crusader tales and [[see:Marco Polo]], its form was shaped by [[see:hashish]].

[[see:Aristophanes]]'s comedy of 391 BC, which features the absurdly long name of a fictional dish.
Anyone or anything that provides information to a secret service; like [[see:agent]], an originally neutral term that spy fiction has tied to spycraft.

Means star-shaped, though asteroids ultimately aren't; formed with [[from:-oid]].
British name for a [[equivalent:Chiron]], after the supplier Aston Broadcast Systems.
Via French, literally to be thundered at; the -ton- is the Latin word for thunder.
In English from the 14th century, divided into [[see:natural astrology]] and [[see:judicial astrology]]; long confused with [[see:astronomy]], the two swapping places many times.

Confused or disorganised, from the older dice phrase [[from:set on six and seven]]; Francis Grose (1785) applied it to scattered furniture and unsettled business.

With [[see:aponia]], one of the highest goals of [[see:Epicureanism]].

River in The Lord of the Rings, surely an Anglo-Saxon reference to springs like [[see:bourne]].
The name for people from Birmingham.
A British accent that gets little love; listeners unfamiliar with British accents rate it against [[see:received pronunciation]] arbitrarily.
A well-known food portmanteau of breakfast and lunch.
Means battle-ready in armour, or armour battle.
A Germanic name whose element hild relates to battle, the name meaning literally armed for battle.
Place name used for B in the earliest, place-name-based spelling alphabets.
Trojan who, according to [[see:Geoffrey of Monmouth]], founded New Troy in London and gave his name to [[see:Britain]]; the hosts dismiss the story.
The French word for heather, a survival from [[from:Gaulish]].
The Korean band say in English that it stands for 'beyond the scene', but the initialism comes from Korean for bulletproof boy scouts.
Nickname for tiny post-war European microcars such as the [[see:BMW Isetta]] and the [[see:Messerschmitt]] KR200.
One of the genericized trademarks Jess found most surprising.
Literally one who roasts meat on a [[from:boucan]]; the word is specific to the Caribbean.
Contains the same goat word as [[same-root:butcher]].
Related to Finnish [[same-root:pukki]], goat; discussed in other episodes.
Related to [[same-root:butcher]]; not a goat in English today, but compare Afrikaans [[same-root:bok]].
Rival of [[see:butt naked]]; Jess believes it is a racist Americanism about Native Americans, perhaps referencing buckskin.
The comic where [[see:zap]] was first used as an illustrated onomatopoeia.
From Spanish [[from:vaquero]], cowboy, where v and b sound alike; related to French [[same-root:vache]] and cow words like [[same-root:vaccination]].
Unrecorded before 2006 despite older [[see:kick the bucket]]; even the OED traces it to the film The Bucket List, though people insist otherwise, a [[see:Mandela effect]].
A term for the [[see:monosyllable]], after [[see:Matthew Buckinger]], born without hands or legs, who married a tall, handsome woman.
A shield, the second part of [[gave:swashbuckler]].
A small shield, the second element of [[gave:swashbuckler]].
American slang for money; Rob feels clever using it with his international friends.
English name for sparkling wine and orange juice, the [[equivalent:mimosa]]; the hosts don't know who the buck is.
Rob's name for the sparkling wine and orange juice drink that menus call a [[equivalent:mimosa]].
Vanilla Ice's pet [[see:wallaroo]].
Means pleasantly pastoral, literally cow-tending, from the Greek elements [[from:bous]] and kolos.
A city named after several cities, Buda, Óbuda and Pest, joined as a compound rather than a [[see:portmanteau]]; saying 'Budapesht' in English can sound pretentious.
From an unidentified Australian Aboriginal language, combining words for good and cockatoo, so basically good parrot; Americans call them [[see:parakeet]]s.
An Australian term, which leads to the origin of [[see:budgerigar]].
Not named for its air but after Santa Maria del Buen Aire, the sailors' Madonna of [[from:Bonaria]], who brought fair winds.
True buffalo live outside America and look more like cows; the word can also be a place name and a verb meaning to bully.

term: Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo

mentions.note: A grammatical sentence built from the animal, the city and the verb meaning to bully: bison from Buffalo whom other Buffalo bison bully also bully Buffalo bison.
From Italian via French [[from:bouffon]], perhaps onomatopoeic, its first syllable evoking puffing out your cheeks to get a laugh.
The TV show with the first pop-culture use of [[see:Google]] as a verb.
An example of [[see:-verse]] meaning world or realm.
A fictional universe named with [[from:-verse]].
Scientifically a member of [[see:Hemiptera]], defined in the 18th century; earlier, Middle English bugge meant a scary bogeyman-like spirit, the sense in a bug in the system.
Contains the old scary-thing sense of [[same-root:bug]].
Contains the old scary sense of [[from:bug]]; originally a permanent imaginary terror, now softened to a pet peeve.
Originally an evil spirit that stole and ate children from their beds; also a word for a scarecrow.
Rated mild on Ofcom's list, though Rob would never have said it in front of his nan.
A 1600s word for the vulva, also bugle-boo, quoted from a poem on [[see:Hero and Leander]].
Means fire meat.
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
Like [[see:eggplant]], an American name made by combining existing English words.
Another word with the diminutive [[see:-ock]].
An example of the diminutive suffix [[see:-ock]].
US hobo slang for police; railroad bulls guarded trains against robbers and people riding illegally.
One of the string of insults in a [[see:William Shakespeare]] history-play rant quoted by Jess.
Used casually in 1970s America, then replaced by [[see:homeless]], an example of the [[see:euphemism treadmill]].
Another of Grose's terms for a schoolmaster, accusing them of indecency.
Paired with [[see:bunch]] to show how [[see:lunch]] relates to lump.
American football term that sounds naughty if you're only half listening, noted down by Jess while watching NFL games.
One of Grose's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]], among many rabbit jokes.
Bunch is to [[see:bump]] as [[see:lunch]] is to lump.
To give someone a bunch of fives is to punch them, with a hand of five digits.
North Carolina county addressed in an 1820 congressional speech; its misspelled name gave [[gave:bunkum]].
Glossed as a German state when introducing the meat-labelling law [[see:Rindfleischetikettierungsüberwachungsaufgabenübertragungsgesetz]].
An obsolete American English word for nonsense, short for [[from:bunkum]]; an orphaned negative that [[gave:debunk]].
Means nonsense; a misspelling of [[from:Buncombe County]], to which a North Carolina politician addressed a long, boring speech in Congress in 1820.
Named after [[from:Robert Bunsen]].
Colourful sandstone, one of the three German rock layers behind the name [[see:Triassic]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.
Not one of the original Greek forms; rule by desks, from French [[from:bureau]], a desk or wardrobe, meaning rule from an office.
A rebracketing of [[from:hamburger]], so even a [[see:beef burger]] or [[see:cheeseburger]] is named after Hamburg.
A purely American and fairly recent verb; British English uses [[see:burgle]].
A rare Old English–Latin hybrid: the Normans added a Latinate ending to [[from:burh]] from [[from:burhbrecere]]; it means breaking in rather than stealing.
The British verb, which sounds odd to American ears, unlike [[see:burglarize]].
Named after the wine from the [[from:Burgundy]] region.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified, walled settlement, found at the end of place names like [[see:Edinburgh]], [[see:Peterborough]] and [[see:Canterbury]], and in [[gave:burglary]].
The Anglo-Saxon word for a fortified town, appearing in place names as burgh, bury and borough: [[see:Peterborough]], [[see:Edinburgh]], [[see:Bury]].
The pre-Norman word for a burglar; the Normans Latinised its first part, giving [[gave:burglary]].
Italian for joke or mockery, also a comic interlude or practical joke inserted into a performance, often in [[see:commedia dell'arte]]; root of [[gave:burlesque]].

Via 16th-century French from Italian [[from:burlesco]], ludicrous, from [[from:burla]]; first an English adjective meaning droll, later a variety show, with striptease added in late-19th-century America.
To polish something until it shines; it originally meant the same thing as [[same-root:brown]].
The trilled Scottish R, probably like the historical English R from which today's weaker British and American Rs developed.
A college treasurer; an Anglo-Latin word first spelled with -er that reverted to the Latin spelling of [[from:bursa]], a bag or purse.
Shares the -ar agent-noun-looking ending with [[see:caterpillar]].
The form with the R that gave [[gave:bust]] when R began dropping before S in the 1600s.
The R-ful form of [[same-root:bust]].
A place named simply from [[from:burh]], a former Anglo-Saxon fortified town.
English place-name ending equivalent to German [[same-root:-berg]].
From a diplomatic custom among North American Indigenous nations, especially the [[see:Iroquois Confederacy]], of burying war axes to make peace, though the record is largely oral.
An expression using the newsroom sense of [[see:lede]].
Short for [[from:omnibus]].
One of Grose's terms relating to breasts.
A joke [[see:oxymoron]] poking fun at the idea.
Implies [[see:busyness]]; ferret owners call even two ferrets a business; also called a [[see:fesnyng of ferrets]] from the book's spelling.
A collective noun in the [[see:Book of St Albans]] whose garbled spelling produced [[gave:fesynes]].
The collective noun for ferrets, a favourite of the hosts.
A Gen Z slang term said to come from Black music and culture.
An R-dropped form of [[from:burst]], found in 1600s writing, when R began disappearing before S sounds.
A variant of [[same-root:burst]] that lost its R, like [[see:cuss]].
Jess jokes that, like the [[see:ruff]], it is named for what it does: it busts out your behind.
The state of being busy, distinguished in Middle English from business as an occupation; played on in [[see:business of ferrets]].
From French, originally someone who dealt only in goat meat, from [[from:buck]], a male goat; related to [[same-root:springbok]]. It replaced Old English [[see:fleshmonger]].
From French [[from:bouc]], goat: the first butchers sold only goat meat; the same word appears in [[same-root:buck]] and [[same-root:springbok]].
Related to Finnish [[same-root:pukki]], goat; discussed in other episodes.
Discussed before as basically meaning goat preparer, showing how important goats were.
Came in after the Norman Conquest, replacing [[see:fleshmonger]]; named for dealing in goat meat, its butch- related to [[same-root:buck]].
A cask of fresh drinking water aboard a ship, which gave [[gave:scuttlebutt]].
Nobody, including Mark Liberman, knows whether this or [[see:buck naked]] is correct; both work.
B in the WWI Royal Air Force spelling alphabet, after [[see:Apples]].
A yellow and white wildflower, also called [[equivalent:yellow toadflax]], that looks like butter and eggs.
Another name for the [[see:avocado]], from its buttery inside.
A past name for the [[see:butterfly]].
Old Dutch name for the butterfly, either because they supposedly ate butter off windowsills or because their yellow excrement looks like butter.
Commonly traced to Hindus throwing ghee at statues of gods; the hosts prefer the idea of lavishing someone with valuable butter.
Another old Dutch name for the butterfly.
An old name for the butterfly, tied to the myth of witches turning into butterflies to steal butter.
One of the old Dutch names for the butterfly, alongside [[see:butter witch]] and [[see:butter shite]].
A third made-up dish in the US Army survey, alongside [[see:funistrada]].
Not a spoonerism of [[unrelated:flutterby]]; an Old English word with Germanic cognates like Dutch [[same-root:botervlieg]].
Present in Old English and not a reversal of [[unrelated:flutterby]]; possibly named for buttery wing colours or myths of butterflies or witches stealing butter.
Not a spoonerism of [[unrelated:flutterby]]; from myths that butterflies eat butter, or their yellow colour; compare Dutch [[see:boterschijte]].
An announcer forgot their ever-changing name and used their song title Butthole Surfer; some TV and radio stations refused to say it.
The little bits that make up your butt, formed with the diminutive [[see:-ock]].
An example of the diminutive suffix [[see:-ock]].
A bird you don't want to see every day, given as another negative word with the [[see:-ard]] ending.
One of the crimes [[see:James Hardy Vaux]] lists in his autobiography.
Place names ending in -by are Old Norse in origin, found along a strip down the east of England.
Old Norse settlement suffix found in Danelaw places such as [[gave:Derby]] and [[gave:Grimsby]].
The form used by people born before 1970; [[see:on accident]] took over among younger, probably mainly American, speakers.
The older form that [[see:on accident]] is shifting away from, mentioned from the grammar episode.

term: by the skin of your teeth

mentions.note: From the Book of Job's [[from:with the skin of my teeth]], meaning gums as one's last flesh; popularised by [[see:The Skin of Our Teeth]].
From the Book of Job in the King James Bible, originally 'with the skin of my teeth'.
A Phoenician port in modern Lebanon that exported Egyptian papyrus, probably the ultimate source of [[gave:Bible]], so the Bible is named after a shipping hub.
Bye wasn't a word before [[from:goodbye]]; bye-bye just references it.
Originally eight [[see:bit]]s.
Greek settlement on the Bosphorus founded around 600 BC, supposedly named after legendary founder [[from?:Byzas]], or from a Thracian name; later renamed [[see:Constantinople]].
Legendary founder of [[see:Byzantium]], said to be the son of [[see:Poseidon]] and a nymph, after whom the city was supposedly named.
Originally a picture of a stick; it triumphed over [[see:K]] in Latin, and the hosts suggest keeping C for the ch sound only.
Technically the smallest British road class, which people rarely talk about.
Charles Talbut Onions, OED editor from 1922, wrongly said to be behind [[see:know your onions]], which is recorded before he went to university.
Both question and answer, so a whole conversation can be held with it; a shortening of the formal [[from:comment allez-vous]].
Not an acronym of five plotters against Charles II (Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley, Lauderdale); probably from Hebrew [[from:kabbalah]], received law.
What you might expect the Spanish knight to be called, instead of [[see:caballo]].
The Spanish name for the chess knight, which means horse rather than [[see:caballero]], since the piece only shows a horse.
Satirical Swiss club, also a publication, where [[see:Dadaism]] was founded.
One of the many American slang words for money.
A common British term for drunk from the linguists' list.
One of the British words for [[see:drunk]].
American word for the staffed car at the back of a train; originally a Dutch word for a ship's galley, later slang for the backside.
Not inherently 'the end': first a ship's galley, then a train's galley or staff car, often but not always at the back.
Spanish insult meaning big goat, related to [[same-root:chupacabras]].
Related to the root of [[same-root:cacophobia]].
Grose's term for eggs; [[see:Polari]] speakers later also called eggs cackle farts.
An inappropriate name, sharing its first element with [[same-root:cacophony]], a bad sound; contrasted with [[see:euonym]].
Fear of ugliness, from Greek [[from:kakos]], bad; related to [[same-root:cacophony]] and [[same-root:caca]], from a PIE root meaning defecate.
A bad sound, used to explain the first element of [[same-root:caconym]].
Bad sound, from the same Greek kakos as [[same-root:cacophobia]].
Amazon's original name, short for [[from:abracadabra]], dropped because people misheard it as [[see:cadaver]].
What people misheard [[see:Cadabra]] as, prompting the name change.
From French [[from:cadet]], a junior person, which was pronounced much like caddie.
An animal abandoned by its mother and reared by hand; Johnson's dictionary defines [[see:pet]] as a cade lamb, and the two were used almost interchangeably.
Named after [[from:Antoine Laumet de La Mothe Cadillac]], a figure in New France and the founder of [[see:Detroit]].
Named after [[from:Cadmus]], via Cadmea, the Theban citadel where he supposedly ruled.
Legendary founder of Thebes, supposedly responsible for bringing the Phoenician alphabet to the Greeks; gave [[gave:cadmium]].
Means fort, seen in [[see:Cardiff]] and the English city [[see:Carlisle]].
A hereditary [[see:cognomen]]; its meaning is uncertain (thick hair, grey eyes, cutting); Romans pronounced the C as K, as in [[gave:Kaiser]].
Shifts each letter a fixed number of places; [[see:Julius Caesar]] used it with allies during his campaigns in Gaul, often with a left shift of three.
Fits the probably inaccurate theory that [[see:Caesar]] is related to cutting.
Named after sky blue, one of several elements named after colours.
Example of a straightforward borrowing, in contrast to a [[see:calque]].
A Chinese [[see:eunuch]] serving the emperor who invented [[see:paper]] by pulping mulberry bark, hemp, rags and fishnets with water and drying the film.
Brazilian cocktail whose name means a young peasant lady, perhaps for its cheapness.
Typeface named after Egypt's capital because it was designed for Arabic script.
Named by the Fatimid dynasty; medieval writers wrongly linked it to [[see:Mars]]; the English form drops the article, maybe via Egyptian Arabic.
From Arabic [[from:al-Qahira]], the victorious, given by the conquering Fatimid caliph; medieval writers linked it to an Arabic name for Mars rising at the conquest.
From Latin [[from:calamarius]], pertaining to pens, ultimately from [[from:calamus]], reed; unrelated to [[unrelated:calligraphy]].
From [[from:calamus]], reed or pen, because squid squirt ink and are pen-shaped; unrelated to the calli- of [[unrelated:calligraphy]].
French for kettle [[equivalent:limescale]].
Related to [[same-root:calculus]], like calculate, both about counting with little pebbles.
Latin for a pebble, also a kidney or bladder stone; diminutive of [[from:calx]], chalk or limestone; named after pebbles used for counting.
From Latin calendarium, an account book or debt register, because interest was due on the [[from:kalends]].
Another verb use Rob resists, a corporate-sounding example of [[see:verbing]].
A short-lived English word meaning warm or hot, taken more directly from Latin [[from:calere]], source of [[same-root:nonchalant]].
Title of Sunni Muslim leaders meaning successor; disagreement over who succeeded Muhammad as first caliph split [[see:Sunni]] and [[see:Shia]] Islam.
A Germanic word that shares a Proto-Indo-European root with Latin [[same-root:calare]], behind [[see:kalends]].
Paired with [[see:collar]] as an example of the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Means beautiful writing and is unrelated to [[unrelated:calamari]], despite Rob's first guess.
Its calli- means nice, and despite appearances it is unrelated to [[unrelated:calamari]].
In American football, a change made at the line after reading the defence; figuratively, a change of plan in response to new information.
Having beautiful buttocks, named after the [[from:Callipygian Venus]] statue of Aphrodite.
One of Jess's favourite words, discussed in an earlier episode.
A statue of Aphrodite whose lost head was supposedly reattached so she looks back over her shoulder at her shapely buttocks; it gave [[gave:callipygian]].
Translating a word's elements rather than borrowing it; French for copy, from calquer, to trace by rubbing, itself from Italian, possibly related to [[same-root?:chalk]].
Another plural showing the f-to-v change seen in [[see:wolf]].
Latin for chalk or limestone, which gave [[gave:calculus]] and is related to German [[same-root:Kalk]].
Apparently means trouser leg, perhaps because a folded calzone resembles folded trousers, though this is debated.
Means a trouser leg or stocking, because it is stuffed like a foot in a sock, the same idea as French [[equivalent:chausson]].
The river through Cambridge, formerly called the [[see:Granta]]; it was renamed to match the town's Norman-altered name.
The river's current name, which it shares with [[see:Cambridge]].
Spelled like the French word but often treated as if it began with Latin com-; it's closer to [[same-root:camera]], meaning people sharing a chamber.
Means chambered lizard, after the large holes in its skull; its skulls were wrongly put on early [[see:Brontosaurus]] mounts.
Another rendering of the same word as [[same-root:Cymru]].
Its name may have shifted because the Normans struggled to pronounce the earlier form, after which the river was renamed the [[see:Cam]].
Originally [[from:Grantabridge]]; reportedly the Normans couldn't say Granta, so the city and the river became [[see:Cam]].
Rhyming slang for a [[see:brown]], a penny.
An old name for the giraffe, literally camel leopard; it is also a southern hemisphere constellation that could have featured in their space episode.
Related to [[same-root:camaraderie]] through the idea of a chamber.
A little pinhole camera, the other possible starting point for animation.
From a Portuguese word for shrimp, meaning river of shrimp; an example of African country names telling a European story.
Driver and maker of [[see:La Jamais Contente]], nicknamed [[see:Le Diable Rouge]] for his red beard and record runs.
Originally in the sense of a battle, from Latin on the continent before English existed; related to German [[same-root:Kampf]], [[same-root:campaign]] and [[same-root:champion]].
Suggested by Jess as a potential third doublet of [[same-root?:champion]] and [[same-root?:champignon]].
Related to [[same-root:camp]] but adopted later from French, one of many doublets from borrowing the same word repeatedly.
Means little bells.
Its plural campuses, like [[see:virus]]es, is a Latin -us word with an English ending, which supports octopuses as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
Another -us word whose Latin plural English never bothered to adopt.
From St. Lawrence Iroquoian [[from:kanata]], village, recorded by [[see:Jacques Cartier]] in 1535–1536. The word for one village came to name the whole country.
From St Lawrence Iroquoian [[from:kanata]], village; [[see:Jacques Cartier]] used it for one area, and a false story derives it from Spanish or Portuguese 'nothing here'.
Named after the [[from:Canary Islands]], which are named after dogs, so it is indirectly a dog bird.
Literally the dog islands, sharing a root with the canis of [[same-root:Canis Major]].
From Latin for island of dogs; the islands gave their name to the [[gave:canary]].
Australia's chosen capital, probably from an Aboriginal name meaning meeting place; rejected names included [[see:Kangaremu]], [[see:Meladneyperbane]] and [[see:Sydmelperadbrisho]].
Both the crab constellation and the disease, named because swollen vessels around cancerous cells resembled crab legs; from Greek [[from:karkinos]]; German uses one word for both.
Discussed with [[see:karkinos]] in a previous episode.
From a term for a white cloth, because Roman candidates for office often wore bright white; compared with [[see:diaper]].
From Sanskrit via Persian qand, cane sugar, and Arabic qandi; it came from [[from:sugar candy]] after 'sugar' was dropped, and Americans favour it over [[see:sweets]].
Confirmed on the spot as related to [[same-root:cannon]].
Another name for the [[equivalent:dog days of summer]]; canicular means doggy, related to Latin canis.
Shares a root with the canis of [[same-root:Canis Major]].
Related to [[same-root:hound]].
Related to [[same-root:hound]] through the same C/H shift that links [[see:head]] and [[see:capital]].
Latin for dog; its K sound corresponds to the H of Germanic [[same-root:hound]] under [[see:Grimm's law]].
One of [[see:Orion]]'s two hunting dogs; canis shares its root with the [[same-root:Canary Islands]] and [[same-root:canine]].
The constellation containing [[see:Sirius]].
The other of [[see:Orion]]'s two hunting dogs, alongside [[see:Canis Major]].
An old name for the [[see:dandelion]], meaning something like crab grass, linked to [[see:cancer]].
Another name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]].
Related to [[same-root:canvas]], a cloth made of hemp.
Related to [[same-root:canvas]], practically a doublet.
A common British term for drunk from the linguists' list.
The annual creativity festival in France with the best [[see:swag]], where Jess got a free tattoo at the Pinterest booth.
Prison slang for drunk, now died out, missing from the hosts' earlier list of British words for drunk.
From Latin [[from:canna]], reed or tube, and related to [[same-root:cane]].
The same word as [[same-root:cañón]], both meaning tube.
Slang language, from the same song root as [[same-root:accent]], probably from the sing-song way such languages were spoken.
From the same source as [[same-root:chant]], Latin [[from:cantus]]; possibly tied to beggars repeatedly chanting appeals for alms.
In-group jargon of a particular group; perhaps from Latin [[from?:cantus]], song, via mockery of friars' chanting, and perhaps influenced by Gaelic words for speech.
Criminal slang deliberately designed to be obscure to outsiders, from the Latin for sing, like chanting.
Slang language, previously discussed, also from the Latin for singing, like [[same-root:incantation]].
From the 16th century: apprentices held candles over a master's work, so it means not even good enough to be the helper.
Someone from Cambridge, from [[from:Cantabrigia]], the Roman name for the city.
A place name ending in [[from:burh]].
Organisation set up to colonise part of New Zealand, many of whose members went to Christ Church, Oxford, hence [[see:Christchurch]].
Entered English from French in the 14th century, literally meaning made of hemp, so related to [[same-root:cannabis]]; became popular with painters because Venice had plenty.
From Old French, literally 'made of hemp', so related to and practically a doublet of [[same-root:cannabis]].
Canvassing opinion is the same word as [[same-root:canvas]], evoking gathering opinions in a cloth bag; spelled with two S's to tell them apart.
The same word as [[same-root:cannon]], meaning tube; the English Y spells out the sound of Spanish cañón's [[see:eñe]].
One of many head-related words from the same source as [[same-root:capitulum]].
Ultimately goes back to the same root as [[same-root:head]].
The half cloak that [[see:Saint Martin]] kept, treated as a sacred relic by Frankish kings; the place it was kept was the original [[gave:chapel]].
From a Latin word meaning to leap or skip; first adventurous pranks, then entertaining crimes like jewel thefts thanks to crime fiction and films.
Related to [[same-root:head]] despite having no consonant in common with it, because of the H/K sound shift.
One of the obvious English derivatives of Latin [[from:caput]], head.
Writing the first-person singular pronoun as a capital is an example of an arbitrary written-English rule based on conditions long ago.
So called because it stands at the head of a word or sentence.
To bow your head, sharing its origin with [[same-root:capitulum]].
Means header; a red C-like mark added later by another scribe, whose omitted gap gave paragraph indentation; same origin as [[same-root:chapter]] and [[same-root:capitulate]].
Also contains the goat word found in [[same-root:chupacabras]].
One of many head-related words from the same source as [[same-root:capitulum]].
One of the Latin-derived words related to [[same-root:head]], from Latin [[from:caput]].
A rank that just means head, one of the many English derivatives of Latin [[from:caput]].
A mischievous Christmas man of the Tudor and Stuart eras who presided over feasting and entertainment.
Australian rhyming slang for a look, only coinable in the Antipodes.
A shabby, ill-dressed fellow.
Latin for head, a recurring topic for the hosts because of its many English derivatives, including [[gave:captain]], [[gave:chapter]], [[gave:capital]] and [[gave:decapitate]].
Not short for [[see:carriage]] but older in English; from Latin for a chariot, perhaps via Irish, and long used for any wheeled vehicle.
Pronounced with and without R as an example of [[see:rhoticity]].
A joke drunk word from [[see:Michael McIntyre]], who suggested you could be thoroughly car-parked.
In French, to have caractère is to have a terrible temper, from the idea of distinctive behaviour.
Given as a possible relative of [[same-root?:mousse]].
People argue over its pronunciation: three syllables in the US South and New England, two in the Midwest and West, a regional case of [[see:syllable reduction]].
His first name was Michelangelo, a name already taken; known for dramatic lighting, [[see:tenebrism]].
From the Latin for coal or charcoal; many European words for coal resemble it.
Also from Greek [[from:karkinos]], like [[same-root:cancer]].
Also from Greek [[from:karkinos]], like [[same-root:cancer]].
With card sharp, an example of the original human sense of [[see:shark]].
Lost play Shakespeare wrote together with [[see:John Fletcher]], which brings his total to about 41.
The Welsh capital: [[from:caer]], fort, plus a Welsh form of [[see:Taff]], meaning fort on the River Taff.
Means heart-shaped; Rob uses it to lead into [[see:pyriform]] and [[see:go pear-shaped]].
Named after the [[from:7th Earl of Cardigan]], whose men in the Crimean War seem to have pioneered this warm garment.
From Latin [[from:cardinalis]], from a word for a hinge, because cardinals were pivotal to the church; the bird and the colour are named after cardinals' red robes.
Numbers like one, two, three, four, named with [[see:cardinal]] in its sense of pivotal or important.
Related to [[same-root:heart]] through the regular C/H consonant shift.
Related to [[same-root:heart]].
