Another German Christmas emblem, literally the Christ child, also called [[see:Christkindl]].
Form of [[see:Christkind]] where Kindl means a really little kid; it gave us [[gave:Kris Kringle]].
From Old English Cristes mæsse, Christ's mass or celebration; since the 1500s it has also been used as a verb, to Christmas.
Decorating trees goes back to Roman Saturnalia; people bought them in the 1500s, and German and French law limited people to one tree of no more than eight shoe lengths.
A saint's name from Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; saints' names tend to be Greekified, then obscured by Latin.
Rob says his name means a column, in passing while separating the two kinds of [[see:colon]].
Reached the Caribbean in 1492, before Vespucci's voyages. His surname means dove, from Latin [[from:columba]], and he [[gave:Colombia]] and [[gave:Columbia]] their names.
An Oxbridge-educated candidate in the authorship question; Jess wonders whether he wrote Macbeth's witch scenes.
Modern Greek for Christmas, Christ plus a root meaning birth or generation, the source of [[same-root:gender]], [[same-root:genre]] and [[same-root:generation]].
A Chinese-named dinosaur meaning legendary dragon, ending in [[from:long (Chinese)]].
The base of [[see:chuckle]].
Jess's only word for a ball-throwing stick, which she thinks is a brand name; the hosts imagine it becoming generic.
An imitative word, [[from:chuck]], to breathe suddenly and sharply, plus the frequentative [[see:-le]]; blended into [[gave:chortle]].
Example of the frequentative -le: to [[see:chuck]] often, cited when discussing [[see:truckle]].
Short-lived Gen Z term, supposedly coined by a student in 2013, for slightly off-trend people, especially millennials; a shortening of nothing.
No longer heated, from Old Norse [[from:kumba]], a block of wood, so a chump is literally a blockhead.
To vomit, now in British English; thought to come from [[from?:Chunder Loo of Akim Foo]], rhyming slang for spew.
Cartoon character from an advert, thought to be rhyming slang for spew and the source of [[gave?:chunder]].
Used on Bone Apple Tea in place of [[see:capybara]] under a capybara picture.
Coined in Puerto Rico in 1995, reportedly by [[see:Silverio Pérez]]; Spanish chupacabras is singular, wrongly clipped in English; victims were probably mauled by mangy coyotes.
Probably coined in 1995 by Puerto Rican comedian and DJ [[see:Silverio Pérez]] as [[from:chupacabras]], 'goats sucker'; English misread the final S as a plural.
Referred to the building first; from Greek kyriakon doma, the Lord's house, so going to God's house is quite literal.
Set up by [[see:Henry VIII]] so that he could divorce [[see:Catherine of Aragon]]; it is the 'establishment' in [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]] and remains the official church.
Anglican church set up by [[see:Henry VIII]] to get a divorce the pope refused. Rob finds it very tame, largely about lemon drizzle cake.
Once meant a non-gentry person before turning negative, like [[see:vulgar]].
A [[from:Yiddish]] word that spread from New York slang.
Literally means slave, from [[from:schiavo]] and medieval Latin sclavus, as in your obedient servant; now a near-universal hello or goodbye across Europe.
Rob has discussed before how it is a handy multi-purpose word.
Related to [[same-root:cricket (insect)]], with a similar imitative sound; Jess confused cicadas with locusts as a child.
Roman who said only the rhythm of a text should guide reading aloud, which is why the Romans dropped the Greek pause marks.
An ending for killing found in about 50 English words, from [[gave:homicide]] and [[gave:regicide]] to [[gave:pulicide]] and [[gave:verbicide]].
The modern French word for [[equivalent:cicada]], from [[from:Provençal]].
Noble title beneath the [[see:tlatoani]], named after a deity, sharing its serpent element with [[same-root:Quetzalcoatl]].
American name for coriander leaves, the Spanish word, from the same Latin [[from:coriandrum]] as [[same-root:coriander]].
American name for the leaves, the Spanish-derived form of [[from:coriandrum]]; a doublet of [[same-root:coriander]].
The [[see:verlan]] form of merci, used to say thanks.
Formerly [[from:Losantiville]], renamed after the [[from:Society of the Cincinnati]], ultimately from [[from:Cincinnatus]], whose name means curly-haired: the curly hair city.
Roman hero who left farming to save the city in days; his name comes from cincinnus, curly hair, and gave [[gave:Cincinnati]] its name.
A spin-off of [[from:photography]], meaning drawing with movement.
Also from Arabic [[from:sifr]], closer to the original; besides a code, in 14th-century English it meant the symbol for [[same-root:zero]].
From Arabic [[from:sifr]], like [[same-root:zero]]; meant any numeral by the 15th century, then a coded message, as French [[see:chiffre]] did first.
A more direct borrowing of Arabic sifr, empty or void, the same source as [[same-root:zero]].
Comes from the same Proto-Indo-European root, [[from:kʷekʷlo-]], as [[same-root:wheel]], so the two words are related despite looking totally different.
The hosts take it to mean putting something off indefinitely, or a way of not embarrassing someone in a group meeting.
The 'little hat' on French vowels, added in a spelling reform to mark a removed S, as in [[see:hotel]] versus [[see:hostel]].
First found in its modern sense in Shakespeare, though the word circumstance already existed with a different meaning.
Sex workers hung out under its arches, giving [[see:fornix]] the sense of brothel.
A hybrid cloud name meaning a heap of curls.
A hybrid cloud name meaning spread-out curls of hair.
Means curl of hair in Latin; one of the cloud names coined by [[see:Luke Howard]].
An alternative code name for the [[see:tank]] that didn't stick.
A Middle English name for [[see:orange]], named after a fruit or plant.
The founding family's name goes back to a Dutch word for a lemon, which is funny since a bad car is a [[see:lemon]].
Nickname for [[see:Prague]] from a count by [[see:Bernard Bolzano]]; today about 500 are estimated.
Given as a common example of a [[see:palindrome]].
One of [[see:George Puttenham]]'s English names for [[equivalent:asteismus]].
A dialect word Rob associates with [[see:cloying]].
The mollusc is named from an Old English word meaning grip or grasp; the coincidence with the Latin for secretly came up in an earlier clam episode.
Literally means to constrict, clinch or pinch, which is what a clam does; discussed in a previous episode.
In 14th-century English an interjection meaning be quiet, possibly from Latin; the sea creature's name is unrelated to Latin [[unrelated:clam (Latin)]].
Latin for secretly, which gave the diminutive [[gave:clanculum]]; the 14th-century English interjection may refer to it.
Latin for secretly, the source of [[gave:clandestine]]; by coincidence the same as the name of the shellfish, but not the source of [[unrelated:clam up]].
Relatively modern slang that pictures a clam shutting its shell.
Comes from being like the shellfish, not from the Latin word for secretly.
Doesn't need the idea of a [[see:clam]] to make sense, since clam itself means to constrict or clinch.
One of the many American slang words for money.
Family dynasties in western Scotland, some set up by Norse settlers, such as [[see:MacIver]] and [[see:MacAulay]].
Means secret or clandestine, from Latin [[from:clanculum]], a diminutive of Latin [[see:clam (Latin)]]; Johnson defined it using the harder word [[see:clandestine]].
Loosely related to [[same-root:clancular]] and used by Johnson to define it.
Called needlessly Latinate by [[see:George Orwell]].
In use since the 1560s, meaning secret or furtive; based on Latin [[from:clam (Latin)]], secretly, an adverbial form linked to [[from:calare]], to hide.
Literally a rabbit's nest or warren, a euphemism for a brothel, which gave [[gave:the clap]].
Meant both a rabbit warren and a pleasure house, giving [[gave:the clap]].
The form that [[see:Modern Standard Arabic]] is a modern adaptation of.

term: Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue

mentions.note: [[see:Francis Grose]]'s very funny dictionary, which the hosts are thinking of covering in a future episode.
[[see:Francis Grose]]'s 1785 dictionary of street slang and cant, gathered from ordinary speakers rather than literature, expanded in 1811 and prefaced with apologies for its rudeness.
[[see:Francis Grose]]'s 18th-century dictionary of slang collected around London, its docks and universities; it's unclear how much he invented.
Pronounced V as W and C as K, unlike [[see:ecclesiastical Latin]]; Rob jokes he was speaking the latter when he said via strata.
Its use for classified documents is an American take on the word.
Unpronounced hieroglyphs showing the theme of a word, like drawing a gift or a clock beside [[see:present]].
One of the many bird terms in the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Impressionist whose paintings were targeted in the review that coined [[see:impressionist]].
Streamer famed for his jawline who was said to be [[see:frame-mogged]] by a judge in an alligator-shooting case.
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the sticking sense of [[same-root:cleave]].
Required by the one-syllable rule, though the guest prefers 'more clear'.
Means both to split and to cling, from two similar Old English verbs; the sticky one relates to [[same-root:clay]], the splitting one to [[same-root:clever]].
Meaning mercy, still in use and sharing its origin with [[same-root:inclement]].
Claimed authorship of [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]] and, being of German descent, changed the Dutch reindeer names to [[see:Donner (reindeer)]] and [[see:Blitzen]].
From French, via Latin clericus, from Greek [[from:klēros]], lot or inheritance, after Deuteronomy's Levites, whose inheritance was the Lord. Clergy were spiritual heirs.
Popular from the 1620s, from Greek klērikos, belonging to the clergy; perhaps an overcorrection after [[same-root:clerk]] went secular.
Shares a root with [[same-root:clergy]]; in the 1200s it meant a priest. It became secular because literate clergy worked as record keepers, accountants and royal scribes.
Shares a root with the splitting sense of [[same-root:cleave]]; originally referred to manual dexterity rather than intellect.
Called by Johnson a low word with no settled meaning; it then meant manual rather than intellectual dexterity.
Pronounced differently in America; Rob can tolerate the American version as it fits words like [[see:plaque]].
Originally a French past participle imitating the sound of casting type; part of [[see:stereotype]] printing.
Its printing origin was discussed in an earlier episode.
Listed as the copulation of foxes, then used in a cant sense for that of men and women.
One of several topographical words from Old Norse.
Greek for ladder; its use as a synonym for [[see:orgasm]] is partly thanks to [[see:Marie Stopes]].
From Greek klinike techne, bedside or sickbed practice: where you lie down to be examined; related to [[same-root:incline]] and [[same-root:lean]].
Novel by [[see:Jules Verne]], inspired by the spiralifer inventions, whose 1887 translation gives the first [[see:aviator]]; its flying machine is the [[see:Albatross]].
A word for testicles Rob found in Le Roux's dictionary and had to check with his wife.
Most likely means a little hill, which also explains a town called Clitoris; Jess's Words from Hell entry opens with 'Congratulations, you found it.'
A verb in Le Roux's dictionary for which, the hosts say, English has no straightforward equivalent.
Meaning clothing, from old London prison slang.
One of the historical names for the [[see:dandelion]].
Imitates the sound of an early square sheet-metal bell; adopted in the 14th century probably from medieval Latin, possibly borrowed earlier from Celtic; compare German [[same-root:Glocke]].
Means to notice someone or figure them out, as in 'he clocked me'.
Means someone figured you out; heard from 13-year-olds, who mime a teacup while saying it; it builds on [[see:clocked]] and [[see:tea]].
A [[see:flat adverb]] next to 'closely', used differently: 'stay close' but 'look closely'.
A [[see:retronym]]: all diapers were cloth until disposable ones were invented.
Compared with [[see:easel]]: both name a carrying animal for something that holds things.
In Old English it meant a rock, hill or heap; the hosts argue the word should really be [[see:wolcen]].
Covered before; from cloud altitude classifications, nine being very high; the phrase has also been [[equivalent:on cloud seven]].
A form of [[same-root:Lewis]].
The courtesy books' collective noun for cats, a variation on [[from:clutter]].
Originally a clumsy country peasant, like [[see:villain]]; Germanic, probably meaning lump, perhaps related to [[same-root?:clue]]; the OED rejects a link with [[unrelated:colonist]].
An old word for a thief, apparently from a word meaning to grip or grasp, like [[same-root:cloying]].
Too sweet or too much, apparently from a word meaning to grip or grasp, related to [[same-root:cloyer]].
The weapon, a word from Old Norse.
Old word for a ball of twine, like the one [[see:Ariadne]] gave [[see:Theseus]] to find his way out of the [[see:labyrinth]].
The US name for [[see:Cluedo]], perhaps changed because Americans don't know [[see:Ludo]]; also a film Jess calls one of her favourite comedies.
A ball of thread, like the one leading through the Minotaur's labyrinth; its ball or lump sense may connect it with [[same-root?:clown]].
A blend of clue and [[from:Ludo]], patented in the 1940s by a British musician inspired by murder mysteries and the parlour game [[see:Murder (game)]].
An unpleasant nickname for a doctor that Rob prefers not to explain.
From the Greek for nettle, since many sting; the group includes [[see:jellyfish]], [[see:anemone]]s, hydroids and corals.
Old English word for knighthood, an example of [[see:-ship]].
The source of the colour sense in [[see:colly birds]].
A blue and a steel-grey metal, from German [[from:Kobold]], household goblin; silver miners' term for rock laced with arsenic and sulphur that could make you sick.
From German [[from:Kobold]], goblin, because arsenic-laced cobalt ore made miners ill; also discussed in their colour episode.
The OED rejects linking [[see:cobbler]] to cobble together; cobble, meaning mend, is recorded only from the late 15th century and may be a back-formation from [[from?:cobbler]].
An example of the gender-neutral or masculine -er ending, in contrast to [[see:-ster]].
A shoe mender of uncertain origin, perhaps French for to couple; recorded from the 14th century. Also a dessert named for its cobblestone-like topping.
Means nonsense; it is rhyming slang from cobbler's awls, rhyming with [[see:balls]], meaning [[see:bollocks]].
Recorded in the 14th century, for stones set together to form a street; Jess sees support in it for the cobble-together theory of [[see:cobbler]].
Simply a spider web, from [[from:cop]], and related to [[same-root:attercop]].
Simply means spiderweb, its first part being the [[same-root:cop]] in attercop.
Proposed in an ICAO South American variant; changed to [[see:Charlie]] very late in the NATO alphabet's development.
Early Coca-Cola contained [[from:cocaine]] and was named after it, perhaps created as a [[see:coca wine]] without the wine.
Named from coca leaves and the [[from:cola]] nut, its first stimulants; created by John Pemberton in 1886 as an alcohol-free alternative to [[see:coca wine]].
The former UK name for [[see:Diet Coke]], still used in much of Europe.
A popular wine and patent medicine containing coca, notably [[see:Mariani wine]].
The drink that [[see:Coca-Cola]] was made as an alcohol-free alternative to.
From coca leaves chewed for energy in the Andes, isolated in 1855; its ending echoes [[see:morphine]]; the DEA lists almost 500 street names for it.
The genus of the [[see:ladybird]], reflected in the French [[same-root:coccinelle]].
French for a ladybird, the same word as [[same-root:cochineal]], though ladybirds were never crushed to make [[see:crimson]] dye.
French for [[equivalent:ladybird]], the source of English [[gave:cochineal]].
Insect the hosts identify with the one crushed for [[see:crimson]] dye; French uses the same word, [[same-root:coccinelle]], for the ladybird.
A red dye whose name comes from French [[from:coccinelle]], though the dye comes from a different red insect, not ladybirds.
An early English word for the penis, now more vulgar; originally a male bird that struts, like a rooster.
Originally a rooster; early penis uses were metaphorical or in [[from:pillicock]]; taps called cocks, like [[see:stopcock]], were rooster-shaped, not phallic.
Stale beer and bread fed to fighting roosters, one proposed source of [[see:cocktail]].
A name for a very small printing house.
Rob thinks it should be cockapoodle; Jess says it ends in -poo to sound like a bird.
Basilisk-like creature hatched from a cock's egg by a snake, once interchangeable with [[same-root:crocodile]]; thought to come from Latin [[from:calcatrix]], one who tramples.
A big European beetle Jess calls the rudest; its cock may refer to a crest-like look.
Someone born within the sound of [[see:Bow Bells]], most likely from [[from?:cokeney]], a cock's egg, unkindly applied to city dwellers; possibly from French [[from?:coquin]].
Says 'water' with a [[see:glottal stop]] and is judged lazy, though posh R-dropping is an even greater weakening.
Used constantly in Britain but, apart from [[see:blow a raspberry]], barely caught on in the US, which makes Rob doubt it explains [[see:know your onions]].
Rob tests Jess with examples from a Victorian glossary, often based on famous people, foods and London places, sometimes layering slang on slang.
First a pit for cockfighting; 17th-century sailors used it for the cramped coxswain's station near the stern, and early 20th-century, WWI-era aviation took it up for the pilot's area.
From Spanish [[from:cucaracha]], reshaped by English speakers into cock plus roach, a simple [[see:folk etymology]].
A folk-etymological mangling of Spanish [[from:cucaracha]] into cock and roach, neither related to the Spanish.
From Spanish [[from:cucaracha]], assimilated into English as two existing words that have nothing to do with the insect.
Since a cock can't lay eggs, it meant dodgy offspring like a petulant child or runt; it is the leading theory for [[gave?:Cockney]].
One of the words on [[see:seven words you can never say on television]].
Most likely from French [[from:coquetier]], an egg cup in which Sazerac cocktails were first served in New Orleans.
Jess notes that [[see:hoax]]es made it hard to work out where cocktail comes from.
Origin disputed, muddied by [[see:H. L. Mencken]]; likeliest from French [[from?:coquetier]], egg cup; other theories: docked horse tails, [[see:cock ale]], a feathered regiment.
Most likely a mangling of French [[from?:coquetier]], cited as a parallel to [[see:cockchafer]].
Meaning scrotum in [[see:codpiece]], possibly related to [[same-root?:cuttlefish]]; the fish might be named after it, making it a ball sack of the sea.
Probably related to the cuttle in [[same-root?:cuttlefish]].
Means tail, the concluding passage of a piece; indirectly related to [[same-root:coward]] via French.
One of the earliest works in [[see:cuneiform]], written in Akkadian, like the [[see:Epic of Gilgamesh]].
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Its [[see:cod]] is not the fish but a word meaning scrotum.
Known locally but doubted by zoologists until seen, as [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]] wrote.
City in the Netherlands from which the Dutch surname behind [[gave:Vancouver]] comes.
From Turkish kahve, from Arabic qahwa, thought originally to mean wine; English's O vowel is unexplained. A rival theory links it to [[from?:Kaffa]].
The stereotyped New York 'cawfee' reflects a wider vowel pattern tied to the [[see:cot–caught merger]], and incomers adopt it first.
In Dutch, as in Amsterdam, a shop selling cannabis rather than coffee, though coffee is usually available.
Linguists' term for a word sharing a common source with another, like English and French [[see:magazine]].
A word with ultimately the same origin, such as [[see:bask]] and [[see:bathe]]; discussed in an earlier episode.
The third element of a Roman citizen's name, originally a family name that became hereditary, like [[see:Caesar]].
From Latin [[from:cuneus]], corner; in 14th-century English it meant wedge, then a stamped piece of money, after the wedge-like dies used to stamp metal.
French for a corner, not money; a coin is a [[see:pièce]].
Shakespeare was the first to use it to mean something other than coins.
Shakespeare first used it for something other than coins in [[see:Hamlet]]: 'This is the very coinage of your brain.'
Meaning to be identical in substance or nature, popularised through astronomy along with [[see:coincidence]].
Popularised through astronomical language, implying coincidences were caused by the stars.
Something that befalls you; shares the root meaning to fall with [[same-root:deciduous]].
Probably the most clinical term for sex, yet still euphemistic because it means a coming together.
Short for [[from:Coca-Cola]]; in the American South it can mean any soda, so asking for a Coke may get you a Pepsi.
One US regional word for a soft drink, alongside [[see:pop]] and [[see:soda]], showing a vocabulary difference in [[see:dialect]].
Coca-Cola's sugar-free drink, marketed to men with black branding, unlike [[see:Diet Coke]].
The cola nut, chewed in West Africa as a stimulant, distinguishing [[gave:Coca-Cola]] from coca wine; later cola names refer to Coca-Cola itself.
An American expression for very cold; "as balls" is a general intensifier among millennials, related in sense to [[see:brass monkey]].
The fictional Louisiana prison in Stephen King's book, home of [[see:the green mile]].
Probably because someone withdrawing from drugs looks pale and clammy like a plucked turkey; popularised by Lennon's song [[see:Cold Turkey (song)]].
John Lennon and Yoko Ono's song with the Plastic Ono Band, which helped popularise [[see:cold turkey]].
From Philip Horky's 1997 poetry collection Child's Reflections, Cold Play; earlier names were [[see:Big Fat Noises]] and [[see:Starfish]], plus the joke name Pectoralz.
The study of beetles.
Another Dutch word that, like [[see:cookie]], entered English in the United States.
The Old English name for a caterpillar, literally cabbage worm, known from the hosts' food episode.
Expressing several concepts with the same word, as many languages do with one colour term covering both blue and green.
A programmer and Reddit user who in 2022 assembled a grid of the most common [[see:compound insult]]s on Reddit.
Also literally means working together, like [[see:synergy]].
Identical in construction to [[see:synergy]], from Latin rather than Greek elements.
A fancy-sounding French technique name that just means gluing.
Paired with [[see:caller]] as an example of the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
The episode's topic: words for groups of animals or people, also called [[see:nouns of assembly]] or [[see:terms of venery]], many from the 15th-century [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Discussed in an earlier Words Unravelled episode.
From the same Latin root as [[same-root:couch]], meaning to place together.
Words that sound right together because they have been repeated together for so long, such as [[see:deeply regret]], which makes things harder for learners.
Words habitually paired even when other words would do, like [[see:pay attention]]; Jess says [[see:taken aback]] is a real idiom, not just a collocation.
The original lyric, misheard as calling birds: blackbirds, collie meaning [[same-root:coal]]-coloured.
A reduplicative word for irritation, depression or bad temper from the [[see:dictionary of reduplicative words]].
Mixed up with [[see:colon]] in a recurring malapropism, 'I like the smell of your colon'.
Named after [[from:Christopher Columbus]]; proposed in the late 18th century by [[see:Francisco de Miranda]] for a unified, independent state of Spanish colonies.
From a Greek word for limb or member, a part of a verse; one of the three pause marks of [[see:Aristophanes of Byzantium]].
The intestine comes from a Greek word meaning food and is unrelated to the punctuation mark or [[unrelated:semicolon]]; the two Greek words converged in English.
Pronounced 'kernel' from French [[from:coronel]], but spelled after Italian [[from:colonnello]] during a vogue for Italian warfare; the head of a column of soldiers.
Italian spelling with French pronunciation (French had an R), adopted when military historians became keen on Italian tactics.
A [[see:Cluedo]] character originally called Colonel Yellow; Rob thinks Colonel Mustard is a much better name.
The second part of [[see:Lindum Colonia]], described somewhat confusedly as a military depot for centurions.
An older suggested source of [[unrelated:clown]], since it also meant farmer; the OED rejects it because the chronology doesn't fit.
Closely related to [[same-root:culture]], originally land tended by farmers or settlers, such as a [[from:colonus]], a tenant farmer settling new lands around Rome.
Spelled without the U in America thanks to [[see:Noah Webster]], which brings it closer to Latin; once spelled many ways, such as coolor and colur.
Late-18th-century poetic name for the US, from [[from:Christopher Columbus]]. It appears in Washington DC's full name and was a female personification before [[see:Uncle Sam]].
Columbus, Ohio, was named long after Columbus, because an Ohio lawmaker who admired him persuaded others; compare [[see:District of Columbia]].
Given alongside the punctuation colon when distinguishing it from the intestinal [[see:colon]].
For Jess, distinct from an [[see:op-ed]]: usually written by a recurring contributor.
Already had a silent B, which printers copied onto [[see:thumb]].
Shares a root meaning to beat or fight with [[same-root:battle]]; literally fighting together.
Sounds almost bureaucratic, but comes from King Lear.
A rumoured but false expansion of [[see:CQD]].
A feminine job title that is falling out of use.
From Greek [[from:komoidos]], a performer at festivals and revelries who put on komoidia, an amusing spectacle; a comedy need not be funny, but should be fun.
A medieval word for a stranger, meaning someone who has come; one of the many old [[see:-ling]] words.
Means long-haired, for the tail streaming behind it; comets are made of dust and ice.
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
Johnson gave it a 750-word explanation.
Has the same -able ending as [[see:vegetable]].
A common metathesised pronunciation of comfortable, more natural in rhotic American accents.
The plain English equivalent of [[equivalent:Bildungsroman]].
A spelling of comics in early and mid-1900s cartoonist culture, perhaps echoed in the ending of [[see:grawlix]].
Greek for something cut off, also a clause or line of poetry; first a short pause dot, its mark later developed from the slash-like [[from:virgule]].
French for ordering food, without literally commanding the server; English [[see:order]] works similarly.
Title taken by Caliph Omar, showing that al- can follow amir, as the theory about [[see:admiral]] requires.
Early professional Italian theatre, popular across Europe, with improvised formulaic scenes, masked stock characters and recurring routines; the source of many English comedy words.
A French-derived near-synonym of [[see:begin]].
The formal version behind [[gave:ça va]], itself said to be short for [[from:comment allez-vous à la selle]].
Related to [[same-root:mercenary]].
Grose's usual word, besides the [[see:monosyllable]], for a woman's genitals.
An old name for the [[see:sweet potato]] when it was more popular than the white potato.
A French-derived word that takes [[see:-est]], one counterexample to Rob's Germanic-versus-Romance theory.
TV show whose German character wishes there were a word for enjoying someone else's misfortune, Jess's favourite joke about [[see:Schadenfreude]].
From the Latin word for bread, literally someone you share bread with, like [[same-root:company]].
Means someone you eat bread with, leading from the count to other bread people like the [[see:lord]].
Literally someone you share bread with, related to [[same-root:panini]], [[same-root:empanada]] and [[same-root:pantry]].
From the Latin word for bread, like [[same-root:companion]]: someone you share bread with.
First made in Han China from floating [[see:lodestone]] pointing south; the word meant a mathematical instrument that steps together, and passed to the round navigational tool.
Literally means hanging together, so the hosts call theirs a compendious friendship.
One of the fourteen words from [[from:pendere]], to hang, in Jess's passage.
One of the fourteen words from [[from:pendere]], to hang, in Jess's passage.
Johnson said this was the proper form, meaning something superfluous or more than enough; a doublet of [[same-root:compliment]].
Saying someone has a complex uses Jungian vocabulary.
Johnson defined it as civility involving some hypocrisy; an etymological doublet of [[same-root:complement]], reshaped via Italian and disliked by him.
One of Jess's favourite insult phenomena, pairing words like fart with nugget; [[see:Colin Morris]] charted the commonest ones on Reddit, and the more unexpected, the funnier.
Shares its root verb with the verb to count.
Like computing, from Latin [[from:computare]], to reckon together; French deliberately avoids it, saying [[equivalent:ordinateur]].
Spelled differently from [[same-root:camaraderie]], which keeps the French spelling.
A French swear word for an idiot that ultimately shares the meaning of [[same-root:cunt]].
The con is short for confidence, as in confidence trickster or artist, because you win someone's confidence to swindle them; unrelated to [[unrelated:ale conner]].
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists, alongside its variant com-.

Earlier name for the condition Bleuler renamed [[see:schizophrenia]].
Shares the Greek root demos with [[same-root:demonym]].
Rule by the people, the demos, whose root may mean city; in [[see:Plato]]'s scheme it follows [[see:oligarchy]] and degenerates into [[see:tyranny]].
Shares the Latin 'show' verb with [[same-root:monster]]; Jess says it contains no demon but does contain a monster.
A TikTok commenter asked why it contains a [[unrelated:demon]]; it doesn't, but it does contain [[same-root:monster]], from the old French word meaning to show.
A classical Renaissance borrowing that [[see:inkhorn]] purists objected to, now taken for granted.
The name for people from a place, coined in its current sense around 1990, from Greek [[from:demos]]; in the 1890s it meant someone named after a place, or a pen name.
A word for people from a place, discussed in an earlier episode.
A later Egyptian script for the Egyptians' day-to-day language, used in the middle section of the [[see:Rosetta Stone]].
Historically a word that boxed women in, it was ironically reclaimed in a TikTok meme by [[see:Jools Lebron]], which Jess discussed on BBC World Service.
Scientific term meaning tree-like, from the same PIE root as [[same-root:tree]].
Dating by trees, for example by counting their rings; from the same PIE root as [[same-root:tree]].
Used in Germany for mixing German (Deutsch) and English.
From [[from:serge de Nîmes]]; in Webster's 1864 dictionary it meant a coarse cotton for overalls, as the fabric changed in America but the name stayed.
Named after the French city of [[from:Nîmes]], 'de Nîmes'.
Thought to have been coined by Shakespeare.
Comes from French [[from:dénouer]], to untie.
Considered as the French for 'unravelled' in the show's intro; it means to untie and gave English [[gave:dénouement]].
Another ghost word from misreading [[see:Francis Bacon]], meant to refer to tooth cutting.
The French phrase that English borrowed directly as [[gave:dandelion]].
French source of [[gave:dandelion]], after the tooth-like serrated leaves; French now prefers [[see:pissenlit]].
Related to [[same-root:tooth]] through the same D/T shift that links [[see:foot]] and [[see:pedal]].
Named after [[from:James W. Denver]].
Suggested as the American counterpart of the British [[see:Home Office]], in charge of police and the like.
The feeling of strangeness at being somewhere other than home; not quite the same as [[see:homesickness]].
One of the fourteen words from [[from:pendere]], to hang, in Jess's passage.
Former name for [[see:oxygen]] given by [[see:Joseph Priestley]], meaning air lacking [[from:phlogiston]]; the hosts debate its pronunciation.
Compared with the old punitive sense of [[see:transportation]]; shares the carry root despite seeming linked to [[see:port]].
A cab for hire that worked around a train depot; the term evolved into [[gave:station wagon]].
Means completely crooked, from a Latin word [[from:pravus]] meaning crooked.
Being 'a bit depressed' is cited as casual [[see:therapy speak]] that drains clinical precision.
One of the models on which [[see:width]] was formed.
Rob's home town in the Danelaw, a Viking place name ending in [[from:-by]].
Rob's home city in the Danelaw; with the Old Norse suffix [[from:-by]], it means place of the [[from:deer]], or of beasts.
Spanish for breakfast, meaning to break one's fast, with the negative des-; like [[same-root:déjeuner]], it shares a Latin root with [[same-root:dinner]].
Means a place deserted of people, not a sandy place; from Latin [[from:deserere]], to unjoin, related to [[same-root:series]]; equated with [[see:wilderness]].
Comes from a Latin root, meaning to join together or put in a row; a deserted place is severed from humanity, unrelated to [[unrelated:dessert]].
Meant an island that is deserted, not a sandy island, as the hosts point out about [[see:desert]].
A French-derived near-synonym of [[see:wish]].
In the plural, desserts reads backwards as [[see:stressed]], the longest [[see:semordnilap]] the hosts found.
The last course, eaten after the table has been cleared of everything else; it comes from the same serving verb as [[same-root:just deserts]], and is unrelated to [[unrelated:desert]].
From Latin [[from:destruere]], to tear down or unbuild; the oldest of its group, arriving in the 1200s with Norman French spelling.
Formed after 'destruction', an example of [[see:back formation]].
A back-formation from [[from:destruction]], not a verb until 1958, and less used because English already had [[see:destroy]].
Entered English before its verb, giving [[gave:destruct]] by back-formation.
One of the English words built on [[from:tenere]], to hold.
An 11-letter palindrome, past tense of detartrate, taking tartrate out of a juice or wine to make it less tart.
According to a 1905 New York Press piece, the [[see:Pinkerton Detective Agency]] made the word so offensive that many detective agencies dropped it.
Literally means something like to thunder down.
Founded by the man after whom [[see:Cadillac]] is named, which explains the French name.
Slang for a twopenny piece, rhymed by [[see:bottle of spruce]].
Means Germanic people, the same word as [[same-root:Dutch]]; the Germans adopted it for themselves when their states united.
What Germans call themselves and their language, a unifying name for the confederated states' shared language; related to English [[same-root:Dutch]].
German name for the [[see:Great Dane]], using a borrowing of English [[from:dog]], which other languages apply to big dogs like mastiffs.
German name for Germany, from the same word as [[same-root:Dutch]].
The Germans' own name for their country, from [[from:Deutsch]].
From Latin [[from:via]], way or road; a deviant is one who strays off the figurative moral path.
Straying from the moral path, built on [[from:via]] like [[same-root:devious]].
To stray away from the course, from [[from:via]].
Doesn't have to mean the Devil, since it can be any demon or pixie-like being; it is often used as an emphatic expletive, which is behind many idioms.

term: devil finds work for idle hands

mentions.note: One of the many idioms involving the [[see:devil]] that the hosts call relatively self-explanatory.
Imagines the devil as a hypothetical being who might care about consequences, implying that no one worth worrying about cares at all.
Recorded in 1616 for someone pleading for Satan's kingdom; the Catholic Church's term for whoever argued against a canonisation or miracle probably gave the modern sense.
Named for its aggressive behaviour and long body shape.
One of the obvious, familiar street names for [[see:cocaine]] on the DEA list.
An old name for the [[see:dragonfly]].
A past name for thirteen, like [[equivalent:baker's dozen]].
Straying from the moral path, built on [[from:via]] like [[same-root:deviant]].
Thought to have been coined by Shakespeare.
Accents or marks above or below letters, one way to spell sounds Latin lacked; Czech prefers this route.
Ends in Greek gnosis, knowing; means to tell two things apart.
Covers differences between varieties at every level, including syntax, vocabulary and pronunciation, so it takes in [[see:accent]].
Contains the same measurement element as [[same-root:geometry]].
An American word that is older than the British [[equivalent:nappy]].
From a Greek word meaning thoroughly white or white mixed with colours; first a costly patterned silk, then fine napkins shaped like a baby's diaper.
Originally a patterned white cloth; from French, meaning thoroughly white, from Greek; used by Shakespeare; Jess dislikes the word.
Means flowing through, from the root shared with [[same-root:rhythm]].
Originally meaning lasting one day, from [[from:dies]]; a doublet of [[same-root:journal]], also mentioned in a previous episode.
Not an animal but an alga, often made of two symmetrical halves, that produces 20 to 50% of Earth's oxygen.
A regional word for rain used in Shropshire.
A slang word for money from Rob's list.
A long chemical name for a gas that, according to the hosts, is used as a fire repellent on submarines and aircraft.
A fairly mild insult; the nickname for Richard, used as an everyman name like Jack in [[see:Tom, Dick and Harry]], then for the penis, like [[see:Johnson]].
An old word for the periwinkle, showing [[see:dick]] used as a generic name.
An old name for a will-o'-the-wisp, another use of [[see:dick]] as a generic name.
German for fat, a relative of English [[same-root:thick]], since English th often matches a Germanic d.
Once a popular name for the everyman, which is why we have [[gave:spotted dick]].
An old term for a jackass, in which [[see:dick]] works like Jack as an everyman name.
German for buttermilk, considered fatty milk, from [[from:dick (German)]].
Another name used for donkeys, cited with [[see:jackass]] and [[see:neddy]] as support for the [[see:Duncan]] theory of [[see:donkey]].
Another example of the stress difference in two-syllable -ate verbs.
Shares the dict, meaning said, of [[same-root:verdict]].
An example of a form of rule ending in [[see:-ship]].
A 20th-century dictionary Joshua owns and loves, exhaustive and full of treats like [[see:heebie-jeebies]] and [[see:habdabs]].

term: Dictionnaire comique, satyrique, critique, burlesque, libre et proverbial
translation: comic, satirical, critical, burlesque, free and proverbial dictionary

mentions.note: [[see:Philippe-Joseph Le Roux]]'s dictionary of Parisian underworld terms, credited by Grose as the model for his own.
One of Grose's terms for breasts.
A less elegant theory derives [[gave?:dildo]] from a corruption of diddle.
Probably imitates the instrument's sound and appeared in English in the early 1900s; claims that it means hollow bamboo lack evidence.
Typeface named after a French dynasty of printers.
A German band whose name means the doctors.
Pointed out in passing as the correct singular of dice.
The singular of dice, which is what the Arabic source of [[see:hazard]] meant.
Popular German band named from the idiom [[from:tote Hose]].
Simply saying someone died can seem rude in many situations, so people use euphemisms like [[see:passed]].
A satirical character in Washington Irving's hoax stories who popularised [[see:Knickerbocker]].
[[see:Washington Irving]]'s character, given a deliberately preposterous Dutch-sounding name, who gave his name to [[gave:knickerbockers]].
[[see:Washington Irving]]'s New York Dutch caricature, illustrated in knee-billowing trousers, who gave [[gave:knickerbockers]].
Washington Irving's character and pen name, whose distinctive trousers, baggy around the knee, became baseball pants.
Sound that exists within the story world, like character dialogue, as opposed to [[see:non-diegetic]] sound.
A form of [[same-root:James]].
Spanish name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], also meaning lion's tooth.
An extremely productive Latin root in English, behind the doublets [[gave:diary]] and [[gave:journal]] and the related [[gave:meridian]].
Day of Mars, a counterpart of [[equivalent:Tuesday]] (called Greek by the hosts); source of French [[gave:mardi]].
Used on both sides of the Atlantic; named after [[from:Rudolf Diesel]], the German inventor of an internal combustion engine.
Named after [[from:Rudolf Diesel]], who developed it.
Once called [[see:Coca-Cola Light]] in the UK, since diet seemed too clinical; long advertised at women, unlike [[see:Coke Zero]].
Used on both sides of the Atlantic; Rob finds it the most logical, matching comparatives like [[see:apart from]].
American usage; Jess says critics object because both words are comparative, so the comparison is repeated.
A British usage that American viewers criticise Rob for; Britain has different to and [[see:different from]], America has [[see:different than]] and different from.
The Latin genus name of the [[see:foxglove]], after the finger-like digits of its bell-shaped blooms.
The Latin name for the rude finger gesture, meaning the impudent or indecent finger.
Several letters standing for one sound, the alternative to [[see:diacritics]]; in English [[see:H]] is the combiner par excellence.
Began as a filler sound in songs, like tra-la-la; [[see:The Choice of Valentines]] first used it for a sex toy in 1592.
Already discussed before; first found in a 1400s-era poem as a nonsense refrain, and Grose claims it evokes [[from?:diletto]], a woman's delight.
Older than expected, probably from an Italian word for delight or perhaps from [[from?:diddle]]; an earlier nonsense word in ballads like [[see:fa la]], also discussed before.
From an Old Norse word meaning to soothe; present in Old English, with cognates across Germanic languages, unlike the Mediterranean herb names.
A playful example of [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
No one knows what it means; proposals include gratitude, barely fills your stomach and close to the heart, probably because it comes from a longer phrase.
Means tenth, from Old French [[from:disme]] and medieval Latin [[from:decima pars]]; first spelled disme to rhyme with team; related to [[same-root:tithe]] and [[same-root:decimal]].
Ultimately related to [[same-root:month]].
A measurement word related to [[same-root:month]].
Jess's favourite dinosaur-like non-dinosaur, alligator-sized with a sail possibly for heat regulation, display or intimidation; unrelated to [[see:Spinosaurus]].
A Latin-derived word now used in contexts where abate, the source of [[see:bated breath]], once was.
The area's earlier name, with Din a form of [[from:dun]]; it gave [[gave:Edinburgh]] and was echoed in New Zealand's [[gave:Dunedin]].
Its use for a restaurant, rather than a person who dines, is an Americanism.
The French name for their last meal of the day, from the same Latin root as [[same-root:déjeuner]], so the French break their fast twice.
Like [[same-root:déjeuner]], it ultimately means to break your fast, but it has moved so far into the day that other words have had to replace it.
Example of German d matching English th under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Qing dynasty official who was particularly fond of the dish believed to be named after him, [[see:kung pao chicken]].
Reversed as 'dong ding', it sounds deliberate, showing the [[see:ablaut reduplication]] order.
From 1838 a drink and placeholder name; later typographic ornaments, a muffin, an insult, genitalia; a fool via [[see:The Dingbat Family]]; precursor to [[see:emoji]].
Etymologically the first meal of the day, sharing a Latin root with [[same-root:déjeuner]] and [[same-root:desayuno]]; it moved to midday, then to evening around the Industrial Revolution.
Mentioned with [[see:supper]] as words for the extra meals of wealthy French speakers.
The more formal British English term, which oddly covers the whole outfit, not just the jacket.
Means terrible lizard, coined in 1842 by [[see:Richard Owen]] from Greek [[from:deinos]], terrible, and [[from:sauros]], lizard; terrible meant awe-inspiring, and dinosaurs aren't actually lizards.
Means double beam, after paired chevron bones under the tail that Marsh thought unique; its pronunciation is disputed, with the BBC and the Natural History Museum differing.
The Natural History Museum's [[see:Diplodocus]] skeleton, sold as replicas; it was replaced in the main hall by a [[see:blue whale]] skeleton.
The study of flies, mosquitoes and midges.
Directly related to [[same-root:dirigible]].
Shares its root with [[same-root:dirige]] and [[same-root:dirigible]].
A corruption of [[from:dirige]], paralleling how [[see:placebo]] also came from the first word of a funeral psalm.
Moroccan currency from the same weight as [[same-root:dram]].
Moroccan currency related to the [[same-root:drachma]].
A funeral rite named after the first word of its psalm, Dirige Domine, direct me O Lord; it gave [[gave:dirge]].
From French [[from:diriger]], to direct, related to [[same-root:direct]]: a steerable airship, unlike a balloon; Jess once punningly called a project dirigible.
A directable balloon, discussed before, from the same root as [[same-root:dirige]].
A printed sheet ruined by errors.
Latin prefix meaning not or away, as in [[gave:distribute]]; French words beginning [[see:de-]] or des- carry it through a French filter.
Literally ill-starred, from [[from:aster]]: a terrible event foretold by the stars or caused by their bad alignment.
Referred to as one of the hosts' favourite etymologies from earlier discussions, compared with [[see:influenza]].
Disaster plus catastrophe, used to stress something is really bad but saying the same thing twice.
Released without bail, your signature being the [[see:recognizance]], a promise to come back.
One of the playful, Latin-sounding words with nonsense elements coined by playwrights around 1800 and given to American characters like the [[see:Davy Crockett]] types.
A 1960s religion holding that order and disorder are human-made grids imposed on deeper chaos; it inspired [[see:The Illuminatus! Trilogy]].
Another everyday long word, built from prefixes and suffixes.
The Victorian movement to undo the establishment of the [[see:Church of England]] as the official state church; related movements existed in Ireland and Scotland.
The dis- intensifies rather than negates, as in [[see:distribute]]; gruntle means to grunt, so it is to be grumbly like an irritated pig.
Arrived in the late 16th century from French desgouster, to dislike the taste, ultimately from Latin [[from:gustare]], to taste; it has no natural opposite.
In Jess's family, the plainer towel used for drying dishes, distinct from a [[see:tea towel]].
From medieval Latin [[from:dies mali]]; first a noun in the phrase in the dismal, then an adjective in dismal day, a tautology meaning bad day day.
From medieval Latin [[from:dies mali]], evil days (two per month on calendars); first 'in the dismal', so 'dismal day' is tautological.
The British form; to disorientate is to undo having found east, whereas to disorient is never having found it—a minute difference from [[see:disoriented]].
Being unable to tell where you are, literally not knowing which way east is; preferred in America over British [[see:disorientated]].
In the US, a place selling legal medical or recreational cannabis, unlike a [[see:drugstore]].
One of the fourteen words from [[from:pendere]], to hang, in Jess's passage.
To carry someone away from what they normally do, with the port of [[same-root:transport]]; Chaucer used it in 1386, and it gave [[gave:sport]].
The older verb form of [[see:disrupt]], which Rob would like people to start using again.
So clichéd it's undisruptive; a back-formation from disruption, older [[see:disrump]], from a root meaning break with dis- meaning apart.
Related to [[same-root:corrupt]].
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
A rarer change where a sound is altered to avoid repeating it, as when Latin [[see:medidies]] became [[see:meridies]], giving [[see:meridian]].
A general term for birds, which make up much of the book's list.
Pronunciation mostly used in Spain, which separates an s sound from a th sound, so [[see:caza]] and [[see:casa]] differ; contrasted with [[see:seseo]] and [[see:ceceo]].
Shares the twisting root of [[same-root:extortion]].
Example of dis- meaning widely rather than negating, cited to explain [[see:disgruntled]].
Discussed before; its dis- means widely or apart rather than a negative, as in [[see:disrupt]].
From [[from:dis-]]: essentially to tribute away or broadly.
One of the best-known places named after Columbus, like [[see:Columbus]], Ohio.
From the same Latin root as [[same-root:turbulence]], making turbulence hard to define without its relatives.
The Old English doublet of the Old Norse [[same-root:dyke]].
A hymn sung to Dionysus, a predecessor of [[see:tragedy]], usually with a chorus of people dressed as [[see:satyr]]s.
Borrowed from Latin and cognate with [[same-root:journal]]; feels like it should relate to two but just means daily.
Persian and Arabic, first a bundle of sheets or collection of poems, then an account book, customhouse and council chamber, and finally a seat.
Compared with [[see:disport]]: the same idea of something that diverts your attention.
Its use as a verb, to divorce someone, is credited to American English.
Used for a taxiway D at the [[see:Delta Air Lines]] hub to avoid confusion with the airline; later dropped for its Confederate associations.
From French [[from:disant]], one who speaks, spelling influenced by [[see:dizzy]]; first a court storyteller, then a fool and an insult; now lost.
Thought to have influenced the spelling of [[see:dizzard]].
The Egyptian word for brick that gave [[gave:adobe]]; its eh vowels are only Egyptologists' placeholders, since the real vowels are unknown.
Australian rhyming slang meaning to bolt or disappear, also 'doing a Harry', after Prime Minister [[from:Harold Holt]].
To trick or fool someone; origin unknown, possibly vaudevillian, where a number is a song, or perhaps boxing; compared with British [[equivalent:stitch someone up]].
A silly, philosophical little palindrome.
A [[see:collocation]] meaning to spend time in prison; there is no necessary reason it uses 'do' rather than 'spend'.
A Nissan Micra advertising campaign built on coined portmanteaus like [[see:spafe]], inspiring Rob's schoolfriends to coin their own.
The joke punchline "do you think he saw us", for which [[see:Eunotosaurus]] sounds like an alternative.
A variant of [[same-root:Robert]] that sounds like a pet name; Rob's dad had a toy called Dobbin the Donkey, then named his son Robert.
Named after the breeder [[from:Karl Friedrich Louis Dobermann]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
Latin for teacher; meant an adviser or religious teacher long before a medical practitioner, though it is still used loosely for anyone with a PhD.
Existed as an academic title before it meant a medical practitioner, from a root meaning to teach; the old English word for a doctor was [[see:leech]].
Asking for a doctor, in France or in English, might get you someone with a PhD who can't help in an emergency.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used as the second reference to [[see:Daleks]].
A Britishism Jess nearly had to say in an advert; it means [[equivalent:shifty]], or [[equivalent:shady]] in American terms.
Mocked by Europeans who ate the bird to extinction; the name is a Portuguese take on another word and may mean stupid person.
As in doffing your cap, a contraction of do off; the hosts wonder whether [[gave?:doffer]] comes from it too.
A worker who swapped full bobbins on a spinning frame for empty ones; also a carding-machine comb that strips off fibre; perhaps a do-offer, from [[from?:doff]].
The 'dog mystery': the word's origin is unknown; other Germanic languages use [[see:hound]]-type words, and its -og ending appears in other unexplained animal names.
Like [[see:body]], an English word whose history can't be traced back past a certain point.
Used as a verb by Shakespeare, an example of [[see:verbing]].
D in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]].
Jess's other example of a basic word going from English into French, though much later than [[see:nord]] and the other compass points.
Of unknown origin, one of the Old English words ending in a doubled G; it likely began as a cutesy diminutive that replaced [[see:hound]].
Not the direct source of [[same-root?:cynicism]], which comes from the Greek for dog, though Rob suspects the two are related far enough back.
Along with lost and fog, a word Americans mispronounce in an old-fashioned way when imitating British accents, because the vowel is alien to them.
Discussed before as having no relatives in other languages, so their versions are borrowings, used for big breeds like [[see:mastiff]]s.
[[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for the telephone, given as an example of how much the British use it.
From the rising of [[from:Sirius]], the dog star; folk etymology links it to dogs suffering in the heat.
Discussed before; the season is linked to the influence of the dog star [[see:Sirius]], visible in late summer. Also called [[equivalent:canicular days]].
A name for the [[see:dandelion]] in some forms of Italian, because they're yellow and grow along roadsides.
Johnson admitted 'of this word I know not the meaning'.
An intense, tangled close-quarters fight in the air, named on the same model as [[see:cockpit]].
One of the separate names once given to kinds of [[see:shark]], still used for certain species.
An older specific name that is still used for a type of [[see:shark]].
What the sharks once called [[see:sea dog]]s are still sometimes called.
Printers' rude alliterative name for the [[see:exclamation mark]], alluded to but not said; compared with the cat's-tail theory of the [[see:question mark]].
A French breed name borrowed from the English [[from:dog]].
Borrowed from English [[see:dog]], it usually means a mastiff, since mastiffs were the dogs most associated with Britain.
Nothing to do with dogs: originally dag tree, a stabbing tree, used for butchers' skewers, like a [[see:dagger]].
Probably from [[from?:dull]] with the ending of [[see:tantrum]]; the hosts argue the calm sea region took its name from the word, not vice versa.
From Middle English [[from:dole]], grief, sorrow or mourning; Jess used to confuse it with [[see:baleful]].
An anglicization of [[from:Taler]], short for [[from:Joachimsthaler]], which came via Low German before the US existed; the American dollar later followed the [[see:Spanish dollar]].
Named after a Czech valley: from [[from:Joachimsthaler]], coins of silver mined at Joachimsthal, now [[see:Jáchymov]].
From [[from:Joachimsthaler]], big coins minted in the Joachimsthal valley, shortened to Thaler and eventually dollar; probably covered in their money episode.
No one knows its origin; theories include PS for [[see:peso]], the [[see:Pillars of Hercules]], a serpent on a cross on [[see:Taler]] coins, and [[see:Ayn Rand]]'s squashed U.
An older expression contrasting cash with something trivial, like [[see:dollars to donuts]].
From the 1920s, pitting serious cash against cheap, zero-shaped donuts; preceded by [[see:dollars to buttons]] and [[see:dollars to dumplings]].
An older version of [[see:dollars to donuts]], dumplings being cheap.
A railroad-style cart for tracking shots; all dollies go back to devices with limbs like a child's doll, beginning with the [[from:dumb dolly]].
The person who operates the [[see:dolly]] used for tracking shots.
Also jumped on the bandwagon of saying [[see:ay up me duck]], though no one knew what it meant.
A shot moving on a track, related through [[see:dolly]] to the [[same-root:Barbie doll]].
In an earlier episode the hosts wrongly said a dolphin is a type of [[see:porpoise]], and they still aren't sure of the relationship.
A toothed whale, named from Greek [[from:delphis]], womb, perhaps for giving live birth; unlike a [[see:porpoise]], it has a sickle-shaped fin and cone-shaped teeth.
[[see:William the Conqueror]]'s big volume recording who owned what land, mentioned alongside [[see:doom]].
A French adjective used for the Anglo-Saxon noun house.
Name of a particularly large ballista in a 1330 Windsor Castle munitions inventory, an early link between [[see:Gunnhilda]] and [[see:gun]].
Looks like the source of the -dom in [[unrelated:kingdom]] but isn't.
The first example of the [[see:-trix]] ending that came to mind.
Looks like the source of the -dom in [[unrelated:kingdom]] but isn't.
Looks as if it shares the -dom of [[unrelated:kingdom]], but it doesn't.
The US president, whose surname Brits find funny because [[see:trump]] means fart in British English.
A British cultural reference to [[see:trews]] that always has to be said in a very strong Scottish accent.
Example of a two-syllable verb ending in -ate that Americans stress on the first syllable and Brits on the second.

translation: Association for subordinate officials of the main electric services of the Danube steamship company

mentions.note: A famous hypothetical German compound: technically possible but not really used, it packs a whole English phrase into one word.
Job title its holders could theoretically have used from 1829 to 1991; Donau is Danube, Dampfschiff steamboat, Fahrt journey, Gesellschaft society, Kapitän captain.
A hill fort near Bombay where the British traded for tough cotton, giving [[gave:dungarees]].
One of Reese Witherspoon's two donkeys, the other being [[see:Honky]].
First found in Francis Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue, spelt like [[see:monkey]] but pronounced dunkey; probably a pet form of [[from?:Duncan]], like [[see:jackass]] and [[see:neddy]].
The French word for data, literally things given, which matches the etymology of [[equivalent:data]]; related to [[same-root:donner (French)]].
Santa's reindeer, originally Dunder and Blixem; the names combine Dutch [[from:donder]], thunder, and German Blitzen, lightning. Covered in their Christmas episode.
The French verb to give, related to [[same-root:donor]] and [[same-root:données]].
Example of German d matching English th under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
German for thunder; originally the Dutch [[from:Dunder]] in the poem, changed by [[see:Clement Clarke Moore]] via an intermediate form.
Named as related to [[same-root:data]] and to the French verb [[same-root:donner (French)]].

term: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
original: Nikkō o mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare
translation: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko

mentions.note: Japanese saying that nothing beats [[see:Nikko]]'s beauty, rhyming through a pun on [[see:kekkō]]; compare [[equivalent:see Naples and die]].
A slogan that was originally an anti-littering campaign, which surprised Rob.

term: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge

mentions.note: An Irish saying advising you to stay out of other people's business.
Ending for poodle crosses, taken through [[see:rebracketing]] of [[from:Labradoodle]], whose D belongs to Labrador; some crosses, like the [[see:Puggle]], are true portmanteaus.
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode about [[see:portmanteau]]s.

A [[see:sniglet]], dork spelled with two Os, for a person who pushes on a door marked pull.

From German, literally a double walker or double-goer; first meant a ghostly apparition of a living person in English, and meeting yours supposedly means you'll perish.
Named after the Austrian physicist [[from:Christian Doppler]].
An accidental ghost word for density, from a garbled 'D or d' slip by [[see:Austin M. Patterson]]; it stayed in print for years.
A [[see:ghost word]] in a much later dictionary, created when slips reading 'D or d' (for density) got mixed up.

A stylised, pointy question mark proposed by [[see:Hervé Bazin]].
One of the many American slang words for money.

Computer scientist credited with coining [[see:ambigram]] in the 1980s.
Mars chocolate sold in the US, called [[see:Galaxy]] in Britain; Rob guessed it was because of Dove soap, which the US also has.

Named as related to [[same-root:data]].
Female rogues in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy, alongside [[see:morts]].
A palindromic novel of about 31,900 words whose title is also a tongue-twister.

Old Greek currency from the same weight as [[same-root:dram]].

Related to [[same-root:trek]].

Greek word, possibly just 'snake' in the Iliad, perhaps from a verb meaning to see clearly; came via Latin [[from:draco]] and French into English.

A word for a dragon in its own right, related to Latin [[same-root:draco]].

A US word for [[see:curtains]] that Jess uses.

Related to [[same-root:trek]] and [[same-root:train]].

An expression with negative connotations from the Jonestown mass suicide; Kraft insists [[see:Flavor-Aid]] was used, not Kool-Aid.
Won Forbes's 2012-ish jargon tournament by beating [[see:leverage]] in the final; the hosts find its persistence, given its very dark reference, brutal.
A sign wording that pedants criticise but that is grammatical, because [[see:slow]] is a [[see:flat adverb]].
A [[see:Kama Sutra]] position that Jess calls pretty standard.
One of Britain's many words for rain.
Created by rebracketing [[from:android]].
A one-humped camel known for its speed, related through Greek dromos, a running, to [[same-root:palindrome]].

One of the weather words that has barely changed since Old English.

The American word for a pharmacy, which Rob teasingly calls moronic.

Recorded as early as 1848 in Indiana; Jess thinks it's simply fanciful.

Another simile from the poem that gave [[see:cool as a cucumber]].
Appalachian expression Jess prefers over [[see:drunk as a lord]], mainly because it rhymes.
Frequent 1800s US expression, after fictional [[from:Cooter Brown]], who supposedly stayed drunk to avoid being drafted by either side in the Civil War.

Someone who drinks too much, an example of [[from:-ard]].
An example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] suffix.
Someone who drinks too much, an example of [[see:-ard]].
Words for being drunk, the subject of a Rob newsletter; [[see:Michael McIntyre]] joked that English speakers can turn almost any word into one.
From the [[see:Book of St Albans]], evoking cobblers drinking together and making [[see:shoddy]] shoes.
From would rathers, as in to have one's druthers, common in the American South; a born fossil.

A wood nymph or nymph of the trees, from the same root as [[same-root:tree]].

One of the French titles that came in with the Norman nobility.

New Zealand city known for rugby, another rendering of the old name for Edinburgh, [[from:Din Eidyn]].

German for [[equivalent:unicorn]], literally one horn.

Welsh for gorse, a rough bush, similar to the probable source of the Edin- in [[gave?:Edinburgh]].
Sounds like [[see:jactitation]]; it now has an almost solely crude meaning but used to mean simply to exclaim.

Means pertaining to amber, from Greek [[from:elektron]], because early static electricity experiments rubbed wool on [[see:amber]].

The adverb form of electroencephalograph, a device that records brain waves.
A real word in the same dictionary, given as a contrast to the fake [[see:esquivalience]].
A naturally occurring gold-silver alloy named for its colour after amber, Greek [[from:elektron]], as covered in an earlier episode.

An example of a Latin-derived -tion noun adopted directly from French, with the verb made later.
The American word for a British [[equivalent:lift]]; Rob mocks it for having four syllables.
From the 1600s, a person or muscle that lifts things, as in elevator muscles; extended in the late 1700s to machines such as grain elevators.
