A very old word with relatives such as Dutch [[same-root:oog]], German [[same-root:Auge]] and Latin [[same-root:oculus]]; its root also appears in [[same-root:synopsis]] and [[same-root:myopic]].
An old name for the [[see:dragonfly]].
Anglo-Saxon for window, literally an eye hole to glance through, used before English took the Danish-derived [[see:window]].
The Icelandic volcano that baffled newscasters; its name breaks down into island, mountain (related to [[same-root:fell]]) and glacier, and its double L sounds like T.
Present in the archaic [[see:Greek alphabet]] but later dropped by the Greeks as unnecessary, though it survived in the Roman alphabet.
Descends from the same ancient forked letter as [[same-root:U]], [[same-root:V]], [[same-root:W]] and [[same-root:Y]], with the fork leaned over.
A ballad filler implying something else happened, comparable to the earlier nonsense use of [[see:dildo]].
Loosely related to [[same-root:hacienda]] through the Latin word for making and doing.
Previously discussed; it no longer has to involve a fable, showing why etymology can't dictate meaning, as with [[see:decimate]].
In the same group as [[see:ludicrous]], because it is related to the word [[from:fable]].
Like [[same-root:face]], it means the part that can be seen, here of a building.
The face is named as the part that faces someone, the thing people see, a logic shared by [[equivalent:visage]] and [[equivalent:Gesicht]].
Means the thing opposite or facing you, which is why a watch or clock has a face.
Possibly from a military trial where the accused soldier faced the drum squad as charges were read out; one theory, but a good one.
Latin for to make or to do, related to [[same-root:fiat]] and discussed before; it gives French [[gave:faire]] and Italian [[gave:fare (Italian)]].
Something fact-shaped that is not a fact, a parallel to [[see:asteroid]].
Often taken as a cute little fact but meant as something not quite a fact, another -oid example alongside [[see:opioid]].
Mandarin name for France: a sound similar to France plus [[see:guó]].
German verb for going by some means of transport, as opposed to [[see:gehen]], on foot; English [[same-root:fare]] has the same element.
Named after [[from:Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit]].
German for a journey or way, from the verb [[from:fahren]], to go or drive; Jess's family joked about 'Fahrt, Germany' on exit signs.
Said of people who succeed despite failing, offered by Rob as a parallel to [[see:glida in på en räkmacka]].
The noise of the fair helped make sense of [[unrelated:fanfare]] as a loud celebratory sound, though the two are not related.
French verb that comes from [[from:facere]].
A cute former name for the [[see:foxglove]].
An even cuter former name for the [[see:foxglove]].
Refers to blades, meaning its claws.
Also named after hookiness, like [[see:griffin]].
The US name for the season, suggesting decay and dying; like [[see:autumn]], unusual among Germanic languages, which mostly called it [[see:harvest]].
Compared with [[see:autumn]] as a word kept in American English, which feeds the myth that Americans sound like Shakespeare.
Somebody who takes the fall for a crime, another word for a [[equivalent:patsy]].
A [[see:false friend]] whose resemblance is coincidental because the words come from completely different sources.
A word in another language that looks or sounds like one you know but means something else; some are also [[see:false cognate]]s, many are true [[see:cognate]]s.
A word that looks like one in another language but means something different, like [[see:empathy]] and modern Greek [[see:empatheia]].
Shakespeare character to whom Jess suspects most of the single-phrase insults belong, given his huge insult-filled rants in the history plays.
The character behind many of the most famous insults, launched at others in the history plays.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] for Kermit the Frog, one of [[see:Gonzo (Muppet)]]'s friends.
One of the English words [[unrelated:fanfare]] was conflated with, though it has nothing to do with them.
Rob's example of [[see:tmesis]], which he thought a bit near the knuckle.
Probably from imitative Arabic farfar, chatterer, via Italian and Spanish words for a braggart; a boastful sound, later rationalised as [[see:fan]] plus [[see:fair]].
Means the backside in America but the female genitals in Britain; most likely from the novel [[from?:Fanny Hill]], though an earlier source is possible.
From [[from:Fanny Hill]]; in Britain a fairly rude word for female genitals, in the US a milder word for the backside, and also a nickname for Frances.
Means the front in Britain, where it is mild, but the back in America; probably a name euphemism like [[see:Johnson]].
A 1748 novel, also called Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure, named after a person; an early work of literary pornography that prompted obscenity debates and laws.
A 1748 novel, Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure, among the first novel-length English pornography, now public domain; its heroine gave us [[gave:fanny]].
Polari for perfect, as in 'absolutely fantabulosa'.
Swedish for your father's brother, almost a portmanteau; English can't distinguish paternal from maternal uncles.
From Latin [[from:farcire]], to stuff, like French [[same-root:farci]]: first a silly interlude stuffed between serious plays, now comedy of escalating chaos and misunderstandings.
From French for 'to stuff', because farces were comic relief stuffed into serious productions to pad them out, such as during set changes.
The French word for a dish with something stuffed inside, still the French word for stuffing, related to [[same-root:farce]].
Dialect way of saying farthing, rhymed by [[see:Covent Garden]].
As in how do you fare, an English survival of the element in German [[same-root:fahren]]; also in [[see:farewell]].
Italian verb that comes from [[from:facere]].
Contains [[see:fare]], one answer to a question raised a few episodes ago.
Bow-tie pasta, whose name is Italian for butterflies.
A Latin-derived name for an ironworker, named after iron, who mostly made horseshoes because they were in such demand; also covered in the periodic table episode.
From the Arabic name for [[from:Pars]], since Arabic has no P sound; Farsi and [[same-root:Persian]] are the same language and essentially the same word.
Very old; found in an old Middle English translation of Aristotle describing farting by the [[see:fundament]], and possibly in [[see:partridge]].
A valet or footman, so called because they walk behind their master or mistress.
An example of a [[see:compound insult]] formed by matching fart with words like muffin, goblin, waffle or nugget.
An IKEA workbench whose name, meaning speedy, sounds unfortunate in English.
The smallest pre-decimal British denomination, two to a [[see:ha'penny]]; in Middle English sometimes called a [[see:quarter]].
A very wide hooped Elizabethan skirt; a folk etymology of French [[from:vertugade]], from Spanish [[from:verdugado]], rod or sapling; unrelated to [[unrelated:farthing]] or [[unrelated:gale]].
From Latin [[from:fascinare]], to bewitch; once witches' power to enthral, positive since the 1800s; likely related to [[from?:fascinum]].
From Latin for bewitch, first used of witches' power to enthral; the positive sense came in the early 1800s. Probably related to [[same-root?:fascinum]].
The divine phallus symbolising the god [[see:Fascinus]]; Roman penis effigies, some winged, invoked his protection; probably behind [[gave?:fascinate]].
The divine phallus, a winged symbol on Roman amulets invoking the protection of the god [[see:Fascinus]].
Roman god symbolised by the [[see:fascinum]].
The phallic god whose protection the [[see:fascinum]] amulets invoked.
Existed before Shakespeare, but his works have the first known use in today's sense.
Means both swift and firmly attached, from an Old English sense of vigorous or strong; [[see:Anglish]] uses it for castle.
Another [[see:flat adverb]], as in 'drive fast'.
Can mean tight or stuck; the speedy sense comes from sticking to an intense pace, a contronym Rob covered in a video; compare German [[see:fast (German)]].
German for almost, so a German who has done something fast hasn't done it.
English equivalent of [[equivalent:attache ta tuque]], warning of something dramatic ahead.
Quebec French for preparing for something dramatic or exciting, like [[equivalent:fasten your seat belt]]; a [[see:toque]] here is a winter hat.
Swedish for your father's sister, paired with [[see:farbror]].
Roman calendar lists of official and religious events, where [[see:dies mali]] were recorded; Jess relishes the fasti of [[see:Furius Dionysius Filocalus]].
Cantonese for to show or exhibit, unrelated to the other words spelled fat.
In Albanian and Catalan, luck, chance, fate or destiny, related to [[same-root:fate]].
In Norwegian and Swedish a plate, saucer or barrel, related to English [[same-root:vat]].
Related to the Albanian and Catalan [[same-root:fat (Catalan)]], luck or destiny.
One of the Germanic words for close family; combined with French in [[see:grandfather]].
Probably went through the same D-to-TH change as [[see:weather]].
The same word as Latin [[same-root:pater]], with P to F and T to TH under [[see:Grimm's law]], showing English is Germanic.
The traditional English name for the Christmas gift-giver, preferred by some over the Americanism [[see:Santa Claus]]; compare French [[equivalent:Père Noël]].
Russian gift-giver resembling Father Christmas who brings presents on New Year's Eve rather than at Christmas.
Applied to animal life by [[see:Carl Linnaeus]]; from Fauna, a Roman fertility goddess linked to [[see:Faunus]].
Roman forest god connected to the goddess behind [[see:fauna]]; his Greek counterpart is [[see:Pan]].
Its similarity to [[see:Johann Fust]]'s name fed superstitions that printing was devilish.
Landmark case over a radio broadcast of [[see:seven words you can never say on television]], which found it indecent but not obscene, so it could air outside safe-harbor hours.
A French word for a meal, sharing a source with [[same-root:fete]] and [[same-root:festival]].
Arabic term for Christmas, the Christian celebration of Jesus's birth, alongside Islam's [[see:Eid al-Fitr]] and [[see:Eid al-Adha]].
From customs of wearing feathers as marks of achievement; a 1599 account says Hungarians wore one feather for each Turk they had killed.
Once existed, meaning effective or efficacious, quoted from 1568: the lost opposite of [[see:feckless]].
Means useless; feck is essentially the same word as [[same-root:effect]], having split off from it.
US slang for federal agencies like the FBI and DEA; in Britain, which has no federal police, it is only used ironically or pretentiously.
A Scottish dialect word for gross, icky rainy weather that sounds like what it means.
A Scottish word for a type of rain, which Rob thinks generally means gross.
Trucker slang for paying a [[see:bear bite]], or ticket.
Dutch for something so obvious you could feel it through wooden shoes, like [[equivalent:sticks out like a sore thumb]].
Origin somewhat unknown, possibly related to Latin [[same-root?:pollex]] and Russian [[same-root?:palec]]; originally literal touching, later sensing in the mind.
Feeling successful or confident; only dated to the 1950s, though 'ten-foot' meant very big much earlier, as in [[see:ten-foot coal]].
From Middle English [[from:fisting cur]], farting dog; it described vivacious little dogs, reportedly after ladies blamed their farts on their lapdogs.
Comes from Latin [[from:felis]].
The classical Latin word for cat, which gave [[gave:feline]], older than [[see:cattus]].
A common cat name meaning happy or lucky, popular thanks to [[see:Felix the Cat]] and its resemblance to Latin [[see:felis]].
The cartoon cat mostly responsible for the popularity of [[see:Felix]] as a cat name.
English word for a mountain, related to the 'fjalla' (mountain) element of [[same-root:Eyjafjallajökull]].
A semi-fossil word meaning wicked or cruel, related to [[same-root:felon]], surviving in [[see:one fell swoop]] and [[see:fell beast]].
Means cruel, vicious or fierce, as in [[see:fell beast]]; related to [[same-root:felon]], unrelated to the past tense of [[unrelated:fall]].
A hill; it has a Scandinavian ring and is an element of [[see:Scafell Pike]].
A particularly wicked or cruel beast, using the same [[see:fell]].
Uses the same [[see:fell]], meaning cruel or fierce, as one fell swoop.
Felling a tree, related to fall, may have caused folk-etymological overlap with [[see:fell]].
Middle English term for sex; the suffix -red was an alternative to -ship, so it amounts to [[see:fellowship]].
What [[see:fellowred]] amounts to, since -red could be used instead of -ship.
From Latin [[from:fello]], evildoer, of unclear origin: maybe Frankish for scourger, Latin for poison, or Latin [[from?:fellare]], to suck, as a joke; also once a boil.
Related to [[same-root:fell]], meaning cruel or fierce.
An Old English word for marsh.
Old word for enmity, discussed in an earlier episode, another example of [[see:-ship]].
Related to the first part of [[same-root:ferocity]], [[same-root:ferus]], wild.
A Roman festival honouring the spirits of the dead, one of the Roman traditions that fed into [[see:Halloween]].
Founder of structural linguistics, the target of the pun 'now I'm not so sure' in Joshua's favourite linguist joke.
The German word for a [[equivalent:telephone]], at least in the past, meaning far speaker.
A yearning to travel and be far away; the flip side of [[see:Heimweh]].
Combines Latin [[from:ferus]], wild (related to [[same-root:feral]]), with a looking element, so ferocious means wild-looking.
Ultimately from a word meaning robber, taken from French [[from:furet]], which Rob links to [[see?:fuir]], to flee.
Term for the penis in the 1500s, often paired with [[see:coney]] for the vulva, as in a ferret hunting rabbits in a warren.
Meant sending your hunting [[see:ferret]] after an animal, since ferrets were domesticated to chase rabbits from warrens.
Jess's surname, which sounds like Latin for iron and Arabic for knight, but really comes from a Scottish name meaning strong or loyal man.
A lover of iron horses, meaning a rail enthusiast, possibly one who likes older trains in particular.
Describes something made of iron, from Latin [[from:ferrum]]; punned on Jess's surname [[see:Ferris]].
Example of Americans reducing the ending of -ile words.
Alternative to [[see:business of ferrets]], arising because business in the [[see:Book of St Albans]] looks spelled this way in early print.
Shares its ultimate French source with [[same-root:fete]] and [[same-root:feast]].
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used for advent calendars.
A ghost word from a misreading, through bad handwriting, of 'business' in [[from:business of ferrets]].
Ultimately from the same French source as [[same-root:feast]] and [[same-root:festival]].
From a Portuguese word for charm, sorcery or allurement; still an object thought to have supernatural power. The sexual sense came in the 1800s, largely through [[see:Havelock Ellis]].
German hip-hop band named after a fan's praise; fett meant great and Brot was slang for hash, so 'really good hash'.

term: few cards short of a deck

mentions.note: English equivalent of [[equivalent:all the Moomins are not in the valley]].
Traditionally used for countable things, or under the Chicago rule for plurals; [[see:less]] in its place has been recorded since the 1500s.
Means fewer in number, unlike [[see:less bad people]]; a Guardian style guide example of where the [[see:fewer]] distinction matters.
Fiat currency is money sanctioned by, say, a central bank; from Latin for let it be done, related to [[same-root:facere]].
DuPont's working name for the fibre while developing it, before it became [[gave:nylon]].
The German word for the act, which would connect to [[same-root:fuck]] if fuck comes from a Germanic source describing rapid movement.
A Germanic word whose cognates are thought to share a root with [[same-root:violin]] and [[same-root:viola]]; the hosts trade jokes about how a fiddle differs from a violin.
Compared with [[same-root:Fido]].
Related to the dog name [[same-root:Fido]].
A classic dog name meaning faithful or trustworthy, related to [[same-root:fidelity]].
Classic dog name from Latin [[from:fidus]], faithful, related to [[same-root:fidelity]]; a famous 1940s Italian Fido waited daily for his dead owner and has a statue.
A top British rank, though marshal comes via French from a Frankish word for horse servant, so Rob ranks it lowest.
Code word in the alphabet proposed by the ICAO South American Regional Office.
Aviation pronunciation of five, because five sounds too much like 'fire', also why countdowns often skip five.
Means shape, so a figment of your imagination is a shape it takes; sometimes eggcorned as [[see:pigment of the imagination]].
From Latin, literally something invented, formed or fashioned, close to modern [[see:invention]]; in English it also came to mean myths and falsehoods, hence figments of imagination.
Jane Austen's novels contain jokes about people misusing figuratively and [[see:literally]].
An old name for a thief.
A thickener made from the sassafras tree and contributed by the Choctaw; filé is a French term related to [[same-root:filament]], meaning ropy or threadlike.
Hanging precariously, as if by a thread, from filament plus pendulous; homework for listeners.
A joke in the Philippines that Filipino time means being late; compare [[equivalent:Indian Standard Time]].
Paired with [[see:full]] as a vowel-change parallel to [[see:pride]] and [[see:proud]].
The usual British word, as old as English itself: Old English [[from:filmen]] meant a membrane or tissue, and specifically the foreskin.
From Latin for end, like [[same-root:finite]]; originally a payment that settled a debt, from finalizing accounts.
A plainer way of saying [[equivalent:possession is nine-tenths of the law]].
Johnson called it an unnecessary word creeping into the language, as he disliked French borrowings.
Thought to come from an ancient root meaning five, the same root as the pent- in [[same-root:Pentagon]].
The original name for the [[see:date (fruit)]].
A former English name for the [[see:foxglove]].
An American alternative name for a [[see:tea towel]].
McWhorter's term for casual online writing, which works like barstool speech, so swearing thrives there.
An old word for a midwife, also a nickname for a pickpocket.
Shares the Latin root for end with [[same-root:finance]].

[[see:James Joyce]]'s work, which contains several ridiculously long words, including the thunderclap word [[see:bababadalgharaghtakamminarronnkonnbronntonnerronntuonnthunntrovarrhounawnskawntoohoohoordenenthurnuk]].
An example of dropping -land from a country named after a tribe.
Not from looking furry: a Norse name for an oak, transferred to other mountain trees.
Sounds the same as [[see:fur]] in American English, an example of vowels merging before R.
A cousin of the [[see:silverfish]] that likes hot places like bakeries and boilers; brat meant a young or mischievous animal.
Anglo-Saxon predecessor of [[see:dragon]], borrowed directly from Roman Latin before the Normans brought the French word.
The front wall of a cockpit protecting the pilot from engine fire, the wall in [[see:balls to the wall]].
The fire-resistant bulkhead between the engine and the pilot, the wall of [[see:balls to the wall]].
Victorian term; to firkytoodle meant to mess about or take liberties. Jess likes it.
Collection of 36 of Shakespeare's plays compiled by friends from sources like actors' copies; no plays in his own hand survive.
Covers a vast array of animals; Old English fisc, sharing an ancient root with Latin piscis and [[same-root:Pisces]], and found across Indo-European languages.
An ancient Indo-European word, cognate with Latin [[same-root:piscis]], once meaning any sea creature; masculine in Old English, so its plural was fishes until relatively recently.
The Old English plural was fishes; using fish as its own plural is a Middle English invention.
When the body cannot break down a compound found in some foods, making you smell of fish.
Stealing, with your five fingers as the discount card.
Slang for police from the 1960s show [[from:Hawaii Five-O]].
An obvious modern borrowing from Norwegian.
Red and white bars with the [[see:George Cross]] in the top corner, not the [[see:Maltese cross]].
From French flacon, a precedent for a C softening to G, as in [[see:sugar]].
Short for German [[from:Fliegerabwehrkanone]], aircraft defence cannon; entered English in 1938 for an anti-aircraft gun, and by the 1940s meant the exploding fire itself.
A German military acronym for [[from:Fliegerabwehrkanone]], anti-aircraft cannon; extended in WWII to the exploding shells, and now to any criticism.
The French name specifies the colour, like English [[equivalent:pink flamingo]].
Surprisingly old; the hosts link it to [[same-root:flamboyant]] and [[same-root:flamingo]], both meaning flaming.
One of the collective nouns in the Book of St Albans alongside [[see:murder of crows]].
Via French flamboyant, flaming or wavy, a 15th-century architectural style with flame-like curves; shares a root with [[same-root:flamingo]].
Spanish for gypsy and the name of the gypsy dance, named after [[from:Flanders]] because it seemed far away and mysterious.
Also meant a person from Flanders, equivalent to [[same-root:Flemish]]; perhaps because Spaniards conflated Flemish and Romani people or used Flemish for any foreigner.
Online harassment resulting in aggressive behaviour, the subject of the [[see:Usenet]] group where [[see:troll]] posted about flames and counterflames.
Means flame-coloured bird, when pink counted as a shade of red; shares a root with [[same-root:flamboyant]].
Means flame-coloured in Spanish and Portuguese, from [[from:flamma]], flame; it's unclear whether it's related to [[same-root?:flamenco]].
Shortened from [[from:inflammable]] for clarity, presumably during the Industrial Revolution when goods were being labelled.
From girls' braids called [[from:flaps]]; once slang for young prostitutes, it became a fashion word from 1895, later used against women wanting the vote, then reclaimed.
Late 1800s word for the braids or ponytails of young girls, unlike women's updos, and the origin of [[gave:flapper]].
The parts that change the wing's shape and surface area, and so its lift, mentioned alongside [[see:aileron]]s.
CIA glossary term for the tradecraft of secretly opening, reading and resealing envelopes or packages without the recipient knowing.
Early slang of Australia's convict community, recorded by [[see:James Hardy Vaux]].
British for an [[equivalent:apartment]]; from Old English [[from:flet]], a dwelling, especially on the ground floor, with a Proto-Indo-European root suggesting an area spread out.
An adjective used as an adverb, like [[see:slow]] or [[see:close]]; these are legitimate English and were once more common, as in 'violent hot' and 'horrid angry'.
Patrolling police, perhaps because walking flattens their feet or because they are bumbling and clumsy.
Someone from Illinois, named for how flat the state is.
An example of the Latin ending meaning full of, also seen in [[see:cromulent]].
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.
A rival drink that Kraft says, rather than [[see:Kool-Aid]], was used at Jonestown.
A schoolmaster, probably a play on [[see:phlebotomist]], suggesting indecency like [[see:bum brusher]].
Describes very fine spotty patterns on horses and dogs, and once discolourations on human skin; linked to the flea-bite sense of [[see:puce]].
[[see:George Puttenham]]'s English name for [[equivalent:mycterismus]].
A London street once full of print houses and newspaper offices, the hub of British print journalism within Rob's lifetime.
The equivalent of [[same-root:flamenco]], which once also meant a person from Flanders, a place Spain controlled.
Crayola colour shortened from [[from:Flesh Tint]] in 1949, briefly [[see:Pink Beige]], then renamed [[gave:Peach]] in 1962.
An old contemptuous term for a doctor, alongside [[see:leecher]].
What meat in today's sense was called when [[see:meat]] meant any food, much like the German and Dutch words for meat meaning flesh.
Old term for what we now call [[see:meat]].
A grim 17th-century term for a surgeon.
Crayola name from 1903 to 1949 for a white skin colour, later shortened to [[gave:Flesh]].
The excitement of a successful beginning, from being fleshed; Rob thinks it sounds like something zombies do.
The old word for a [[see:butcher]] before English took that word from French.
An old word for a butcher, discussed on an earlier episode, in line with [[see:flesh meat]].
Lost English word for a [[see:butcher]], replaced after the Norman Conquest.
French word for river alongside [[see:rivière]]; Rob thinks one is bigger than the other.
Rob's grandma went to the flicks; flick is still heard and survives in [[see:Netflix]].
Another name sometimes given to [[see:printer's devil]]s, the little urchins doing the drudge work.

term: flies don't enter a closed mouth

mentions.note: Spanish advice to keep your mouth shut to stay out of trouble.
A reduplicative word for irritation, depression or bad temper from the [[see:dictionary of reduplicative words]].
Like [[see:flip your wig]], probably from the 1940s or later.
Related to [[see:flip your wig]], since lid is also a word for hat.
Being so angry you dislodge or throw down your wig; relatively recent, probably 1940s, like [[see:flip out]]; related to [[see:flip your lid]].
German for a pinball machine, with a whole park near Berlin devoted to them; Rob finds it more pertinent than [[see:pinball]].
Johnson defined it as a pert young hussy.
A relationship of flirting that goes no further.
An old word for a bat, preferred by the hosts to [[equivalent:chauve-souris]].
The act of estimating something as worthless; an Eton coinage stringing together Latin words for trifles from William Lily's grammar, such as [[from:floccus]] (lock of wool) and [[from:nihil]].
A made-up word meaning to esteem something as worthless, built from a pile of terms meaning nothing, including the nihil of [[same-root:nihilism]].
Used for sheep, goats, birds and Christians; Old English flocc, perhaps from Old Norse [[from?:flokkr]] brought by the Vikings.
A modern Scandinavian borrowing for ice.
Viking who tried unsuccessfully to settle there and named [[see:Iceland]] after seeing its ice.
One of the British words for [[see:drunk]].
From Flora, Roman goddess of flowers celebrated at [[see:Floralia]]; paired with [[see:fauna]] by [[see:Carl Linnaeus]].
Journalistic jargon for flowers, which Rob particularly hates; journalists have their own jargon but resist the corporate kind.
Festival of the goddess Flora, behind [[see:flora]].
Became a woman's name after [[see:Florence Nightingale]], named for the city; Rob's French wife finds it strange, since in French Florence is a man's name.
Named after the city where she was born, she popularised [[see:Florence]]; the lady of the lamp worked in Derbyshire, whose hospital bears her name.
From Latin [[from:florem]], meaning strikingly beautiful, though Jess thinks it sounds worse because it rhymes with livid and horrid.
From Spanish for flowery, either for its many flowers or because the Spanish landed around [[from?:Pascua Florida]].
Britain's suggestion for the [[see:euro]], since many European cultures have had one; in pre-decimal Britain it was worth two [[see:shilling]]s.
Originally the same word as [[same-root:flower]], only splitting about 200 years later; sifted meal was the 'flower', or finest part, of the grain.
Medieval phrase for cream, the best part of the milk that floats on top, using the 'finest part' sense of [[see:flower]].
One of the Latin-derived 'flo' words related to [[same-root:flower]].
Borrowed from French, ultimately from Latin [[from:florem]], suggesting something at its best; originally the same word as [[same-root:flour]] and from the same root as [[same-root:bloom]].
German for a refugee, someone who is fleeing, an example of the Germanic [[see:-ling]] suffix.
From the Latin for to flow, which the hosts link to [[see:phloem]].
A rarely used phrase showing that [[see:aback]] isn't quite a fossil word.
Named because it flows; it was used as a [[see:flux]] in smelting to remove impurities and make metals more fluid.
One of Jess's favourite terms for drunk.
Its root means to flow, implying agitated water.
A playful coinage combining [[from:fluster]] and [[from:frustrate]].
A charming but false claim that [[see:butterfly]] is its spoonerism.
Wrongly claimed to be the source of [[see:butterfly]]; it has only been used in the past couple of centuries.
Popularly but wrongly thought to be the source of [[see:butterfly]].
A Latin word for the river water itself, unlike the bank word behind [[see:river]].
Also meaning flow, a smelting substance; explains [[see:fluorine]].
Rob's word for the [[see:zipper]] on trousers, which Jess finds an odd choice.
Used by both hosts for a trouser opening; they don't know why and ask viewers to explain.
One of several Latvian phrases for daydreaming, similar to [[equivalent:have your head in the clouds]].
Covered in a recent episode: it comes from poor-quality homemade axes, probably from the American Civil War, whose heads would fly off.
The day in Britain when flying ants seem to climb to the tips of grass blades and all take off at once.

term: flying by the seat of your pants

The Old Norse word for [[equivalent:shark]], related to the Dutch [[same-root:haai]] and the German [[same-root:Hai]].
Scandinavian king, to all intents and purposes a Viking, defeated by [[see:Harold Godwinson]] in 1066.
Once neutral: someone sent ahead to arrange lodging, or an innkeeper; from a French verb meaning to provide lodging, related to [[same-root:harbor]] and [[same-root:auberge]].
Contrasted with a [[see:port]], which is an entry point, while a harbour is where you actually stop.
Related to the French lodging word behind [[same-root:harbinger]].
Related to the havn in [[see:Copenhagen]].
Believed to be linked to [[same-root?:haven]]; both mean a place of shelter.
One of the many baseball idioms Jess lists as common in American everyday language.
Brand name from the first syllables of [[from:Hans Riegel]], its founder, and Bonn, where he founded it.
A Bergamese manservant of commedia dell'arte, invisible to [[see:Pantalone]] and so free for mischief; the name also covers his patterned costume and now suggests a jester.
Looks as if it is wearing a little harlequin costume.
A comic stage form based on commedia dell'arte figures, closely tied to British [[see:pantomime]], in which [[see:Harlequin]] gets a magic wand and drives chases and transformations.
A word for someone with a lot of sexual experience, unlike the missing word for a non-[[see:virgin]].
Johnson's description of a [[see:lexicographer]], which lexicographers today happily use for themselves.
Means army commander; its ending means strong, as in [[same-root:Ronald]], [[same-root:Gerald]] and [[same-root:Arnold]].
Anglo-Saxon king of England in 1066 who defeated [[see:Harald Hardrada]] in the north before heading south to fight [[see:William the Conqueror]].
Australian prime minister who vanished, presumed drowned, while swimming off Victoria in 1967, inspiring [[gave:do a Harold Holt]].
An Old English word whose root was adopted into Latin and Italian, giving [[gave:harpsichord]] and ultimately [[gave:arpeggio]].
Given as an English [[see:hybrid word]].
Its first element comes from the Germanic word [[from:harp]], one of the few Germanic terms in the episode.
The full Italian name that was shortened to [[gave:pianoforte]].
One of many insulting words for women, defined by Johnson as a decayed strumpet.
Often credited with sayings about freedom she never said; she was not known for being verbose.
A multi-toothed farm tool dragged over soil; Hamlet's 'harrow up thy soul' first used it figuratively, which gives today's harrowing.

term: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

mentions.note: Retitled the Sorcerer's Stone in America, apparently because publishers doubted children knew what a [[see:philosopher's stone]] was.
The first Harry Potter book's title was changed for Americans, a transatlantic difference the hosts have covered before.
A two-game series that brought rugby-style handling into US colleges and helped set [[see:gridiron football]] apart from association and rugby football.
What English called the season before [[see:fall]] and [[see:autumn]], as many other Germanic languages still do.
Rob's name for the wingless long-legged arachnid others call [[equivalent:daddy longlegs]].
Another name for the # symbol, which Americans call a [[see:pound sign]] and many now call a [[see:hashtag]].
Not the source of [[see:assassin]], but it influenced the English form of that word.
Derogatory name a Fatimid caliph gave the Nizaris; Europeans wrongly claimed they took hashish before killing, giving [[gave:assassin]].
Now a common name for the # symbol, though Rob insists it's only a hashtag when followed by a word, a tag with a [[see:hash]].
An old word for a liar that Jess doesn't fully understand yet; she learned it from the card game League of the Lexicon.
One of Jess's favourite Shakespearean insults.
A neck protector, from Old Frankish.
Originally meant to frequent, as in Middle English 'haunt school', a sense surviving in 'your usual haunt'.
An insult once used to describe [[see:Jacob Rees-Mogg]], which the hosts call fabulous.
French haut, high, plus bois, wood, for a high-pitched wooden instrument; the source of [[gave:oboe]] and [[gave:hautboy]].
French for high wood, or high-pitched wood; source of [[gave:hautboy]], [[gave:hoboy]] and [[gave:oboe]].
Named for its high register among woodwinds; it gave English hautboy and, via Italian, [[gave:oboe]].
The older English name for the [[see:oboe]], an anglicised rendering of French [[from:hautbois]].
The original English word for the [[see:oboe]], an English attempt at French [[from:hautbois]], discussed in a past episode.
Rob's British phrasing, as opposed to [[equivalent:take a bath]].
British phrasing, while Americans say [[equivalent:take a shower]].
An old swing idiom meaning to have freedom of action, scope or licence.

term: have one's tongue in one's pocket
original: avoir la langue dans sa poche
translation: have one's tongue in one's pocket

mentions.note: Quebec French for someone shy or silent, less mocking than [[see:cat's got your tongue]].
To have worked someone out, knowing them so well you'd know their phone number.
An old swing idiom meaning to exert physical and social power over something; to Jess it suggests a swinging bell.

term: have your bread buttered on both sides

mentions.note: To benefit from two conflicting parties at once, the opposite of [[see:there will be no butter cleave on my bread]].

term: have your head in the clouds

mentions.note: The English equivalent of [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].
Wrote many problematic books about sex and largely brought the sexual sense into [[see:fetish]] in the 1800s.
Cognate of the havn in [[see:Copenhagen]], once meaning a port or harbour.
From Old Norse, probably related to [[same-root?:harbor]], a sheltered place for a boat; the same word ends [[see:Copenhagen]].
Originally a bag for oats, like a horse's oat bag; German Hafer is oat, as in [[same-root:Hafermilch]].
Cockney rhyming slang from Barney Rubble, rhyming with trouble; the hosts note it must be modern because it uses an American TV character.
British phrase that baffles Jess; it means having a shockingly bad day or week, an exaggeration unlike typical British understatement.

term: having your work cut out for you

mentions.note: From 16th–17th century tailoring: assistants cut out the pieces, leaving the master the real work of assembling and stitching.
Originally an Anglo-French war cry ordering soldiers to pillage, hence Mark Antony's "Cry havoc" in [[see:William Shakespeare]]'s Julius Caesar.
Means to grasp.
Also named after hookiness, like [[see:griffin]].
Paired with [[see:hock]] as an example of the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Another proposed source of [[see:hocus pocus]], which the hosts call gibberish.
The Armenian name for Armenia.
Cheap springy wire for binding hay bales, used for makeshift repairs; going haywire comes via the [[from:haywire outfit]].
Probably from logging: a poorly equipped operation held together as if with haywire, linking the wire to modern [[gave:haywire]].
A medieval dice game named via French hasard, luck, from Arabic for a single [[see:die (dice)]]; its H is an overcorrection and its D comes from [[see:-ard]].
From Arabic [[from:al-zahr]], the die, via French; first a dice game, then a risk, and the pronounced H is an overcorrection.
For eyes, originally red-brown, now more green-brown, after hazelnuts; [[see:Mercutio]] says [[see:Benvolio]] would quarrel with someone cracking nuts because he has hazel eyes.

term: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket

mentions.note: Welsh for someone stingy with money, who avoids reaching into a pocket where a hedgehog would prick them.

term: he that lies down with dogs shall rise up with fleas

mentions.note: A [[see:Benjamin Franklin]] aphorism about the company you keep.
Once [[see:witch]] became associated with women, male witches were called he witches, which shows when the shift happened.
From Old English heafod and related to Latin [[same-root:caput]] through a regular H/K consonant shift, so it is a cousin of [[same-root:capital]] and [[same-root:captain]].
A friend's job title; head of execution sounds like a beheader, and executing a strategy could also imply cutting it off.
Compared with the old idiom [[equivalent:tit over thumb]].
Middle English headling, from [[from:-ling]], originally meaning headfirst.
Jess says [[see:ay up]] evokes [[see:what's up]] or heads up.
Someone's picture; the spelling [[see:hed]] avoids confusion with it.

term: headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile

mentions.note: [[see:Mrs Malaprop]]'s malapropism, using allegory for alligator.
What the Anglo-Saxons called an [[see:archbishop]] before they used the Latin-derived arch- form.
Paired with [[see:hale]] as a vowel-change parallel to [[see:pride]] and [[see:proud]].
In Old English also the seat of soul, will, courage and intellect; through the C/H shift related to [[same-root:cardio]], [[same-root:courage]] and [[same-root:credible]].
The plain Old English word, contrasted with the weightier Latinate [[see:cardiovascular system]] used to be taken seriously in medicine.
Used when your courage fails, echoing the stomach-dropping feeling of fear.
Where the heart is supposed to be, the hosts joke, among all the idioms that move it around the body.
One of many idioms that move the heart around the body, since the heart was seen as the seat of life, mind, will and courage.
Used when fear rises and the heart climbs into your mouth, echoing what fear feels like physically.
Echoes the physical feeling of fear, when you can feel your heartbeat rising in your chest.
Another historical placement of the heart, which was treated as the seat of life, mind and will.
Describes the feeling of your whole body sinking, another idiom that moves the heart around.
In news writing, debates are always heated.
One of 552 synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]] listed in Farmer and Henley's slang dictionary.
The Old English word for sky, replaced by Norse [[see:sky]] but still used in other contexts.
The Anglo-Saxon word for the sky generally, replaced by Old Norse [[see:sky]]; not as closely linked to [[see:haven]] as it looks.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used for [[see:Darth Vader]].
A [[see:knobbly monster]] phrase used for [[see:Darth Vader]].
One of the many baseball idioms Jess lists as common in American everyday language.
British swimming pool signs saying no heavy petting meant no snogging, because in Britain you stroke a pet rather than [[see:pet]] it.
The German word for the midwife who visits new parents several times after a birth.
In [[see:A wounded deer leaps highest]], consumption, whose flush makes a cheek reddest where it hurts most.
Newsroom spelling of head(line): shorter for margins and avoids confusion with words like [[see:headshot]] or adding head to the text.
Looks like hedge plus hog, but possibly a folk etymology of Slavic words related to [[same-root?:urchin]] and [[same-root?:igil]].
The original land [[see:urchin]].
Originally called an [[see:urchin]].
Means pleasure; going further than [[see:Epicureanism]], its followers held that the only intrinsic good is pleasure, meaning positively enjoyable sensations, not just absence of pain.
A Germanic personal name containing a word for war; it basically means fighting a battle.
Means war struggle, or struggle struggle.
A reduplicative word for irritation, depression or bad temper from the [[see:dictionary of reduplicative words]].
The original name for the condition later rendered as [[gave:nostalgia]]; the flip side of [[see:Fernweh]].
From a [[from:Frankish]] root meaning hate.
Noun matching the verb [[same-root:hoist]], literally a lifting, like lifting something off someone.
Basically a noun form of [[from:hoist]]: lifting something big, a bigger theft, like thieves lifting things from pockets.
A variant of [[from:hoist]], to lift, with the same logic as [[see:lift]] meaning steal.
The noun related to the verb [[same-root:hoisting]], meaning to steal.
Greek for a hundred, related to [[same-root:hundred]].
Norse goddess of the underworld, spelled with one L, whose name gave [[gave:hell]].
Splits as helico- plus -pter from Greek [[from:helix]], spiral, and [[from:pteron]], wing, meaning spiral wing, but copter gets rebracketed onto other words.
Greek helico-, spiral, plus pter-, wing, wrongly rebracketed as -copter; coined by [[see:Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt]] and popularised by [[see:Jules Verne]].
Brought up to show that splitting [[see:Diplodocus]] into its parts for pronunciation would also change how we say helicopter.
Contains the same pter, wing, as [[same-root:Megaptera novaeangliae]].
Named after [[from:Helios]], Greek for the sun, because it was detected in the solar spectrum during an eclipse in 1868.
Named after sun god [[from:Helios]] because it was identified in the sun's corona before being obtained; assumed to be a metal, hence [[see:-ium]].
The only other English word from Germanic gods Rob found: the name of [[from:Hel]], Norse goddess of the underworld.
One of Farmer and Henley's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]].
Given with [[see:damn]] as traditional [[see:profanity]] that breaks religious rules but no longer shocks.
Where worn-out and broken type was thrown, for the [[see:printer's devil]] to sort through.
The Greek name for Greece, which is why English uses [[see:Hellenic]] for things Greek.
Jess thinks it also sounds like an insult: a hell bore.
English word for things Greek, related to [[same-root:Hellas]].
Became a standard greeting only in the 1870s with the telephone, proposed by [[see:Thomas Edison]]; it varies older hailing calls [[from:hallo]] and [[from:hollo]].
[[see:Thomas Edison]] persuaded telephone companies to recommend opening calls with hello; people did not say hello before the telephone.
The name for the telephone operators who connected calls, almost all young women, after the [[see:hello]] they said.
Name for US telephone operators, because [[from:hello]] became so closely tied to telephone conversations.
Another word using the -scape taken from [[from:landscape]].
The 1950 Guardian style guide demanded "help them to finish" instead, requiring the extra "to" of the infinitive.
Typeface named after the Latin name for Switzerland.
The group a true [[see:bug]] must belong to: piercing, sucking mouthparts, four wings thickened at the base, and [[see:incomplete metamorphosis]].
Names both poison hemlock, which [[see:Socrates]] drank, and an unrelated nonpoisonous evergreen; 'hem' probably means poison, so the tree is unfairly named.
Means flowing blood, from the root shared with [[same-root:rhythm]].
One of Britain's many regional words for rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
Another name for [[equivalent:maitake]]; grows on the ground and looks feathered, not to be confused with [[see:chicken of the woods]].
Literally one by means of two: two words joined by and to express one idea, like [[see:nice and warm]] for nicely warm.
A soldier the English sent in 1386 to infiltrate French noble households; executed in Paris, his interrogation exposed a large English spy network in France.
Scientist who proposed that [[see:foxglove]] was originally [[see:folk's glove]], which the hosts joke was an attempt to distance himself from the flower.
Reformer whose anti-monopoly single tax theory [[see:The Landlord's Game]] was designed to illustrate.
Man of Dutch descent whose family claimed he wrote [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]], citing the original Dutch reindeer names.
Welsh journalist who renamed Kinshasa [[see:Leopoldville]].
Journalist who coined [[see:abominable snowman]] and later apologised for the translation.
Used [[see:palindrome]] in 1638 essays, discussing a Latin palindrome he painted above a schoolhouse door in a town of rude people.
Founded the [[see:Church of England]] to break with Rome so that he could divorce [[see:Catherine of Aragon]].
Set up the [[see:Church of England]] because he wanted another divorce and the pope wouldn't allow it.
An obscure street name for [[see:cocaine]] that baffles the hosts.
Married one of his wives on the strength of a [[see:portrait miniature]] and was upset when she arrived.
One of Britain's many regional words for rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
Old English pronoun used where we now say [[see:their]].
One of the Old English words for [[see:deer]], today's hart; also the name of the hall [[see:Heorot (hall)]].
The hall in Beowulf, named for the stag ([[from:heorot]]) because royalty was associated with stags.
Goddess who cursed [[see:echo]] over suspicions about [[see:Zeus]]'s affairs with nymphs.
Overreacting as ever, she took away [[see:Lamia]]'s children.
A [[see:theophoric]] name beginning with the goddess [[see:Hera]]'s name.
From Old French without an H, spelled erbe in Middle English; Americans drop the H, a split the hosts attribute to transatlantic pro- and anti-French pettiness.
Its split US/UK pronunciation is compared with [[see:lieutenant]], reversed.
From the rhyming verse in the [[see:Book of St Albans]] instructing readers which group words to use.
Given as a familiar everyday collective noun.
Lost Old English word for an army, replaced by French [[see:army]]; preserved in [[see:Hereford]].
An example of the legal [[see:pronominal adverbs]].
The [[from:ford]] where an army crossed, from Old English [[from:here]].
A legal anaphoric adverb, compared with condensed journalistic phrases like [[see:crisis talks]].
Johnson defined it as private men's opinion differing from that of the Catholic and Orthodox church.
French word briefly borrowed for a hedgehog, a variation on [[same-root:oursin]]; also the spiked part of a turnstile.
French for hedgehog, spelled with an H; drop the H and it sounds much like [[same-root:oursin]], which is the same word.
Surprisingly the same name as [[same-root:Arminius]].
Used [[see:dingbat]] ornaments that became [[see:Zapf Dingbats]], and also created [[see:Optima]].
A falling-out-of-use word combining [[from:Hermes]] and [[from:Aphrodite]], named after their son [[from:Hermaphroditus]].
Son of [[see:Hermes]] and [[see:Aphrodite]], after whom [[gave:hermaphrodite]] is named.
God of science and art, part of [[gave:hermaphrodite]] and source of [[gave:hermetic]].
Greek god associated with the Roman Mercury, a very fast traveller, explaining [[see:mercury (quicksilver)]]'s name.
Called 'thrice blessed Hermes', said to have invented an airtight glass tube, explaining [[see:hermetic]] sealing.
From [[from:Hermes]]; first about occult science and alchemy, now airtight, as in hermetically sealed, from an airtight tube credited to [[see:Hermes Trismegistus]].
The woman [[see:Lysander]] asks for bedroom in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
From the Greek for desert or uninhabited place, so literally a person of the desert. Christianity took it up through stories of wandering the desert for trials.
An old word for the brain, easier for speakers of other Germanic languages to recognise because it resembles German [[same-root:Gehirn]].
A poem quoted for [[see:bugle-bow]]: 'one hand he put upon her toe, the other on her bugle-bow'.
An ancient inventor behind early [[see:vending machines]], a coin-operated holy water dispenser, and steam-driven temple [[see:automatic doors]].
Coined by [[see:Bayer]] from the Greek root of hero, almost certainly blending [[from:heroine]] and [[from:morphine]]: a drug that heroically rescues you from pain.
The female hero, whose feminine ending differs from the chemical ending of [[see:heroin]], though the drug name puns on it.
Borrowed from Greek, meaning creeping; in Greek it meant shingles, now [[see:herpes zoster]]; used for many skin conditions, even in oysters.
Today's name for shingles, zoster being Greek for belt or girdle from where the disease commonly appears; see [[see:herpes]].
Perhaps a diminutive of a word meaning army, because they school, or with [[see:-ing (noun suffix)]] meaning the fish associated with the army.
Named after [[from:Heinrich Hertz]].
French writer, died 1998, whose 1960s book proposed new marks including the [[see:love point]] and [[see:doubt mark]].
A line the audience shouts at a [[see:pantomime]].
A back-formation younger than [[from:hesitation]].
The evening star, brother of [[see:Phosphoros]].
An early letter, already in the Phoenician alphabet; when the [[see:Ionians]] lost its h sound it became the vowel letter [[gave:eta]].
Describes a word that doesn't describe itself, like [[see:oligosyllabic]] and [[see:monosyllabic]].
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode about -nym words.
A word spelling a different word backwards, like [[see:bonk]] and [[see:knob]]; hetero means different.
A word that spells another word backwards, like [[see:bonk]] and [[see:knob]]; also called an [[see:anadrome]].
The medieval six-note series formed from syllables of [[from:Ut queant laxis]]; running the gamut means running its length.
Contains the Greek word for angle, which shares a root with [[same-root:knee]].
Once considered too casual by Jess's teachers, though it and [[see:hi]] are older than [[see:hello]] for saluting someone.
What Jess's teachers said to discourage [[see:hey]] as a greeting in favour of [[see:hello]], ironically the younger word.
The familiar magic phrase using [[see:presto]].
Like [[see:hey]], an older term than [[see:hello]] for greeting someone, even from a distance.
Means to winterise yourself, evoking the French name for winter.
A word for a country person implying loutishness and lack of education, a possible source of [[gave?:hobo]].
What Old English speakers called the body's covering before [[see:skin]].
The Old English word for what we got from Old Norse as [[see:skin]].
An American contribution to English that sounds as if it came from crime films.
Old English pronoun used where we now say [[see:they]].
Sacred or priestly rule, from Greek [[from:hieros]], sacred.
According to Egyptologist Ilona Regulski, this is the wrong word for the signs, which should be called [[see:hieroglyphs]].
The right term, not [[see:hieroglyphics]], says Ilona Regulski; signs stand for words, sounds or themes and face the start of the line; Rob made a video about them.
Once meant German, while [[see:Low Dutch]] meant Netherlandish.
Like [[see:bunch of fives]], refers to the five fingers of the hand.
Like Parisian French, it is one dialect that came to be called simply the national language.
Named for the altitude of southern Germany, not for being further north; it is modern standard German, the dominant dialect.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s Germanic rendering of [[see:grandiloquent]], which Jess likes.
An old meal eaten around six o'clock, which explains why some people call their evening meal [[see:tea]].
Dates from Old English, where high meant main, the main way between towns; Britain uses it in the [[see:Highway Code]].
The British book of road rules, which shows Britain does recognise the idea of a [[see:highway]].
Old English for battle, used in many a [[see:kenning]], like [[see:hildbedd]].
Means battle; related to [[same-root:Hildebrand]], and the element also appears in [[same-root:Matilda]].
A [[see:kenning]] meaning deathbed.
Its brand is related to [[same-root:brandish]] and [[same-root:brand]], from a root meaning burning, perhaps from swords flashing.
A [[see:kenning]] for blood dripping from a sword, evoking cold steel.
A [[see:kenning]] for an arrow, lance or spear.
Weary of fighting; its [[see:sad]] has the old sense of satiated or fed up.
No agreed distinction from [[see:mountain]]: definitions vary by country and surrounding terrain; hill is Germanic, mountain Romance.
A name that can go either way for men and women.
Industry term, also hillbilly music, for bluegrass-style music marketed to white audiences in the South, which turned into [[gave:country music]].
An example of the diminutive suffix [[see:-ock]].
An Old English plural pronoun replaced by Norse [[see:they]] and [[see:them]]; Rob is glad English doesn't still use it as a plural.
Old English plural pronoun used where we now say [[see:them]]; imagine using him as the non-binary pronoun today.
Airship whose sad disaster is part of German and American history, hardly evidence that the [[see:Zeppelin]] was perfected.
A modern parallel to [[see:had-I-wist]].
Being used for India at the moment; it is also what English speakers called India before they called it India.
A reduplicative word for irritation, depression or bad temper from the [[see:dictionary of reduplicative words]].
Often credited to Shakespeare (Othello, The Tempest), adapted from a Middle English noun and the verb [[from:hinten]], to seize; a small graspable bit of information.
Another name for the seahorse, literally horse sea monster; also a seahorse-shaped part of the brain.
Half eagle, half horse, meaning horse [[from:griffin]]; surprisingly recent, from [[see:Orlando Furioso]].
Means river horse; its -potamus part means river, as in [[same-root:Mesopotamia]].
Means river horse; the amphibious biblical [[see:behemoth]] came to be identified with it.
The fear of long words, dismissed as a made-up phobia with silly multilingual roots.
A recent, deliberately fanciful word for the fear of long words, built on [[from:sesquipedalia]]; the hippo and monstro parts are extra hyperbole.
Usually Welsh people's longing for Wales, but more broadly a yearning for any absent person or thing; English has no single equivalent.
Half he-goat, half stag: cervus means stag and hirco- a he-goat; mocked as a boring hybrid, like most antelopes.
Someone who works for hire, an English example of [[see:-ling]].
Means broad island; its [[see:shima]] is the same element as the jima in [[see:Iwo Jima]].
Latin name the Romans supposedly took from a Carthaginian word for land of the rabbits, really of the [[see:hyrax]]; it [[gave:Spain]].
The island shared by French-speaking Haiti and Spanish-speaking Dominican Republic, mentioned in the story of [[see:mambo]].
Johnson noted it cannot be pronounced without making the noise it means, as with many onomatopoeic words like [[see:lisp]].
Would be a lesser shock than [[see:hit for six]], since a ball that bounces before the boundary scores four, but nobody says it.
To be astounded or overwhelmed, from hitting a cricket ball over the boundary without it touching the ground, which scores six runs.
Rob's English equivalent of [[equivalent:under a frog's ass]], which Jess turns into 'frog bottom'.
Jess's further joke variation on [[see:outlaws]] and [[see:yonder laws]].
A common call to railroad workers and a possible source of [[gave?:hobo]]; it reminds Rob of [[see:hautboy]].
Means grey-haired frost, because it looks like grey hair collected on grass and branches; related to [[same-root:hoary]].
Merged with [[see:horse]] in American English.
Describes someone with a big grey beard, like Gandalf; related to [[same-root:hoarfrost]].
Probably comes from [[from:hocus pocus]].
The British word for the cooking top of an oven, which Americans call a [[see:stove]].
A Shakespeare original; it meant 'take it or leave it' or hit or miss, rather than rubbing elbows.
The biscuit, which Rob calls the best biscuit, brought up as what [[see:hobnob]] really means.
Of uncertain origin: perhaps the railroad workers' call [[from?:ho boy]], or [[from?:hick]], a word for a loutish, uneducated country person.
An old English name for the [[see:oboe]], also seen as hoot boy, from French [[from:hautbois]].
Dictionary of Anglo-Indian words rich in etymology and history; its title is a British anglicisation of the Shia cry [[from:Ya Hassan! Ya Hussain!]].
Paired with [[see:hawk]] as historically separate vowels that fall together under the [[see:cot–caught merger]].
Mock-Latin patter used by jugglers performing tricks; one 1694 claim derives it from [[from?:hoc est corpus meum]], another from [[from?:hax pax max Deus adimax]].
Nonsense, once a name for a conjurer; [[see:John Tillotson]] derived it from [[from?:hoc est corpus]], discredited; a 1655 account credits a trickster under James I.

term: hoddy doddy, all arse and no body

mentions.note: A phrase for a short, clumsy person of either sex.
According to [[see:Francis Grose]], 18th-century London slang for a clumsy person.
Samuel Johnson's cat, which has a statue thanks to one of Johnson's biographers rather than Johnson himself.
Since the 14th century, originally any kind of stew, sometimes made with goose, spices and wine; variants include hotchpot and hodgepot.
A word for a random mix, never spelled consistently, with French precursors such as [[from:hotchpot]].
A food word from French that was originally the name of a spiced goose stew.
Example of English p matching a German f sound under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Another unexplained -og word like [[see:dog]]; Old English hog meant the male of almost any farm animal, which argues against a Celtic origin like Welsh [[unrelated?:hwch]].
Another animal word with the unexplained final G sound, like [[see:dog]].
Indigenous culture that built hundreds of miles of Salt River Valley canals, whose abandoned remains inspired the name [[see:Phoenix (city)]].
A Dutch greeting still used today, the Dutch version of hi, and the source of [[gave:ahoy]].
The verb corresponding to the noun [[same-root:heist]].
The verb behind [[gave:heist]].
To lift into the air, the word [[gave:heist]] varies.
From Hamlet's hoist with his own petard, about turning the tables on assassins: blown up by your own bomb.
Originally a Shakespearean phrase, literally blown up by your own [[from:petard]], so jokingly 'by your own fart bomb'.
A crime on [[see:James Hardy Vaux]]'s list; the verb is related to [[same-root:heist]], as [[see:lifting]] means stealing.
The phrase that [[gave:avast]] is short for.
An example of [[see:therapy speak]] used outside therapy sessions.
One of several English equivalents of [[equivalent:pagar el pato]].
One of several number-one idioms the hosts call self-explanatory.
Used as a verb in British English, to holiday somewhere, as the equivalent of the American to [[equivalent:vacation]].

Also Dutch gin: the original, much stronger juniper drink from the Netherlands from which [[see:gin]] developed.
A variant of [[same-root:hallo]] used to get someone's attention from afar; it lies behind [[gave:hello]] and [[gave:hullabaloo]].
Named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm; also discovered in [[see:Ytterby]].
Element also found at [[see:Ytterby]].

Code word in the alphabet proposed by the ICAO South American Regional Office.

One of the many baseball idioms Jess lists as common in American everyday language.
Replaced [[see:bum]] in the 1990s but now sounds as harsh as bum did, so people say [[see:unhoused]].

The feeling of being away and wishing you were home; contrasted with [[see:Fernweh]], [[see:dépaysement]] and [[see:hiraeth]].
Nearly identical to [[see:manslaughter]] in structure and meaning.
One of the few [[see:-cide]] words we actually hear about regularly.
Related to Latin homo, human, as in the original sense of [[see:homophobia]].
Shows the Latin homo, human, which the original sense of [[see:homophobia]] used, related to [[same-root:hominid]].
Offered as an example of a [[see:tautonym]].
Another word with Greek homos, same, unlike the Latin homo of [[see:Homo sapiens]].
Some contronyms are homonyms: words from two different etymological sources that are spelled the same, like [[see:cleave]].
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode about -nym words.
Uses the unrelated Greek homos, same, like most English homo- words, which shifted the meaning of [[see:homophobia]].
Originally fear of humans, from Latin homo, used of animals; reinterpreted via Greek homos, same, as fear and then hatred of gay people.

Disputed as a true badger; Jess finds it shares a subfamily with the [[see:European badger]] but not the [[see:American badger]].
Means fragrant harbour, the fragrance probably from local agarwood trees.
One of Reese Witherspoon's two donkeys, the other being [[see:Donkey]].
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.
Edward Perkins's door-to-door product line, a funny spelling of honor and maid that may have started the trend leading to [[see:Kool-Aid]].
A real medieval Latin word meaning the state of being able to achieve honours, used in [[see:Love's Labour's Lost]] as a joke about pretentious length.
From Love's Labour's Lost: a real Latin word for the state of being able to achieve honours, used there for cheeky effect.
A 14th-century Spanish livestock owners' association whose annual assemblies divided up strays; mesta supposedly comes from Latin for mixed. It gave [[gave:mustang]].
Klondike gold rushers' version of the name of an Alaskan Indigenous people, [[from:Hoochinoo]], whose rum-like liquor was so popular it named unofficial spirits.
Belly-dance-inspired number at the 1893 World's Fair linked to [[see:Little Egypt]]; the name may come from [[from?:Hoochie Coochie Rice]] or [[from?:The Ham Fat Man]].
[[see:Willie Dixon]]'s 1954 song, full of innuendo, which popularised [[gave:cooch]].
Minstrel show performer whose stage name may have influenced the name of the [[see:hoochie coochie]] dance.
The American word for a car's [[see:bonnet]].

A big British proprietary eponym, as in doing the hoovering; in the US it would suggest the president or J. Edgar Hoover.
British word for a vacuum cleaner, named after a specific brand, which gains ubiquity but loses credit when rivals' products are also called Hoovers.
Perrault's tale of a tiny, wise youngest of seven children who steals an ogre's [[see:seven-league boots]].
Also called Hopping Johnny, an American dish of bacon, rice and peas that was sometimes considered the same as [[see:jambalaya]].
Linked jokingly to the [[see:March Hare]] and possibly to [[see:mad as a box of frogs]].
The Spanish word for [[equivalent:hour]], whose H has never been pronounced.
Coined [[see:serendipity]] in the 1700s.
The collective noun for hamsters, in the army sense rather than hoarding, which fits the trampling sense of [[see:hamster]].
A business approach supplying something to all sectors, the line from which the [[see:vertical]]s branch off.
The French word for a clock or timepiece, which Rob compares with [[same-root:horologe]].
The French word for a clock, contrasted with English keeping the Germanic-sounding [[see:clock]].
Appears in the 1687 [[see:hot cockles]] quote about a furious husband, showing that the notion of horniness is old.
The Germanic counterpart of [[same-root:cornucopia]], showing the C to H shift.
A kind of wasp; one theory links it to a horn blower, but etymologists favour an original coinage later reshaped by association with horn.
Spanish for oven, showing the F-to-H shift when compared with Italian [[same-root:forno]].

Another old [[see:flat adverb]] use that has since dropped out.
Still inspires horror, unlike [[see:terrific]], which has undergone amelioration.

Related to the bristling old French words for hedgehogs.

A newer borrowing from French that kept its French spelling.
Sounds the same as [[see:hoarse]] for Americans, though they would have differed in Shakespeare's time.
Shows the [[see:frozen binomials]] tendency to put the more common word first.
Listed with other noun-only [[see:frozen binomials]].
Invented by [[see:James Watt]] as a marketing technique: his steam engine's horsepower was the number of horses it could replace.
A historical name for the [[see:kraken]], implying something that grabs.
The one legwear word that isn't plural, though worn in two pieces; it means a tube, the same word as a garden or fireman's hose.
The German word for trousers, used in the plural, unlike singular English [[see:hose]].
A Cumbrian word for rain.
Not always a place of healing; a place to stay, from a root meaning stranger, guest or host shared with [[same-root:hostile]], [[same-root:hospitality]], [[same-root:hostage]], [[same-root:hotel]].
Jess teases that Rob doesn't drop the H here despite defending h-less [[see:herb]].
Another word where the French circumflex marks a lost S, like [[see:hotel]].
From Latin [[from:hospitalis]], a place welcoming guests, first lodging pilgrims and travellers; [[same-root:hotel]] and [[same-root:hostel]] are clipped versions.
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]].
American slang short for horse, which led Jess to guess [[see:Charing Cross]].
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]].
Given as an early sense of what a [[see:hospital]] could be.
Borrowed from French when it still had its S; a double borrowing with [[same-root:hotel]].
A clipped version of the same Latin word as [[same-root:hospital]].
Sounds like [[same-root?:hostile]] for some Americans, which Jess thinks is a double meaning behind the horror franchise [[see:Hostel (film)]].
Horror franchise whose title Jess thinks is a pun on [[see:hostile]].
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]], one of the members of the family that turned pejorative.
Shakespeare is credited with being the first to import it from French.

What most people in England call the sausage that Americans call a [[see:wiener]].

The phrase that [[see:brat summer]] twists into something more intrusive and in-your-face.
Internet jargon the hosts think predates Gen Z, credited to Millennials.
The toy brand whose looping track inspired the spider name [[see:Hotwheels sisyphus]].

From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]].
Another word where Rob keeps the H, cited against his defence of h-less [[see:herb]].
From French hôtel, whose circumflex marks the lost S of [[same-root:hostel]]; the two are a double borrowing.

A clipped version of the same Latin word as [[same-root:hospital]].

Related to [[same-root:canine]] through the C/H consonant shift.

Related to the Greek word for dog behind [[same-root:cynicism]].
One of the specific names older English used before it had a general word like [[see:shark]].
One of the specific older names for sharks, used before [[see:shark]] became the general word.
A French import that replaced Old English [[see:stound]]; also linked to the clockmaker's word [[same-root:horologer]].

The Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:mansion]].

Old English term for a builder.

Named after [[from:Sam Houston]].

H in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]].

A Shakespearean greeting used in As You Like It and Hamlet (how now, sweet queen), echoed in [[see:how now brown cow]].
The phrase Rob is reminded of by the Shakespearean greeting [[see:how now]].

Antiquated word for a [[see:hullabaloo]] or [[see:kerfuffle]].
Means mind bright, with the same -bert ending as [[same-root:Robert]].
An unofficial collective noun Rob likes.

Human-shaped, which can apply to beings that aren't human; formed with [[from:-oid]].

Like [[see:human]], Danny says it with a palatal sound from H fused with [[see:yod]].
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.

Paired with [[see:hunch]] to show how [[see:lunch]] relates to lump.

[[see:Sir John Cheke]]'s native replacement for [[see:centurion]] when writing about Romans.

A Germanic agent noun with the [[see:-er]] ending.

A made-up word for acting like a hyena, used as an example of a possible [[see:nonce word]].
Danish coziness and more: being indoors by a roaring fire with friends and drink while it's cold outside.
Has the same membrane-meaning element as [[same-root:Hymenoptera]].

Humorous [[see:anagram]] of William Shakespeare.

term: I came, I saw, I conquered

mentions.note: The iconic example of [[see:asyndeton]].

term: I can read him like the back of my book

Apparently a Spanish [[equivalent:Simon says]], though the hosts aren't sure how widely it is used.

term: I desire we may be better strangers

mentions.note: A [[see:William Shakespeare]] insult from Rob's mug, one of his favourites for being so withering.
Martin Luther King's speech, with repeated I have a dream and Let freedom ring, exemplifies [[see:anaphora]].
Brits read it as 'I disagree and don't want to discuss it further'; most Americans took it as accepting the other person's view.

term: I heard it through the grapevine

mentions.note: Goes back to the unreliable 1859 [[from:grapevine telegraph]] line; famous from Marvin Gaye's song.

term: I know what I like and I like what I know

A Germanic vowel change where vowels moved toward an I or E sound, producing [[see:foot]] and feet, [[see:mouse]] and mice; linked to [[see:umlaut]].
English name for [[see:umlaut]], so called because a lost i sound in an ending reshaped the preceding vowel.

A form of [[same-root:James]].

The Latin-derived ending used for the other planets' inhabitants instead of [[see:-ling]].
British journalist behind [[see:Betteridge's law]], stated in a throwaway 2009 blog post; he told Rob he hoped it improved headline writing.
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
The International Civil Aviation Organization, which made English aviation's official language and requires level four proficiency; its four-letter initialism is pronounced 'eye-kay-oh'.
A [[see:sniglet]] for ice at the bottom of an upturned glass suddenly sliding toward your mouth; an ice [[from:avalanche]].
Named by [[see:Flóki Vilgerðarson]] after he saw glaciers, replacing [[see:Snæland]]. One theory says he chose it to deter settlers, unlike [[see:Greenland]].
Named by [[see:Flóki Vilgerðarson]] to scare people off, because it was a terrible place to settle.
A Germanic-style demonym for a country with a Germanic name, contrasted with Latinate ones like [[see:Mauritian]].
A remote, conservative language that best shows what Old Norse was like; it keeps [[see:thorn]] and [[see:eth]], and three genders and four cases.
Freud's German word, simply 'the I', rendered in English as [[gave:ego]].

[[see:Sigmund Freud]]'s own German term, rendered in English as [[equivalent:ego]].
Fish lizards, sea-dwelling, dolphin-like reptiles that aren't dinosaurs; [[see:Shonisaurus]] is a giant example.
Latin-sounding term introduced by Freud's English translators for his plain German [[from:Es]], meaning simply 'the it'.
A Latin term [[see:Sigmund Freud]] never used; he wrote in German and said [[equivalent:Es]], 'the it'.
Promising something absurd if a claim were true; earlier [[from:I'll eat Old Rowley's hat]]; Dickens's Pickwick Papers probably popularised an emphatic usage.
A French word, so purists replacing [[see:logic]] couldn't use it and went back to [[see:witcraft]].
A metaphorical word or phrase, from Latin [[from:idioma]], something used by an individual or small group, going back to Greek idios, private; related to [[same-root:idiot]].
Keeps the 'being the way you are' sense of [[same-root:idiot]]'s Greek source.
Once an actual legal designation, now a milder, less serious insult, like [[see:lunatic]].
From Greek idiotes, from idios, private; the first idiots were private, non-professional people, hence untrained and ignorant; shares its root with [[same-root:idiom]].
From Greek [[from:idiotes]], a private individual, someone in their own world; it later became an insult, a case of [[see:pejoration]].
In the Romance languages, idiotisms are simply sayings or set expressions, keeping the neutral sense of [[same-root:idiot]].
An ending on Latin-derived professions taken directly from French, as in [[see:sommelier]]; the -yer of [[see:lawyer]] and [[see:bowyer]] is a variant, from Latin -arius.
Dr Seuss book using [[see:nerd]] as an imaginary creature's name, not thought to have much influenced the insult.

term: if you fail to prepare, you prepare to fail

mentions.note: Example of [[see:antimetabole]].

term: if you're going through hell, keep going

mentions.note: Often credited to [[see:Winston Churchill]] because people want him to have said it.

term: if you're not a liberal when you're 25, you have no heart

mentions.note: Attributed to [[see:Winston Churchill]], unlikely since he was a Conservative at 15; Rob first heard it credited to someone else.
Another Latin suffix English adds to Germanic nouns, creating a [[see:hybrid word]].
Swedish for hedgehog, from igel, bristly, and a word for pine cone.
Old English for hedgehog, meaning bristling; same as German Igel in [[see:Mettigel]], possibly from the same root as [[same-root?:urchin]].

Fiery-looking phenomena such as shooting stars, the sense [[see:meteor]] has narrowed to.

In the 15th-century sense of [[see:meteor]], lightning and shooting stars.
Via Spanish from the Taíno (Arawakan) name for the animal; [[see:Charles Darwin]] was rude about Galápagos marine iguanas.

Meme acronym for 'I'm a keep it a Gurt', from the same memes as [[see:gurting]].
The soldier among the higher-class stock characters of commedia dell'arte.
A commedia dell'arte scholar or doctor who talks endlessly and presents himself as highly educated.
From Old Norse, originally meaning morally evil; British speakers favour it where Americans say [[see:sick]].
55% of Brits said it meant 'I've forgotten it already', while more Americans took it as sincere; tone can also make it sarcastic.
Earlier version of [[gave:I'd eat my hat]], referring to [[see:Old Rowley]], King Charles II.
The threat that caps a run of [[see:William Shakespeare]] insults Jess quotes.
American football term that sounds naughty if you're only half listening, noted down by Jess while watching NFL games.
Blaming everything on them, which recurred through the 20th century, took off with [[see:Operation Mindfuck]].
A classical Renaissance borrowing that [[see:inkhorn]] purists objected to, now taken for granted.
An example of [[see:softeners]]: at a party you can't just say 'I'm leaving'; you say you're going to head out and leave gradually.
A Taylor Swift lyric that became a meme; Jess picked it up without realising where it came from.
A standard Victorian word for enfeebled, used by the Romans as an insult; probably from Latin [[from?:baculum]], walking stick, someone lacking support.
Once clinical, it has lost its sting because it is foreign and opaque; an [[see:orphaned negative]] whose positive [[see:becile]] referred to being physically unsupported.
An early clinical term for mental disability, once not an insult, that pejorated into one, like [[see:loony]].
From Latin, unstained: unsullied and untarnished; Susie Dent's further example of a word with a lost opposite.

A word that could theoretically exist but doesn't, as with a 'groomal' to match [[see:bridal]], or [[see:liver]] for a living person.
Keywords created by [[see:John C. Wells]] in 1982 for comparing the vowels of General American and RP, such as kit, dress, trap, lot, strut and goat.

Regional Swiss German diminutive suffix making things cute, as in [[see:muesli]]; compare [[see:-lein]] and [[see:-chen]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].

Latin word meaning desire, sharing a distant ancestor with [[same-root:love]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:belief]] and [[same-root:love]], a link also made in the hosts' recent sexy episode.
A set of scales, one of the [[see:zodiac]] signs that isn't an animal.

French for a bookshop, not a library, which is a [[see:bibliothèque]].
Rob says Brits skip so many letters that it might as well be spelled 'libr'.
Spanish for a [[equivalent:bookworm]].
From an Old English word for a corpse, used for undead in fantasy games; cognate with [[same-root:like]], meaning body or form.

German ending, like Dutch -lijk, that is the word [[same-root:like]] and corresponds to English [[same-root:-ly]].

The 17th-century English term for [[equivalent:cunnilingus]].

Title in which 'general' is the adjective placed after the noun, showing French influence on [[see:general]].
Related to the German word for body, [[same-root:Leib]].
A 1991 patent for a wristwatch counting down your approximate remaining lifespan from personal data and demographic mortality estimates.

term: life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness

mentions.note: An example of the [[see:rule of three]].
The British word for what Americans call an [[equivalent:elevator]]; Rob prefers its single swift syllable, and Jess admits she likes it a little better.
Used to mean steal, by the same logic as [[see:heist]].
The British word for an [[see:elevator]], simpler and shorter, though no one mentions that it also lowers you.

term: lift the cat onto the table

mentions.note: Finnish for raising an awkward subject everyone avoids, the [[equivalent:elephant in the room]]; almost the inverse of a [[see:dead cat]].

Means stealing, a parallel for [[see:hoisting]].
Joined letters like the E and T forming the [[see:ampersand]], which Jess scribbles in handwriting.
A character joining two letters, like fi, from Latin [[from:ligare]], to bind; related to [[same-root:alloy]], [[same-root:ally]], [[same-root:liaison]], [[same-root:religion]].
Influenced the spelling of [[unrelated:delight]], which has nothing to do with it.
In the sense of not heavy, related to [[same-root:lungs]].
The source of [[gave:lightning]]; people still often write lightening for lightning.
Simply a [[from:lightening]] of the sky, with the E dropped to tell the two words apart.
Both the Dutch equivalent of the [[same-root:-ly]] ending and a Dutch word for body, the same thing as [[see:lichaam]].
A Dutch ending that sounds like 'like', making the link between [[same-root:-ly]] and [[same-root:like]] more obvious.
The same as German [[same-root:-lich (German)]] and English [[same-root:-ly]], and cognate with [[same-root:lich]], a body, implying similar form.

Cognate with the adverb ending [[same-root:-ly]] in English and other Germanic languages.

One of the other popular girls' names in England and Wales.

Another word for an arm that is also used for the [[see:branch]] of a tree.

An old name for a thief, from twigs smeared with sticky lime used to snare birds.

Roman name of [[gave:Lincoln]], joining a Celtic name containing [[from:lin]] with [[from:colonia]].
The invisible line where each American football play begins, from the earlier rugby term [[from:scrummage]].
