A Germanic diminutive suffix combining Old English [[from:-le]] and [[from:-ing]]; planets named after Roman gods take [[see:-ian]] instead.
The hosts discussed -ling words in an earlier episode.
Old English suffix making directional adverbs, seen in [[gave:groveling]], [[gave:sidelong]] and [[gave:headlong]]; unrelated to [[unrelated:long]].
A suffix that is more clearly diminutive than [[see:-ing (noun suffix)]].
Originally lenger; its spelling was updated when e was raised to i before nasals, unlike [[see:English]].
The British pronunciation is far closer to French than the American one, which Jess doubts she will ever shake.
French for ingot, from l'ingot, another rebracketing like [[see:licorne]].
[[see:Dante]]'s term for languages, Italian among them, that use sì for yes.
The killing of a language, which has happened to many Indigenous languages through conquest and colonialism.
Means little tongues, reportedly referring to snake tongues rather than human ones.
The push to keep English free of foreign, especially classical, borrowings, as in [[see:Anglish]] and the [[see:Inkhorn Controversy]].
The modern forum for corporate parlance and odd job titles; generally positive, it flatters users' egos, and spawned [[see:broetry]].

Swaps names with [[see:leopard]] in heraldry, showing the mismatch between heraldic names and appearance, as with [[see:salamander]].

Shows the Germanic shift of B to P compared with Latin [[same-root:labium]].
Shares the Greek fat root with [[same-root:liver]].
A type of spirit, usually sugary and syrupy, like [[see:Kahlúa]]; pronounced variously.

American usage; British speakers say [[equivalent:spirit]]s instead.

A German dialect name for the ladybird, paralleling English [[equivalent:lady cow]].
Common name for [[see:Ursa Minor]].
Performer said to have inspired the [[see:hoochie coochie]] dance, though whether she was at the 1893 fair is debated.
A Hebrew phrase for the reflection of a person seen in someone's pupil, translated as [[gave:the apple of my eye]].
[[see:Winsor McCay]]'s 1911 animated film.
Looks very like [[unrelated:liver]] but doesn't seem to be related to it.
A verb pair among the [[see:frozen binomials]], ordered by events: you live before you learn.
One of several Latvian phrases for daydreaming, similar to [[equivalent:have your head in the clouds]].
Thought to be related to the Greek word for fat, like [[same-root:lipid]], perhaps because it looks greasy; probably unrelated to [[unrelated:live]].

A name for someone from Liverpool, also called a [[see:Scouser]].
One of several old words for movies that didn't catch on.
Related to Spanish lagarto, the source of [[same-root:alligator]], but took a different route into English.

Listed with gaslighting and narcissism as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].

Gaelic prefix meaning son of, making names like [[gave:MacIver]] and [[gave:MacAulay]] Gaelic-Norse hybrids.
1770s style of towering wigs and tight bright clothes, named after the fancy dish young men brought back from the continent; linked to [[see:Yankee Doodle]].
One of the [[see:frozen binomials]]: the main part of the dish comes first, so 'cheese and macaroni' sounds wrong.
Another suggested background filler phrase that might actually work.
The British name for [[see:macaroni and cheese]], which drops the 'and' but keeps the same order.
Scottish name meaning son of Olaf, a hybrid of Gaelic [[from:Mac]] and a Scandinavian name.
Shakespeare's play, staged using John Dennis's thunder system, which prompted [[see:steal someone's thunder]].
Duncan's praise of Macbeth is dramatic irony, while the witches' prophecy unfolding unexpectedly adds situational irony.
Considered worse than Titus Andronicus, perhaps for its kill count; Jess thinks its witch scenes have a different style, possibly [[see:Christopher Marlowe]]'s.
The best-known [[see:thane]], who becomes thane of Cawdor.
Shares its stain root with [[same-root:immaculate]]; Rob noticed it in a coffee shop.
An ultimately unimportant plot device, loved by [[see:Alfred Hitchcock]], probably coined by [[see:Angus MacPhail]], whose name may have shaped it; guff means nonsense.
A verb for improvising a fix, from the TV character who made tools from gum and duct tape; British English says [[equivalent:bodging]].
In Latin and Greek a device, tool or contrivance, but in 16th-century English any large structure or system, even the whole world as a constructed frame.
Scottish clan name meaning son of Ivar, a Norse name, combined with Gaelic [[from:Mac]].
Another word with the -phage eating element found in [[same-root:sarcophagus]].
Sexual interest in gigantism or excessive growth.
Eye condition where eyesight becomes stained or foggy, showing the stain root of [[same-root:immaculate]].
The missing opposite of [[see:immaculate]], meaning stained.
Early uses referred to animals, mostly rabid dogs; the anger and insanity senses share irrationality. It replaced [[see:wood]] and largely replaced [[see:wroth]].

term: mad as a bag of cats

mentions.note: A riff on [[see:mad as a box of frogs]]: anything that flails.

term: mad as a box of frogs

mentions.note: Origin unknown, mainly British, fashionable in the 2000s; maybe from the hopping in [[see:hopping mad]].
A 14th-century 'mad as' simile.
Predates [[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s Mad Hatter; hatters went mad from mercury poisoning by mercurous nitrate used in making felt hats.
From hatmakers suffering mercury poisoning from the mercurous nitrate used to make felt hats.
A 17th-century simile; the hosts can only speculate about plentiful spring milk or cows protecting their calves.
Named by mistake by [[see:Marco Polo]], who misread an Arabic text about [[from:Mogadishu]]. The islanders had no name for the whole island and adopted his.
Accidentally named after [[from:Mogadishu]], so it means the same.
Given as a common example of a [[see:palindrome]].
A red dye used alongside [[see:woad]] in the medieval era.
Saudi city whose name just means the city, also the word for an Arab city's old town; formerly Yathrib, renamed by the Prophet Muhammad.
A former name of [[see:Madinah]], meaning the city of the prophet.
Danish name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], meaning a jar of milk, after the white sap that oozes from its split stem.
The specific term for the [[see:priest]] who stood at the front of the church and read aloud, as opposed to anyone holding a church position.
Code word in the South American variant that also turns up in other versions of the alphabet.
The word reversed to make [[see:Stromae]].
First recorded in 1875 for a Sicilian criminal society; it is often traced to Arabic because Arabs ruled Sicily, but no convincing Arabic source exists.
Possibly from Sicilian mafiu, which may relate to Arabic marfud, rejected or outside society, though the OED isn't convinced.
French word sharing its source with [[same-root:magazine]] but meaning storehouse or shop, the basic French word for a shop.
Arabic for storehouse, via Italian and Middle French; first a military storehouse (1580s), then a weapon's ammo holder, then periodicals after [[see:The Gentleman's Magazine]].
Originally a storehouse, then a store for bullets or for gathered articles; [[see:The Gentleman's Magazine]] was the first periodical so called; cognate of French [[same-root:magazine (French)]].
French for a shop, from the same storehouse word as English [[same-root:magazine]].
Related to [[same-root:magic]] through Greek magos.
Named after [[from:Magenta]], a northern Italian town where the dye could be obtained.
A variant of [[same-root:Margaret]].
The biblical three wise men, from the plural of Latin magus; also Median and Persian religious specialists in astrology, alchemy and dream interpretation.

Has long meant influencing events or supernatural forces; from Greek [[from:magos]], related to [[same-root:mage]], literally things associated with the [[same-root:Magi]], short for [[from:ars magica]].
The final E that lets English spell more vowel sounds, compared with the role of [[see:H]] for consonants.
One possible starting point for animation, which became the [[see:cartoon]].
What Snow White's stepmother actually says, commonly misremembered as [[see:mirror, mirror on the wall]].
Spelling once common among many variants; [[see:Aleister Crowley]] revived it around 1912 to separate occult practice from stage [[see:magic]].
District of Thessaly, Greece, where a magnetic mineral was supposedly first found; source of [[gave:magnet]], [[gave:manganese]] and [[gave:magnesium]].
Linked to [[from:Magnesia]]; its coiner tried to avoid the confusion with [[see:magnium]], but magnesium stuck anyway.
Named after [[from:Magnesia]], where a magnetic mineral was supposedly first found.
Named after [[from:Magnesia]], like [[same-root:magnet]].
Name the coiner of [[see:magnesium]] preferred, to avoid confusion with [[see:Magnesia]]; it didn't catch on.
Named after [[from:Pierre Magnol]].
Its mag shortens [[from:Margaret]]; such Mag- or Meg- names often marked something disliked, too loud or too busy, and also named artillery.
Mag, a woman's name from Margaret, plus pie, an older word for the bird.
Pie was the original name; mag, short for Margaret and an epithet for a chatty woman, refers to the bird's chattiness.
The Hungarian name for Hungary, after the [[see:Magyars]].
A people whose name appears in [[see:Magyarország]], the Hungarian name for Hungary.
Means good mother; it was the first dinosaur found with seemingly incontrovertible evidence of parenting, young found near an adult.
The American word for what Rob calls the [[equivalent:post]], although Rob's post is delivered by the Royal Mail and Jess's by the US Postal Service.
Where Americans put letters, which the British call a [[equivalent:post box]].
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:mayhem]].
Someone from Maine, who can also be a [[see:Maniac]].
From [[from:tenere]]: literally to hold in the hand, showing how literal these Latin compounds are.
Means dancing mushroom; the same thing as [[equivalent:hen of the woods]].
Rank whose fairly obvious etymology means big.
Joe Biden's dog, whose ceremony prompted the headline pun [[see:indoguration]].
Title in which 'general' is the adjective placed after the noun, showing French influence on [[see:general]].
Golfer who in an 1890 game, thinking of a popular song, called the invincible notional opponent a regular bogeyman, giving [[gave:bogey]].
Used as an example: the only French-derived word in Rob's sentence, showing that everyday speech stays mostly Germanic.
The word for capital letters before [[see:uppercase]], still the right term for handwriting.
Capital letters, the older forms that gave rise to [[gave:minuscule]]; Danny's book says all-capital Roman writing looks like angry shouting.
A simple verb phrase given as an example of [[see:collocation]].
German for time, as in [[see:einmal]], [[see:zweimal]] and [[see:nochmal]]; it shares the Germanic root that gave English [[same-root:meal]], the repast.
Calls someone's motivations into question; the opposite of [[see:bona fide]].
How the French described the name [[see:euro]].
A merging of two commonly used idioms or metaphors, as in [[see:we'll burn that bridge when we come to it]].
A blend of [[from:malapropism]] and [[from:metaphor]] for a mix of two idioms; usually an error, but often used deliberately for humour.
Like eggcorns but goofier, making far less sense; named after [[from:Mrs Malaprop]].
Discussed in an earlier episode.
A more egregious word mix-up, named after [[from:Mrs. Malaprop]] of Sheridan's The Rivals; contrasted with an [[see:eggcorn]].
Disease whose name means bad air, the opposite of [[see:Bonaria]], good air.
Name of a language that is itself a palindrome, a proper-name example of a [[see:palindrome]].
Released by [[see:Nabisco]] in 1913: a graham cracker topped with marshmallow and covered in chocolate, one of the forerunners of [[see:s'mores]].
Justin Bieber's capuchin monkey, named after the rapper Mally Mall who gave it; confiscated in Munich over paperwork, it now lives in a Danish reserve.
Malta's language, a mix of Arabic and Italian, given as a comparison with Sicily's Arabic influence on [[see:mafia]].
The cross of the [[see:Knights Hospitaller]], who ruled Malta, yet it is not the cross on the [[see:flag of Malta]].
Used in French sports scoring for points deducted, the opposite of a [[see:bonus]]; Rob thinks English should adopt it.
The [[see:Twelfth Night]] character who makes a complete fool of himself.
Related to [[same-root:mammal]] through the idea of the mammary gland.
Maybe shares an ancient root with the man- in [[same-root?:Manchester]].
Came via Spanish from Haitian Creole, where, per the OED, it was a voodoo ritual dance or voodoo priestess.
A regular at the Victory Club who asked what the new dish of [[see:nachos]] should be called.
Refers to animals with mammary glands that suckle their young; related to [[same-root:mama]] and to the place name [[same-root:Manchester]].
Shares an ancient root with the man- in [[same-root:Manchester]].
Very distantly related to the man- of [[same-root:Manchester]].
Shares an ancient root with the man- in [[same-root:Manchester]].
A real prisoner kept in an iron mask for 34 years; the [[see:Great Cipher]] points to [[see:Vivien de Bulonde]], but most historians favour [[see:Ercole Antonio Mattioli]].
A TV show whose title was pronounced 'man verse food', the same clipping of 'versus' seen in [[see:versing]].
Like [[see:he witch]], a term for a male [[see:witch]] once the plain word came to imply a woman.

term: Man Won't Stop Coming Up With New Sniglets

mentions.note: A 2001 article in The Onion about a man still inventing [[see:sniglet]]s nearly 20 years after the fad, such as [[see:creamerass]] and [[see:snubbler]].
A place name covered in a recent Rob video, linked to the mammary gland and [[same-root:mammal]] because of nearby breast-shaped hills.
Rob's favourite; the Roman fort ([[from:-chester]]) at the breast-shaped hill, distantly related to [[same-root?:mammary]] and perhaps [[same-root?:mother]].
Means fort at the breast-shaped hill: [[from:chester]] is fort, and man- shares an ancient root with [[same-root:mammal]].
Fans protesting the club's ownership wore red and green scarves as a nod to the precursor clubs that merged to form it.
Someone from Manchester, from [[from:Mancunium]], the Roman name for Manchester.
Another Indigenous name for the [[equivalent:didgeridoo]] given by the hosts.
A collective misremembering, used to describe beliefs about [[see:bucket list]].
Collective misremembering, named after [[from:Nelson Mandela]], whose death and funeral people remembered before he died.
A 17th-century word for a surgeon; the form is unclear in the captions.
Eurovision-winning Italian band whose Danish name was suggested by their half-Danish bassist.
Also named after [[from:Magnesia]] and oddly corrupted; used to remove colour in glassmaking and weakly paramagnetic.
An alternative to [[see:Mainer]] for someone from Maine, which Jess finds perfect.
Compared to the original adjectival use of [[see:panic]].
Its English equivalent on the translated map is Manheim.
Like [[see:house]], it comes from a word simply meaning house, but Norman associations made it seem fancier, showing why Germanic words seem more basic or vulgar.
An alteration of the French word now spelled [[same-root:maison]]; like [[see:house]] it means house, but it is the fancy one.
A Germanic holdover meaning man-kill, now a lesser degree of homicide than [[see:murder]], though interchangeable with it in Middle English.
An Anglo-Saxon legal term that sounds brutal next to French ones, discussed in an earlier episode; unlike [[see:murder]], it does not imply premeditation.
Another Greek name for what we call [[see:oracle]]s, meaning seer.
Shares a root with [[same-root:mentor]].
Means diviner or prophet, from a root behind words for thinking, seeing and divining.
Named as related to [[same-root:money]] and the words for thinking.
The scientific name of the [[see:praying mantis]], which adds to the idea of praying.
Comes directly from French [[from:manteau]], the coat element in [[same-root:portmanteau]].
A [[see:retronym]].
Latin for hand, whose plural is also manus, not mani.
Used for countable things, against [[see:much]] for uncountable ones; used to argue that groceries can be seen as a mass, so [[see:10 items or less]] works.
Basically just means maple.
The old British name for [[see:Snickers]], replaced by the international name.
A French baron, spelled B-I-C-H, who founded the company [[gave:Bic]] and perfected the ballpoint with the [[see:Cristal]].
Creator of [[see:Fountain]], with a female alter ego, [[see:Rrose Sélavy]].
Mad because hares are randy in March, which leads the hosts to [[see:hopping mad]].
Misread an Arabic text about [[see:Mogadishu]] and so coined the name [[see:Madagascar]].
In the 13th century he wrote of a young man drugged with a hashish potion and sent to kill, spreading the [[see:assassin]] story.
The same name as [[same-root:Martin]], meaning Mars, the Roman god of war.
Roman emperor and the most famous stoic, whose Meditations on virtue and resisting temptation shaped modern ideas of being stoical.
French for [[equivalent:Tuesday]], the day of Mars.
Old English for a goblin or [[see:incubus]], probably from a root meaning to harm; replaced in the 1600s, surviving only in [[gave:nightmare]].
Has surprising variants, including [[same-root:Marjorie]], [[same-root:Maggie]], [[same-root:Peggy]], [[see:Daisy]] and [[see:Pearl]], since it means pearl.
Named after the woman's name, though Jess couldn't identify a specific woman.
Rob expects many Margos starting school soon, following the same pop-culture pattern as [[see:Betty]].
Title, close to count, behind the graven in [[see:'s-Gravenhage]]; Rob says English lacks it.
The French form of Margaret and a French name for the oxeye daisy, which is why [[see:daisy]] serves as a nickname for Margaret.
The French name of the oxeye daisy, explaining why [[see:Daisy]] is a nickname for [[same-root:Margaret]].
Etymologically the same name as [[same-root:Mary]].
A [[see:coca wine]] created in the 1860s by [[see:Angelo Mariani]], a French chemist from Corsica.
Female personification of France, compared with [[see:Britannia]] and [[see:Columbia]].
Etymologically the same name as [[same-root:Mary]].
Falsely credited with [[see:let them eat cake]]; she was a small child when the line was recorded.
Polish patriot often assumed French, which may have irritated her; her real name was Maria Skłodowska-Curie, and [[gave:curium]] and [[gave:polonium]] honour her.
Palaeobotanist and women's rights activist who helped make [[see:climax]] mean orgasm and founded Britain's first birth control clinic.
German name for the [[equivalent:daisy]], from a fable in which the Virgin Mary cut her finger picking flowers, giving daisies red tips.
The German name for the ladybird, closer in spirit to [[equivalent:ladybug]].
French word for the couple getting married, which English lacks, a [[see:lexical gap]].
Literally Mary's gold, after the Virgin Mary, likely because it opens by day and closes at night as if driven by God's will.
Wrongly credited with [[see:well-behaved women seldom make history]].
A type of xylophone with a name from Kimbundu: ma- is a plural prefix and rimba means wooden bar, an etymology similar to [[see:xylophone]].
What aquatic turtles were called before [[see:turtle]] took on that meaning.
Rob compares Saul becoming [[see:Paul]] to these characters, where changing the first letter switches between evil and good.
A variant of [[same-root:Margaret]].
Directly related to the German currency [[same-root:Mark (currency)]], whose first coins were cut from marked ingots.
Germany's currency before the euro, as the Deutsche Mark and [[see:Reichsmark]]; related to English [[same-root:mark]], because the first marks were cut from stamped ingots.
Like [[see:Winston Churchill]], someone who has hoovered up many misquotations.
Related to [[same-root:mercenary]].
From [[from:marron]], French for a chestnut; unrelated to [[unrelated:marooning]] or the Bugs Bunny-era insult.
A Bugs Bunny-era insult, saved for a future episode and unrelated to the colour.
Leaving someone stranded on an island; unrelated to the colour [[unrelated:maroon]].
Daughter of [[see:Theodora]], sharing her influence over Rome and the papacy in the [[see:pornocracy]].
Said to have daubed a toll booth and town with red paint after the races in 1837, a story emerging decades after his death.
One of the French titles that came in with the Norman nobility.

term: marriage is a great institution, but I'm not ready for an institution

mentions.note: A Mae West [[see:paraprosdokian]] that Jess links to [[see:zeugma]].
French for a chestnut that also simply means brown; it gave [[gave:maroon]].
Merged with [[see:Mary]] and [[see:merry]] in American English, which shows American speech is not Shakespearean.
Named after the war god, linked with [[see:Ares]], for its red colour visible from Earth; the Greeks called it [[see:Pyroeis]].
Roman war god, equated with [[see:Ares]] and also the red planet; source of [[gave:martial]].
A surname, not the Roman god, naming the Anglo-American company and the British Mars bar, which is the American [[see:Milky Way]].
The vanquishing star, wrongly linked by medieval writers to the name [[see:Cairo]].
Often spelt with a final S in English but not French; a French adaptation of the Greek name [[from:Massalia]].
An Old English word for a wetland, one of many English wetland words.
An earlier version of [[gave:s'mores]]: butter and marshmallow spread on a saltine cracker, toasted, and served with hot chocolate or tea.
Relating to war or the military, from [[from:Mars]], god of war.
The name of the show's third partner; like [[same-root:Marcus]], a [[see:theophoric]] name referencing [[from:Mars]], god of war.
Proposed the [[see:interrobang]] as a tool for copywriters.
Father of Protestantism, whose list of Catholic evils made [[see:poltergeist]] prominent.
Greatly objected to [[see:indulgences]], the idea that you could pay your way into heaven.
French for kingfisher; one theory says it links the bird's sea-calming power to the calm weather of [[see?:St. Martin's Day]].
German cartographer whose 1507 wall map and globe first named [[see:America]]; Rob says his surname means something like forest lake miller.
Existed before the [[see:martini]], complicating the timeline of its name.
Probably named after a place; the Martinez, California theory is debunked; linked to [[see:Martini & Rossi]] vermouth, but a [[see:Martinez cocktail]] predated it.
Leading vermouth brand proposed as the source of [[see:martini]].
A name that might be related to [[same-root?:Myrddin]].
From Hebrew [[from:Miriam]], of uncertain meaning (theories include rebellion, beloved, wished-for child); the top US woman's name of the past century.
Sounds the same as [[see:marry]] and [[see:merry]] for most Americans, a merger that Shakespeare's English did not have.
Probable namesake of the [[see:Bloody Mary]]; no bloodier than her father, but she had about 280 Protestants burned as heretics.
Most American accents merge at least two of Mary, marry and merry; they are distinct in RP, while Jess merges all three.
Apparently played [[see:golf]] quite a bit, and [[see:pall-mall]] too.
A common British term for drunk from the linguists' list.
Cited as one of the few remaining uses of [[see:hysteria]].
What people in Massachusetts call themselves.
Old French mastin meant great [[see:cur]], but it comes from a Latin word meaning tame or gentle.
The kind of big dog other languages call by English [[see:dog]].
Means killer, likely from Latin [[from:mactare]], to kill, but possibly related to Arabic [[from?:mata]], he died, as in [[see:shah mat]].
The American abbreviation of [[from:mathematics]], which Jess defends as logical because abbreviations like econ aren't pluralised; Brits find it irritating.

From Greek [[from:mathema]], science or knowledge, a general word for learning until [[see:Pythagoras]] applied it to arithmetic and geometry; Americans abbreviate it [[see:math]], Brits [[see:maths]].
The British abbreviation of [[from:mathematics]], kept plural because the full word is; Brits often correct anyone saying [[see:math]].
Means mighty in battle, containing the hild of [[same-root:Hilda]].
The killing of a mother, a more specific word than [[see:parricide]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for chemistry, ironic since matter itself is Latin-derived.
Born without hands and legs, he drew coats of arms, toured showing himself for money, and gave his name to [[see:Buckinger's boot]].
From Arabic matrah, a place where something is thrown down, such as a carpet laid on the floor for comfort, much like [[see:sofa]].
Mauna means mountain, so "Mount Mauna Kea" repeats itself; the world's tallest mountain from base to tip, though lower in elevation than [[see:Everest]].
A Latinate demonym for a Latinate country name, contrasted with [[see:Icelander]].
Home of the [[see:dodo]]; it had no native population, which makes the bird's name hard to pin down.
A [[from:Yiddish]] word that spread from New York slang.
The Old English word for the stomach, and later the throat or gullet, was related to maw, which now usually means a mouth.
George Clooney's 300-pound pot-bellied pig.
German placeholder name shown on sample ID and residency cards, its surname meaning template man; like [[see:Joe Bloggs]].
Michigan engineer credited with inventing [[see:painting by numbers]] kits.
A band with an unexplained umlaut over the i, an example of the [[see:metal umlaut]].
The reply to [[see:in bocca al lupo]]; the hosts wonder whether the wolf chokes on the speaker or dies before it can swallow them.
Etymologically the same name as [[same-root:Mary]].
Distress call from French for 'help me', chosen in the early 1920s by [[see:Frederick Stanley Mockford]] because both English and French speakers could say it.
In English and Anglo-French law, injuring someone to make them less able to defend themselves; etymologically the same word as [[same-root:maim]].
Name of the Zoroastrian god of wisdom, chosen because it sounded like the surname of owner [[see:Jujiro Matsuda]].
East Midlands for my dear or my love; men there normally call one another duck too.
A repast, from a Germanic root meaning time, as in German [[same-root:Mal]], which makes mealtime tautologous; unrelated to meal meaning flour.
Related to the mail in [[same-root:blackmail]], implying an appointed time for gathering and eating.
Ground grain such as flour, from a root meaning grind and directly related to [[same-root:mill]]; unrelated to meal meaning a repast, despite the matching spelling.
Name for [[see:Brisbane]] in a local language, meaning spike of land.
Just means spots or blemishes; Middle English measel was an adjective meaning leprous.
In Old English any food, nourishment or meal, from a root meaning moist or wet; by the 1300s it meant flesh, replacing [[see:flesh meat]].
Originally meant any food, hence [[see:green meat]], [[see:white meat]] and [[see:flesh meat]]; it also explains [[see:sweetmeats]].
Somewhere men go to strut; another name for [[see:the Dilly]].
Also called the Turk, a supposedly autonomous chess-playing [[see:automaton]] first displayed in 1770, though apparently it wasn't.
Sexual attraction to cars and machines.
French for a doctor, not medicine.
Books linking mythology and morality to animals, with oddly drawn human-faced lions; Jess suspects overlap with the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Rob calls this an Americanism that Britons wouldn't use.
Greek monster whose name is now the genus name for jellyfish, their tendrils resembling her snaky hair; compare French [[same-root:méduse]].
French for [[equivalent:jellyfish]], which led Rob's wife to call a jellyfish a medusa in English.
A Russian name meaning bear, which Rob tried to link to the rise of [[see:Bear]].
German for [[equivalent:mermaid]], with Meer, the sea, and specifying a young lady.
Ultimately related to the mail in [[same-root:blackmail]].
Pop-culturalised fear of very big things, celebrated on subreddits, like the stomach-drop at a wide shot of a blue whale.
Named in 1824, the first dinosaur named before the word existed; described by [[see:William Buckland]] from Stonesfield fossils and mentioned in [[see:Bleak House]].
The [[see:humpback whale]]'s binomial, meaning great winged of New England, after its long fins; its pter element appears in [[same-root:helicopter]] and [[same-root:pterodactyl]].
A hyphenated Scottish dialect word for a spider, using the Margaret nickname found in [[see:magpie]].
A Scottish dialect word for a centipede, a companion to [[see:meggy-licky-spinny]].
A Chinese-named dinosaur meaning sleeping dragon, ending in [[from:long (Chinese)]].
Mandarin name for America, chosen because mei sounds a bit like America, with [[see:guó]] added.
Proposed name for [[see:Canberra]], blending Melbourne, Adelaide, Sydney, Perth and [[see:Brisbane]].
One of the humours; Jess believes the word means dark bile.
Literally black bile, the humour whose excess caused sadness; the chol- part matches [[same-root:choleric]] and [[same-root:cholera]], the melan- part [[same-root:melanin]].
Often thought beautiful but literally 'black bile', one of the four humours of [[see:humorism]].
A pretentious substitute for 'mix', which is all it means in French.
The dark pigment in skin, sharing the melan- element meaning black with [[same-root:melancholy]].
Named after [[see:William Lamb]], Viscount Melbourne; earlier called [[see:Batmania]], [[see:Bareberp]] and Bearbrass; its Indigenous name is [[see:Naarm]].
Derbyshire village near Rob's home, locally pronounced 'Melbun', meaning mill stream; it gave its title to the Viscount after whom [[see:Melbourne (Australia)]] is named.
A name meaning honeybee, from the Greek word for honey.
The study of bees, from the Greek word for honey, like [[same-root:Melissa]].
Name of dime museums and a Boston music hall, cited alongside [[see:nickelodeon]].
Meaning music plus action, from Greek elements, like [[see:melody]] and [[see:drama]]; existing since the 1700s and common in early silent films.
One of the book's collective nouns for people rather than animals.
Draws on the same Greek word for apple as [[same-root:chamomile]].
Rob speculates that it could be related to [[same-root?:merengue]] through an R and L swap.
Linked at a more basic level to [[same-root:mollusk]].
English town famous for pork pies that claims to be the birthplace of [[see:paint the town red]].
French mythical woman, half two-tailed serpent, who left husband [[see:Raymond]] after he broke his promise not to see her on Saturdays, her bath day.
Coined by [[see:Richard Dawkins]] in 1976 for a unit of cultural transmission, abbreviated from Greek [[from:mimeme]] to sound like [[see:gene]]; internet sense from 1998.
Dawkins said [[see:meme]] could be thought of as related to this French word, though it isn't.
Field arising from Dawkins's book, analogous to genetics, seeking to explain how ideas propagate; derived from [[from:meme]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the mantis in [[same-root:praying mantis]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with the mantis in [[same-root:praying mantis]].
One of the thinking words related to [[same-root:money]].
Dawkins said [[see:meme]] could be thought of as related to memory, though it isn't.
Related to [[same-root:mountain]], sharing its sticking-out sense.
Named after Russian scientist [[from:Dmitri Mendeleev]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
A good guy; borrowed from [[from:Yiddish]], probably in New York, and ultimately from the German for person.
German for person, probably borrowed via [[from:Yiddish]]; used kindly in English, as in a real mensch.
Basically means monthlies, overlapping with [[same-root:month]] and [[same-root:moon]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
Linked to [[same-root:moon]] and [[same-root:month]] through [[same-root:menses]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:mentor]].
A French adjective applied to the Anglo-Saxon noun brain, perhaps because of medicine's love of foreign words.

Botanical name for the [[see:daffodil]], after the youth in [[see:Ovid]]'s Metamorphoses who loved his own reflection and died, a flower growing where he died.
Beautiful youth in love with his own reflection who rejected Echo and faded away, giving [[gave:narcissism]] and the flower [[gave:narcissus]].
Handsome youth of Greek myth cursed to love his own reflection in a pool, loved in vain by [[see:Echo]]; source of [[gave:narcissism]].
Shares the Greek root meaning numbness with [[same-root:narcissism]].
From a Greek root meaning numbness, deadness or stupor; shortened to [[gave:narc]].
The older spelling for a snitch, Victorian prison slang for a policeman's spy, which influenced [[gave:narc]].
A police informer, recorded in the 1800s and thought to come from a Romani word for nose; not ultimately related to [[unrelated:narc]], though influenced by it.
Sexual interest in obscene words.
Most likely corpse whale, because its mottled grey body looked like a corpse under the surface; alternatively linked to [[from?:nál]], needle, for its tusk.
Named after [[from:Francis Nash]].
Italian for Christmas, from Latin [[from:natalis]], birth, like [[same-root:Noël]].
The ICAO spelling alphabet, a century in the making, moving from place names to personal names; words were chosen to be pronounceable across languages.
The German word for [[same-root:adder]], keeping the original initial N.
The branch of [[see:astrology]] foretelling tides, seasons and eclipses.
A [[see:retronym]]: satellite meant any natural orbiting object until Sputnik was launched.
Confused with [[see:naturism]], mirroring the confusion of [[see:astronomy]] and [[see:astrology]].
One of Farmer and Henley's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]].
Confused with [[see:naturalism]], as [[see:astronomy]] is with [[see:astrology]], which can lead people to judge you very differently.
Literally having nothing; went from neutral to negative through [[see:pejoration]], like [[see:villain]].
Greek for ship, the source of many English words connected with sailing, such as [[gave:nausea]] and [[gave:navicular]].
The feeling that you are going to vomit; it literally means seasickness or ship sickness, from [[from:naus]].
Literally means seasickness, so feeling nauseated is feeling as if seasick.
Greek for sailor, from [[from:naus]], and the source of [[gave:nautical]].
Comes from Greek [[from:nautes]], sailor.
The famous boat from [[see:20,000 Leagues Under the Sea]]; its name is basically a poetic form of the Greek word for sailor.
A swirly-shelled cephalopod whose name means sailor; bestiaries described it sailing with outspread arms, an image perhaps from the [[see:argonaut]]. Jess thinks the ship was named after it.
The central part of a church, separated from the [[see:aisle]]s by rows of pillars.
The everyday expression that [[equivalent:omphaloskepsis]] literally means.
Means boat-shaped and comes from the same ship root as [[same-root:nautical]].
Spanish for Christmas, from Latin [[from:natalis]], birth, like [[same-root:Noël]].
Given as an example of a word from the same ship root as [[same-root:nautical]].
Jess calls it 'oceaniness'; the model on which [[gave:aviation]] was coined.
Given as an example of a word from the same ship root as [[same-root:nautical]].
Thought to be from Old Norse, a compound of not and ever, literally not ever; Swedish still says nej; compare Old English [[see:no]].
Comes from the Neander Valley.
Means cloudy; probably cognate with [[same-root?:Neptune]].
Former N, replaced by [[see:November]] because it could be confused with vector and sector and was hard for foreign speakers.
Another name-based word for donkeys, cited with [[see:jackass]] as support for the [[see:Duncan]] theory of [[see:donkey]].
Slang for money that Rob likes, as in not having quite enough needful.
Middle English examples of a negg for an egg, understandable among mostly illiterate people who only heard it.
Back-formed from [[from:negotiation]]; its first known instance is in Shakespeare.
Named after Italian aristocrat [[from:Camillo Negroni]], who had gin added to his usual sweet vermouth, Campari and soda.
German (and Dutch nemen) for to take; these West Germanic languages have no word like English [[see:take]].
German for no, which nine may sound too much like, one suggested reason for [[see:niner]].
Said to a hunter before a hunt, hoping they catch no game or bird; the Russian [[equivalent:break a leg]], answered with [[see:go to hell]].
From Nemesis, goddess of retribution; the Greek means distribution of what is due, related to [[same-root:numerous]].
McWhorter's name for [[see:algospeak]] substitutes, which make speakers look daring, as if they were dodging a taboo.
Means free-market capitalism: deregulation, privatisation and reduced government, the opposite of what Americans call [[see:liberal]] beliefs.
Its etymology literally means new word.
Means new; discovered by [[see:William Ramsay]] and [[see:Morris Travers]], who also found it glows in glass tubes, soon used for neon signs.
A French word for extended family, reflecting the Norman nobility's interest in lineage.
Corresponds to [[see:Poseidon]], name probably cognate with [[same-root?:nebula]]; identified in the 1800s from its pull on [[see:Uranus]], though [[see:Galileo]] had seen it.
Named after the planet Neptune.
A thoroughly ameliorated insult about a century old, once spelled nert, probably a college slang variant of [[from?:nut]]; also appears in [[see:If I Ran the Zoo]].
Emily Brontë's cat, a fitting name for a cat, jokingly fiddling with yarn as Rome burned.
A suffix called the friend of every Scrabble player wanting to extend a word.
Norse word for coastal areas, probably related to the river name [[same-root?:Ness (river)]].
Scottish Gaelic river name, probably meaning fast-moving water; probably related to Norse [[same-root?:ness (headland)]].
Shortening of [[from:Loch Ness Monster]] in use by the 1940s.

translation: Ness dweller with a diamond-shaped fin

mentions.note: Scientific name for the [[see:Loch Ness Monster]], coined in 1975 by [[see:Peter Scott]] and [[see:Robert Rines]], possibly as a joke, to classify and protect it.
Short for the internet, more common decades ago (on the net), now passé like [[see:cyber]]; a brand using it would seem fussy.
A 1998 quotation about a dancing baby animation; early uses of [[see:meme]] specified net or web because memes weren't yet exclusively online.
Like [[see:basketball]] without bouncing or a backboard; players stay still, only the goal attack and goal shooter can score, and Rob wonders which came first.
Its name preserves the old word [[see:flicks]].
Rob's proposed name for the people of the Netherlands, freeing [[see:Dutchland]] for Germany.
A system shaped physically or figuratively like a net, dating back to the 1500s, when spiderwebs and artistic elements were described as networks.
The study of the neurons or nerves, more broadly the brain, contrasted with [[see:psychiatry]].
Formed by putting n- before ever, like [[see:nay]].
[[see:back slang]] for seven.
Original name of the tip of Manhattan, reflecting the Dutch settlement that brought [[see:Santa Claus]] to America.
The Dutch settlement's name, after Amsterdam, which grew from [[see:Fort Amsterdam]] and became [[gave:New York]] under English control.
From Spanish Nueva Guinea, a name given in 1545 by a Spanish explorer who sighted the island's north coast, after [[from:Guinea]].
Named after [[from:Philippe II, Duke of Orléans]], whose title comes from a place; like [[see:New York]].
Compared with [[see:Berlin]] as another city built on a swamp.
John Gay's poem full of elaborate similes, including [[see:cool as a cucumber]] and [[see:drunk as a piper]].
First Dutch [[from:New Amsterdam]], renamed in 1664 after the [[from:Duke of York]], not directly after the city of [[see:York]].
Discussed often in earlier episodes of the podcast.

Simply means new things, like the earlier French [[see:nouvelles]]; not an acronym of [[unrelated:notable events, weather and sports]] or [[unrelated:north, east, south and west]].
Rob and Danny say it with a y sound and Jess without, an example of [[see:yod dropping]].

A neologism coined as a gender-neutral word for a niece or nephew, filling a lexical gap.
Once closer to [[see:naive]]: foolish in the 1200s, then fussy, dainty, precise, agreeable, and finally kind and thoughtful by the 1800s.
A [[see:hendiadys]] meaning nicely cozy.
The OED's example of [[see:hendiadys]], instead of nicely warm.
A biscuit the hosts guess must be named after the French city of Nice, though neither knows for sure.

A [[see:theophoric]] name meaning victory people, whose Nick- is the same as in [[same-root:Nike (goddess)]].

Discussed on the podcast before; the hosts joke about doing a whole episode on Nicks.
Previously discussed as a recurring reference to the devil, recalled by the spelling nickumpoop for [[see:nincompoop]].

A hidden reference to the [[see:devil]], which the hosts say they have discussed a lot before.
Its name has a story very similar to that of [[see:cobalt]].

The metal's name contains the same nickel as [[same-root:pumpernickel]].
From German [[from:Kupfernickel]], copper goblin, named by miners for copper-coloured ore that yields no copper; nickel has long been a nickname for the devil.
Now a pay TV channel; originally a theatre showing films for a nickel, plus a Greek element for a roofed theatre, as in [[see:Odeon]].
Originally an ekename, eke meaning additional; rebracketed, perhaps influenced by folk etymology from [[see:Nick]].

German word compared with [[see:nay]], showing n- added to make a negative.

1940s film, recently remade, that popularised the sideshow sense of [[see:geek]].
A term poets sometimes use for midnight, from [[from:meridian]].

Generator of niter, from Greek [[from:nitron]], sodium carbonate, because the gas was identified in nitric acid and potassium nitrate.

Every Norton is the north [[from:-ton]], or north town.

original: nordmenn er født med ski på beina
translation: Norsemen are born with ski on leg

Means northern [[from:wick]], a city in [[see:East Anglia]].
Another very old word for a part of the face.
The film adaptation of [[see:Dracula]]; possibly from Romanian [[from?:nesuferitul]], insufferable one, or Greek [[from?:nosophoros]], disease carrier.
Latinised Greek for homecoming grief, coined by a Swiss medical student to translate [[from:Heimweh]]; an 1830s medical description helped move it into popular culture.
Middle English citations of nostrich instead of ostrich, a rebracketing that didn't survive into Modern English.

From Old English for 'nose hole'; its ending is related to [[same-root:thrill]].
German for emergency, as in [[see:Notausgang]], not English 'not'.

term: not all who wander are lost

Not playing by the rules or in the right spirit; first said by cricket players about the game itself, as in an 1867 quote, then applied to everyday life.

term: not for all the tea in China

mentions.note: Meaning under no circumstances or at any price, from the late 19th century, because tea was a costly import.

term: not in a Month of Sundays

mentions.note: Sundays dragged because of religious restrictions, so a month of them is very long; an 1849 letter links it to there being no Sunday post.
Another English way of saying something will never happen, like [[equivalent:when pigs fly]].

term: not my circus, not my monkeys

mentions.note: A favourite idiom of Jess's for disclaiming responsibility; Polish had it first, and Jess wonders whether English got it from Polish.
A gentler way of saying no or not precisely, a softening use related to [[see:quite]].

term: not to be handled with a pair of tongs

mentions.note: Dates to 1643; the OED suggests a link to Envy's long tongs of hatred in Chaucer's [[see?:The Parson's Tale]].
A false acronymic explanation of [[see:news]].
German for emergency exit; someone knowing only that Ausgang means exit might read it as 'not the exit' and turn away.
A banknote is essentially a promise to pay the bearer, as British notes state, rather than the money itself.
Called [[from:Snottingham]] until fairly recently, meaning settlement of the people of [[from:Snot]], a fact enjoyed in rival Derby.
The British name for the game whose grid looks like the # symbol; Americans call it [[equivalent:tic-tac-toe]].
Another name for [[see:collective noun]]s.
Earlier French term meaning new things, used in much the same way as [[see:news]].
Name meaning New Rome that Constantine gave to [[see:Byzantium]] before it became [[see:Constantinople]].
Adjective meaning relating to New York, containing [[from:Eboracum]] and the demonym ending [[from:-ensian]].
Compared with the nov meaning new in [[see:Nizhny Novgorod]].
The very last change before the NATO alphabet was finalised, replacing [[see:Nectar]].

term: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
original: nu komt de aap uit de mouw
translation: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve

mentions.note: The Dutch [[equivalent:spill the beans]], possibly from a magic trick; the hosts say it has [[see:let the cat out of the bag]] energy.
Listed in Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall for annoyance, but both forms already existed in Old French, so it may not be English rebracketing.
A placeholder number, as in for the nth time or to the nth degree.
Cute German slang term for sex.
German for pasta generally, even spaghetti, which annoys Rob; related to English [[same-root:noodle]].
[[from:nuron]] with L for R, rejected as too close to an existing trademark and because adverts would say 'new nulon'.
Another word with a silent final MB, compared with [[see:plumber]].
Another of the few French words among the 100 most-used English words, alongside [[see:people]].
Given to English by French; without it, Rob conjectures, we'd probably say [[see:tally]].
Origin uncertain: perhaps a lottery or draft number, or biblical passages about the number of one's days, such as [[from?:Job 38:21]].
To be number one is called too obvious to need explaining, like other number-one idioms.
The creepy inscription at [[see:Belshazzar]]'s feast foretelling his overthrow; mene mene is sometimes said instead of [[equivalent:the writing on the wall]], almost a shibboleth.
Related to [[same-root:nemesis]] through the idea of allocating.
From Greek [[from:nomisma]]; Rob learned it from a coin-collecting YouTube channel, and Jess knew the editor of a numismatics magazine.
Another parental-figure word, related to [[same-root:nana]]; Old English also had [[see:mynecen]], a female monk.
A Middle English word for a noon draught or noon drink of ale, older than [[gave?:luncheon]], which was probably modelled on it.
The flight of male ants and queens, which Jess says isn't confined to a single day, unlike the British [[see:flying ants day]].
[[from:no-run]] turned around, rejected because it sounded like a nerve tonic.
The word Scott actually wrote, misread as the ghost word [[see:morse]].
The usual British term, rather than [[equivalent:kindergarten]].
Meaning head, from prison slang.
The nutshell paragraph explaining a story's essential point; nut is the core essence, and [[see:graf]] is short for paragraph.
Someone from Connecticut, the Nutmeg State, possibly from Yankee pedlars selling counterfeit wooden nutmegs in colonial times, though that may be apocryphal.
N in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet, after [[see:Monkey]] for M.
Not New York plus London: [[see:DuPont]]'s Fibre 66 went from [[from:no-run]] to [[from:nuron]], [[from:nulon]] and [[from:nilon]], taking -on from [[see:cotton]] and [[see:rayon]].

Rob suggests it comes from the Titans, wondering whether the [[see:Cyclopes]] were Titans.
Named after the [[from:Titans]], perhaps for its strength or because they were sons of the earth.
The British form of [[equivalent:tidbit]], which Jess finds hilarious; Rob compares its tit- to the small bird [[see:titmouse]].
The British spelling; Americans may prefer tidbit to avoid saying [[see:tit]], though the hosts doubt it, since Americans still say [[see:titmouse]].
A tenth owed to the church, ultimately from the same root as [[same-root:dime]].
A protein, and a much more concise name for the thing that the enormous chemical word [[see:methionylthreonylthreonylglutaminylalanyl…]] spells out.
The patron devil of printing, blamed for scribes' errors from the 13th century and later for typos in print shops, like 1631's 'Thou shalt commit adultery'.
Shares its Latin origin, titulus, with [[same-root:tilde]].
A very small bird whose name Rob compares with [[see:titbit]].
A bird name Americans still use, which undermines the idea that they avoid [[see:tit]].
A collective noun that makes Rob titter.
The dot on an i or j, added so i could be told apart from u, m and n; paired with [[see:jot]] in Matthew 5:18.
The dot on an I or J, also from Latin titulus like [[same-root:tilde]].
Gave Jess nightmares: obscenely bloody and depraved, with people baked into pies; hard to believe the author of As You Like It wrote it.
Anglo-Saxon god behind [[gave:Tuesday]], related to Norse [[see:Tyr]].
The Germanic god of war after whom [[see:Tuesday]] is named.
An existing British shop whose name is why [[see:TJ Maxx]] became TK Maxx in Britain.
The US store is called [[see:TK Maxx]] in Britain, as it could be confused with the existing shop [[see:TJ Hughes]].
Short for to come, marking something to fill in later, as in pre-written obituaries; spelled TK because that combination is rare in English.
The British name for [[see:TJ Maxx]], chosen to avoid confusion with [[see:TJ Hughes]].
Aztec rulers in the stratum beneath the [[see:huey tlatoani]]; the word means speaker, which sounds very modern.
Ramming a word inside another, as in [[see:unflippingbelievable]], [[see:fan-bloody-tastic]] or [[see:a whole nother]].
The English infinitive particle and Old English preposition; with more Norse influence it might have been [[see:at]], and [[see:till]] took over some uses.
The T is most likely short for [[from?:tittle]], the dot on an i or j.
Not from [[see:badger]]s' behaviour but from the dogs' relentless attacks in [[from:badger baiting]].
Also to have game: an old phrase meaning to have the mettle or fighting spirit for a contest, apparently comparing someone to a [[see:gamecock]].

term: to be or not to be, that is the question

mentions.note: The iconic [[see:hyperbaton]], from Hamlet's soliloquy, instead of the question is to be or not to be.
An Old English way of saying to die, possibly euphemistic, before Old Norse [[see:to die]] took over.
An emphatic phrase implying an advantage, with the same sense found in the source of [[same-root:booty]].
Ruled out as an Americanism in the Guardian's 1950 style guide in favour of "so far", though now widely used in Britain.
Borrowed from Old Norse, possibly as a euphemism; it displaced the Old English verb that became [[see:starve]].
One of the ordinary words avoided in [[see:algospeak]].
Verb from Old Norse; before it, English used the word that became [[see:starve]], like German [[same-root:sterben]].
A big to-do means the same as a big [[equivalent:ado]], made with the English infinitive particle.

A big fuss, essentially the same as [[equivalent:ado]].
Euphemism for sex used from the 1600s onwards.
A verb that sounds modern, but [[see:William Shakespeare]] is its first recorded written user.
False expansion of [[see:tip]]; Rob once objected it should spell TEP, though [[see:ensure]] and [[see:insure]] are etymologically the same word.
To table an idea means putting it forward in British usage but setting it aside in American business usage.
A disliked usage discussed before as a contronym, since it can mean either taking something off the table or putting it on.
An earlier French phrase meaning to make someone angry, perhaps by stealing their goat; a variant of [[equivalent:get someone's goat]].
One of the nouns that [[see:William Shakespeare]] turned into verbs.
For Jess mainly the red-and-white [[see:amanita]]; in England a thin stem with a flat top, something a toad might sit on.

Thought to be related to words meaning to point or show, like [[same-root:indicate]], and perhaps somehow to [[same-root?:finger]]; some languages manage without a separate word.
Spelled with toe, not tow: British naval seamen lined up for inspection with their toes against the seams of the deck.
A First World War name for a large spherical mortar shell, wrongly said to be behind [[unrelated:how do you like them apples]].
Oxford University shortening that Rob thinks referred to a boat in one of the boat races, alongside [[see:soccer]] and [[see:rugger]].
Itself a euphemism, from a French word for a towel.
Flushing toilets date to about 2500 BCE in [[see:Mohenjo-Daro]], long before [[see:Thomas Crapper]], who is falsely associated with them.
English toilet adapted to Japanese syllable rules, an example alongside [[see:bīru]] and [[see:katsu]].
Formerly [[from:Edo]], renamed in 1868 after the Meiji Restoration as the eastern capital, east of [[see:Kyoto]]; the shared kyo explains the anagram.
Paired with tabby and [[see:Tabitha]] as a name for cats.
[[see:Francis Grose]]'s friend, who went out with him at night collecting street speech; the hosts joke about his name.
The best example of [[see:dick]] used as an everyman name.
Listed among the English [[see:placeholder names]] for people.
An insult found in a [[see:nincompoop]] citation ('pitiful lousy Tom Farthing'); it sounds Dickensian or like a [[see:Jack Sprat]]-type character.
An American who supposedly coined [[see:couch potato]] in 1976 for himself and his TV-watching friends, but never explained the name.
A teenage genius inventor in [[see:Edward Stratemeyer]]'s syndicate books whose electric rifle inspired the [[see:taser]].
Fictional character who debuted in novels in 1910, wielder of the rifle behind [[see:taser]] and inspiration for [[see:Tom Swifty]].

term: Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle

mentions.note: Also called Daring Adventures in Elephant Land; involves killing many elephants and native people, with offensive language, and inspired the [[gave:taser]].
A quoted sentence whose attribution makes a pun, as in "We're out of flowers," said Tom lackadaisically; a recurring trope of the [[see:Tom Swift]] books.
Botanically a berry; from the Aztec language, where it means the swelling fruit, and introduced to Europe only after the age of conquest.
In Johnson's dictionary it wasn't specific to girls; a boy could be a tomboy too.
A war nickname compared with [[see:Johnny Law]].
Means the next morning, built on [[from:morrow]].
The precursor of [[gave:town]], as in [[see:Norton]], [[see:Sutton]], [[see:Southampton]] and [[see:Boston]].
Loosely related to [[same-root:thunder]] far back.
Originally spelled tung; the -gue spelling was an overcorrection meant to guide pronunciation, and it makes the word look like French [[see:langue]].
Billy Joel's reversal of [[see:gin and tonic]] in a song, done for the rhyme, which catches the ear.

term: too many irons in the fire

mentions.note: From blacksmithing: with too many irons heating at once, one can burn until it becomes unworkable.
Related to [[same-root:dental]] through regular consonant shifts.
An example of the Germanic habit of compounding.
Spice mix used in Moroccan cooking, supposedly a merchant's mix of their best spices, or alternatively one prepared above the shop.
In [[see:attache ta tuque]] a winter hat; it can also mean a chef's hat or something shaped like one.
Rarest Crayola, made 1997–1998 before becoming [[see:Scarlet]]; named for Paralympian [[see:Gary K. Woodring]], the torch being the Olympic torch.
One of Jess's favourite terms for drunk.
One of Jess's favourite terms for drunk.
An insulting term for a fiddler.
An insulting term for a drummer.
Coined in English in the early 1500s from Spanish [[from:tronada]], thunderstorm, reshuffled by metathesis under [[see:tornar]], to turn; Spanish later borrowed it back.

translation: where there are trees standing in the water

mentions.note: From Mohawk tkaronto for where there are trees standing in the water, describing Wendat fish weirs of saplings between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching; unrelated to [[unrelated:Taranto]].
Often mistranslated as bull lizard but probably from a Greek verb meaning to perforate, after holes in its frill; [[see:Triceratops]] was once wrongly thought to be its juvenile.
Latin for the electric ray, from a word meaning to be numb, like [[same-root:torpor]]; used from 1776 for a floating mine, later self-propelled explosives.
An English place whose name means hill hill hill, an example of a repetitive name.
Related to [[same-root:torpedo]] through the sense of numbness.
Shares the twisting root of [[same-root:extortion]].
Originally fear of being shut outside medieval city gates at night; now anxiety that time is running out for life goals. Jess links it to [[see:panic]].
A made-up disease from South Park, offered as a quiz option.
From Middle English tortuse, with spelling influenced by [[see:porpoise]], and from Latin for twisted, perhaps for their feet, or possibly from [[from?:Tartarus]].
The French word for both turtle and tortoise, misheard in English as [[see:turtle]].
Related to [[same-root:tortoise]] through the sense of twisted.
Johnson called it a cant term, probably derived from an Irish word meaning a savage.
Nonsense, thought to come from the junk the [[from?:tosher]] pulled out of the sewers.
A Victorian who waded through London's sewers for items to salvage and sell; probably the source of [[gave?:tosh]].
Equivalent in origin and meaning to calling someone a [[see:plonker]].
[[see:tabloidese]] for child on British front pages, now dying out somewhat.
Rugby name for the lines at the side of the pitch, not at the end.
A satisfyingly apt but false expansion of [[see:tag (game)]].
A sports term turned corporate jargon, tolerable because it works across contexts.
One of the many baseball idioms Jess lists as common in American everyday language.
One of the American football terms taken from rugby, though Rob hasn't heard it used in modern rugby.
Named after [[from:Georges Gilles de la Tourette]]; poorly understood when [[see:coprolalia]] was coined, it's now known not to require obscenity.
Descends from the place-name ending [[from:-ton]].
Another name for [[see:baseball]] used in New York and the Great Lakes region until the early 19th century.
A [[see:therapy speak]] label now often used to describe people you disagree with.
In French the name is pronounced like merdeux, which roughly means shitty.
Named as related to [[same-root:trek]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]].
Spacing across an entire line, as opposed to [[see:kerning]].
From the same Old English verb as [[same-root:tread]]: your trade is the path you choose to tread in life.
What spies call their work, an example of deliberately dull, non-specific terms chosen so that anyone overhearing them learns nothing.
Term for a brand name becoming the generic word for a thing, as happened with [[see:Hoover]], [[see:zipper]] and [[see:Jacuzzi]].
When a brand name becomes so generic it loses its capital letter and its owner loses the trademark, also called [[see:genericide]].
Another name for a [[see:roundabout]].
Another name for a [[see:roundabout]].
An old British portmanteau of traffic and [[from:indicators]], still used in Nigerian English.
A subreddit mocking creatively spelled baby names, named after a real name supposedly given to a child.
From Greek [[from:tragos]], goat, plus the -ody song ending shared with [[same-root:comedy]]: a goat song, perhaps because a goat was the prize in early ode competitions.
The only fox hunting allowed in England and Wales: hounds hunt a laid trail rather than foxes, though they may still chase a fox they find.
The forced removal after which Creek families from [[see:Tallahassee]] resettled in Indian Territory, bringing the name that became [[see:Tulsa]].
Shares a pull or draw root with [[same-root:trek]]; strictly the whole set of vehicles that trails behind the [[see:locomotive]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]].
British term for enthusiasts who wait by the tracks to spot trains or engines they haven't seen before; the equivalent of a [[equivalent:railfan]].
Disturbing film whose glossary of strong Edinburgh dialect came up when Rob searched for [[see:trainspotter]] jargon.
Typeface inspired by the lettering on [[from:Trajan's Column]] in Rome.
Named for tramping across the country, and once romanticised.
One of the high-yield Latin prefixes Jess lists as basic and easy to guess.
A relationship where you give something to get something.
Compared with [[see:Transylvania]]: 'trans' means across or on the other side.
Patients redirecting feelings from earlier relationships onto the analyst; the English rendering of Freud's German [[from:Übertragung]].
From French, literally to carry across; Britain says public transport where Americans say [[see:transportation]].
Its port is the same element as in [[same-root:disport]], which shows the idea of carrying something away.
Preferred in Britain for public transport because [[see:transportation]] had meant shipping convicts abroad.
Once usual in British English too, but it fell out of use there after becoming the name for the punishment of shipping convicts to the Americas and Australia.
In Britain it came to mean sending convicts to Australia, which is why Britons say public [[see:transport]] rather than public transportation.
One of the [[see:Kama Sutra]] sex positions in English translation.
Etymologically means the same as [[same-root:travesty]], which is a figurative wearing of someone else's clothes.
Basically a doublet of [[same-root:travesty]], with a different ending and sense.
Means beyond the forest; its 'sylvania' matches [[same-root:Pennsylvania]], and 'trans' works as in [[see:transatlantic]].
Means beyond the woods, from Latin [[from:silva]], so roughly the same idea as [[see:forest]].
Jess's other American word for waste, as in trash bag, with a British equivalent in [[equivalent:rubbish]].
Not a name for a waste collector, unlike [[see:garbage person]], because it is an insult.
A common British term for drunk from the linguists' list.
Listed as an example of [[see:therapy speak]].
Also from French [[from:travailler]]; an [[see:etymological doublet]] of [[same-root:travel]].
French for to work, not to move around; the source of English [[gave:travel]] and [[gave:travail]].
A variant of [[same-root:travail]] from French [[from:travailler]], to work, so it implies a rough journey.
Spelled with two L's in Britain but one in America; Jess prefers the double L, since a single L suggests a long E.

From trans and [[from:vestire]], to clothe across, via [[from:travestir]], dressed in disguise; first a burlesque keeping a serious work's characters, then any grotesque distortion; a doublet of [[same-root:transvestite]].
One of the earliest phrases using [[see:travesty]] for a grotesquely inadequate version of something.
Comes from the same Old English verb as [[same-root:trade]].
Danish for making a blunder, like [[equivalent:put your foot in it]]; the hosts don't know why it's spinach and ask viewers.
Related to [[same-root:thesaurus]].
An iconic novel that romanticised the golden age of piracy and popularised many pirate phrases.
From Old English, helped by a similar Old Norse word; traced to a PIE root meaning steadfast, shared with [[same-root:true]] and [[same-root:durable]].
Aviation pronunciation of three, one of the number forms meant to be understood over poor radio.
Shares a root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:true]].
The Old English term for a [[equivalent:carpenter]], which Jess says makes more literal sense than the French word.
Old English term for a carpenter, later replaced by a French word.
Originally travel by ox-drawn cart, from a Dutch word meaning to draw or pull; related to [[same-root:drag]], [[same-root:draw]], [[same-root:track]] and [[same-root:train]].
Originally Dutch for to draw or pull, entering English in the 1850s via [[from:Afrikaans]]; related to [[same-root:drag]], [[same-root:track]] and [[same-root:train]].
The French two dots, which separate two vowel sounds rather than altering the vowel as the German [[see:umlaut]] does.
A Boston street that still carries the name [[from:Trimountaine]].
The Old English word for a carpenter and a favourite of both hosts; it was later replaced by [[see:carpenter]].
In French this relative of [[same-root:trespass]] means to die, to pass over.
German term for thinking of the perfect comeback too late, equivalent to French [[equivalent:l'esprit de l'escalier]].
An old word meaning a sin, as in prayers, from Latin [[from:transpassare]], to pass beyond; in English, to cross a border; compare French [[same-root:trépasser]].
The original Scottish word behind [[gave:trousers]], related to Irish [[same-root:truis]].
The second word of the two-seed [[see:Wordle]] opening, played after [[see:cones]].
From German [[from:Trias]], after three rock layers: [[see:Keuper]], [[see:Muschelkalk]] and [[see:Buntsandstein]]; in this period there was only [[see:Pangaea]].
Means three-horned face; once wrongly thought to be a juvenile [[see:Torosaurus]], and the source of the name [[gave:Sera]].
Shares the horn element of [[same-root:monoceros]].
An example of the now gender-neutral [[see:-ster]] ending.
Same origin as [[same-root:truffle]], meaning a trick or frippery; a layered dessert named after something frivolous, like the [[see:fool]] and [[see:Eton mess]].
Rob's nan's sherry trifle had layers of sherry-soaked sponge, jelly or jam, custard and whipped cream; in America almost anything layered in a clear dish counts.
Possibly named for how fast they move; the reef triggerfish's Hawaiian name is [[see:humuhumunukunukuapua'a]].
Literally triangle measurement, sharing the measurement element of [[same-root:geometry]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:knee]].
Like [[see:digraphs]], combinations of letters standing for one sound.
A hieroglyph representing three consonants at once, like the [[see:scarab beetle]], which can write [[see:kheper]].
On the [[see:long scale]], the number following the British trillion.
An American trillion equals the British [[see:billion]] on the [[see:long scale]].
Means three months, not a division into three, which Rob realised during his wife's pregnancy.
Related to [[same-root:month]].
A French-derived name used by early Puritan settlers for [[see:Boston]]'s hilly peninsula, still carried by [[gave:Tremont Street]].
Three feet, an example of the -pod ending for feet seen in [[same-root:theropod]].
Means three cities, the coastal settlements of Oea, Sabratha and Leptis Magna in the wider region of [[see:Tripolitania]]; from [[from:polis]].
The wider region containing the three coastal settlements that gave [[see:Tripoli]] its name.
Sets of three consonants that carry a Semitic word's meaning; English [[see:woman]] works a little like one.
From [[from:via]]: three roads, a junction where Romans traded goods and news; the fun-fact sense dates from [[see:Logan Pearsall Smith]]'s 1902 book series Trivia.
Describes inconsequential street talk, like the commoners' chatter at the Roman crossroads of [[from:trivia]].
The three classical arts of grammar, logic and rhetoric, studied before the [[see:quadrivium]]; coined in the Carolingian Renaissance and the basis of today's liberal arts.
A Latin-derived feminine ending that has fallen out of use, surviving in [[see:dominatrix]] and [[see:aviatrix]].
Reportedly used for people from Michigan's Lower Peninsula because they live under the bridge.
The monster, which is unrelated to [[unrelated:trolley]].
From a 1992 [[see:Usenet]] user called Troll who incited arguments, evoking both [[see:trolling]] ships and a [[see:bridge troll]]; now any bad-faith online behaviour.
Named because it trolls, meaning strolls or rolls around; unrelated to [[unrelated:troll]] but related to [[same-root:shopping trolley]].
As a ship trolls, one image behind the internet [[see:troll]].
Another word Johnson admitted he didn't know the meaning of, and the hosts think nobody does.
Means a large [[from:trumpet]].
One of the American terms for different kinds of police.
Related to [[same-root:tropics]]; a figurative turn, direction or recurring element in storytelling, probably via Latin [[from:tropus]], a turn of phrase.
The northern tropic at about 23.4 degrees, where the sun appears to turn back at the June solstice; used to explain [[see:tropics]].
The other tropic, named alongside the [[see:Tropic of Cancer]] in explaining the sun's apparent reversal.
From Greek [[from:tropos]], turn, after the sun appearing to turn back at the solstice; related to [[same-root:trope]] and [[same-root:zoetrope]].
Latin for a figure of speech, literally a turn of phrase, probably where the storytelling sense of [[gave:trope]] comes from.
The US name for [[see:Frustration]], which had a cute advertising jingle in the 1990s.
British for what Americans call [[equivalent:pants]]; for Jess it is a more specific word for smart business pants.
A Celtic word from Scotland: a plural of [[from:trews]], already a 'pair', with spelling influenced by French [[see:trousse]]; singular trouser survives in fashion retail.
Known from French lessons as a pencil case, it could also mean a kind of trouser, and its spelling shaped English [[see:trousers]].
Probably from [[from:truckle]], a set of small wheels, hence also the railway [[see:bogie]]; Greek trochos, to run, is a less likely source.
The original word, a group of small wheels to help move something; its -le ending marks smallness, giving [[gave:truck]].
Paired with [[see:truth]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Paired with [[see:truth]] as an example of the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Thought to share a PIE root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:tree]].
Shares a root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:tree]].
Its pairing with [[see:truth]] was the model for pairing [[see:rue]] with [[see:ruth]].
One theory links it to the permanent colour of the sky, another to the permanence of blue dye.
Actually the same word as [[same-root:trifle]], both from words meaning trickery.
The Irish word, spelled out by Rob, alongside Scottish [[same-root:trews]].
The old name for a [[see:trumpet]], a hollow tube; in British English it also means a fart, which amuses Brits given [[see:Donald Trump]].
The horn that [[gave:trumpet]] its name, and also British slang for a fart.
Was originally called a [[see:trump]].
Means a small [[from:trump]] or little horn; [[see:trombone]] means a large trumpet.
From the game of trumps, a parallel to [[see:spoof]] coming from a card game.
An Old Frisian compound meaning drum beat, an example of the Germanic compounds resembling [[same-root:drumslade]].
Paired with [[see:truncheon]] as a model for how [[see:luncheon]] was assumed to extend [[see:lunch]].
Paired with [[see:trunch]] as a model for how [[see:luncheon]] was assumed to extend [[see:lunch]].
From French and ultimately Latin, meaning the body of a tree; related to [[same-root:trump]], a hollow tube.
The American word for a car's [[see:boot]].
Puffy Tudor pants that came before [[see:pantaloons]], worn to show off how much fabric you could afford.
Jess pictures a trunk sloshing with bodily humours.
With true, a model for forming [[see:ruth]] from [[see:rue]].
Paired with [[see:true]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Formed from [[from:true]] with the [[see:-th]] suffix.
Noun from true via [[see:-th]], paralleling [[see:mirth]].
The noun paired with [[see:true]], the model for [[see:ruth]].
Once worth no points: scoring one only earned the chance to try for points with the [[see:conversion]]; now worth four or five points.
Spelled tsar or czar, a rendering of [[from:Caesar]] or [[from:Kaiser]].
The informal you, more common in Spain; in Latin America it can seem over-familiar or rude with people who aren't close, unlike [[see:usted]].
A word for a tube, typical of brass names, which the hosts find straightforward.
A bulbous growth on a plant below ground; Rob had to look it up.
Not about tubes but tubers, swellings and lumps, referring to the lymph nodes.
A 1948 car with a centre-mounted headlight that looked cool.
Entertainment about the people the Tudor elites considered trashy.
Named after the Anglo-Saxon god [[from:Tiw]], related to Norse [[see:Tyr]], a war god like Mars; compare [[equivalent:dies Martis]] and [[equivalent:mardi]].
Named after [[from:Tiw]], the Germanic god of war.
Ultimately from Turkish and Persian words for a [[from:turban]], which it resembles; the flower comes from Central Asia, not the Netherlands.
An orchid that looks like a little swaddled baby when blooming.
Named after a town in central France where it was first made.

A plant such as an [[see:amaranth]] that dries into a ball, lets go and rolls around spreading its seeds; around ten plant groups can become one.
An old word for a [[see:porpoise]], used before people called them porpoises.
Came to English from Spanish, which got it from Arabic, Latin and ultimately Greek, from a root probably meaning to dart or rush.
Swedish for perhaps hard stone, though Swedish calls the element wolfram; its symbol W comes from [[see:Wolfram]].
Central English dialect for a ram; Jess guessed it from the 'tupping' line in Othello alongside the [[see:beast with two backs]].
Draws on the rotational, stirring sense of the Latin root of [[same-root:turbulence]].
Draws on the rotational sense of the Latin root of [[same-root:turbulence]].
Violent disturbance, from a Latin root for crowd or confusion that also gave [[same-root:disturb]], [[same-root:perturb]], [[same-root:turbo]] and [[same-root:turbine]].
A rare three-way portmanteau: a deboned chicken inside a deboned duck inside a deboned turkey, assumed to be an American invention.
The bird is named after the country now called [[from:Türkiye]], probably via Turkish traders; the word first meant [[see:guinea fowl]] before passing to the American bird.
First the name of the [[see:guinea fowl]], because Turkish traders sold them into Europe, before it named the North American bird.
Official English spelling of Turkey, reflecting how locals say it and chosen partly so the country isn't named the same as the bird, [[see:turkey]].
Jess thinks it may overlap in sense with [[see:garboil]].
From [[from:Spinal Tap]]'s amp dial going to 11; Jess compares Chico Marx answering '11' in [[see:Duck Soup]].
The US word for [[see:indicators]].
Another idiom from the [[from:Sermon on the Mount]]: if someone strikes your right cheek, offer them the other.
The first carved [[see:jack-o'-lantern]]s were turnips, like the one [[see:Stingy Jack]] put his coal in.
Only certain US roads, like the New Jersey Turnpike, are called this; in Britain the toll-collecting Turnpike Trusts are gone and the word has slipped out of use.
First meant [[see:turtle dove]], imitating its cooing; it came to mean the reptile in the 1600s when French [[see:tortue]] was misheard as turtle.
Nothing to do with reptiles; named turtur after the sound they make.
What Old English [[see:turtle]] referred to, the word imitating its cooing; discussed in an earlier episode.
Named for [[from:Tuxedo, New York]], a wealthy place near Jess.
One of Grose's synonyms for the [[see:monosyllable]].
Originally a trademark, now generic.
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
One of the genericized trademarks Jess found most surprising.
Pronounced differently by Rob and Jess; perhaps from twixt your legs, or a filler sound in songs like twitty twatty, as with [[see:dildo]] and [[see:nonny]].

Probably Rob's favourite play, mainly for [[see:Malvolio]] strutting around making a fool of himself.
