Old English name for the [[see:zodiac]].
An old time-frame word for a year, which the hosts say makes perfect sense.
Used since Old English for a period of twelve months, distinct from the calendar [[see:year]]; it appears in [[see:All Around My Hat]].
The English version of French [[from:vingt-et-un]], the game's name before [[see:blackjack]] replaced it.
A word for an effeminate-looking fellow, silly now but probably nasty then.
Old Germanic word meaning fork, since twigs fork off.
The light between, when the sun is below the horizon; originally it referred to both morning and evening.
Rob glosses it as two lights; Jess corrects this to between lights, since [[see:between]] is related to two.
Johnson called it a vile word, a ludicrous reduplication of [[from:twattle]].
American slang for a quarter dollar: two one-real pieces cut from a piece of eight, a quarter of its value; from [[from:pieces of eight]].
A self-explanatory number-two idiom that refers to no particular game.
Perhaps doubling [[from?:a penny for your thoughts]], the biblical widow's two coins, a gambler's bets or the [[see:two-penny post]].
The British rude gesture with index and middle fingers, the one actually linked to the Agincourt archer story rather than the middle finger.

term: two nations separated by a common language

mentions.note: A description of England and the United States supposedly coined by [[see:George Bernard Shaw]]; the hosts agree the two speak different versions of English, not different languages.
British 'my two penn'orth', a contraction of two pennies' or tuppence worth, possibly predating [[same-root?:two cents]].
Early English postage cost two pennies, a weakly supported explanation of [[see:two cents]].
The taut fabric that holds the paper ready for printing.
From Greek [[from:typos]], figure, image or form but also a blow; the verb comes from the noun.
Has a printing origin very similar to [[see:stereotype]].
The overall style of a character design, unlike a [[see:font]]; literally the face of the type block that makes the impression.
A mix of Greek [[from?:Typhon]], mythical father of storms, an Arabic word for a deluge found in the Quran, and possibly a Cantonese word for great wind.
Norse war god similar to [[see:Tiw]], connected to Mars.
One of the unusual [[see:-cide]] words for killing.
The tyrannical king, unusual because people call it by its full genus-and-species name; it lived closer to us in time than to [[see:Stegosaurus]].
What [[see:democracy]] degenerates into in [[see:Plato]]'s scheme: rule by a [[see:tyrant]].
Someone who seizes power without the legal right to it.
French itself added a T to form it, as it did with [[see:peasant]], the same addition English made to [[see:ancient]].
Originally the same letter as [[same-root:V]], from the ancient forked letter.
Another word English has borrowed from German.
Freud's German term meaning the super I or above I, translated into English as [[gave:superego]].
[[see:Sigmund Freud]]'s own German term, rendered in English as [[equivalent:superego]].
Jess wonders whether it boosted [[see:mensch]]; originally Nietzsche's idea, later associated with the Nazis.
The German word for the day after tomorrow, still in use; the equivalent of [[equivalent:overmorrow]].
Freud's German word for [[gave:transference]], literally a carrying over or 'over-dragging'; also used for transferring money.
From Old Norse [[from:uggligr]], dreadful; unusually based on fear rather than misshapenness, so it implies looks that strike dread.
The German word for a [[equivalent:watch]], which simply means a clock or a time.
Hawaiian for jumping flea; Rob plays one, and the tuning chant [[see:my dog has fleas]] nods to the meaning.
Survives only in ulterior motives; built on [[from:ultra]], beyond, meaning further away than [[see:exterior]].
British designation for 1940s wartime signals intelligence, which decrypted enemy radio and other communications; [[see:Boniface]] was its cover name.
James Joyce's novel, which contains one of the first recorded colloquial uses of [[see:loo]].
Related to [[same-root:somber]] through the idea of shade.
A humble dish of [[from:umbles]] baked in a pie, whose sound made an irresistible pun giving [[gave:humble pie]].
Entrails, usually of a deer, a lowly food given to servants after aristocratic hunts, eaten long before the phrase [[see:humble pie]] existed.
Related to [[same-root:somber]] through the idea of shade.
Means something that shades you from the sun, oddly parallel to [[see:parasol]].
Related to [[same-root:somber]] through the idea of shade.
Both the two dots over a vowel and the phenomenon of vowel change German uses in plurals, which Old English shared, as in [[see:foot]] and feet.
Vowel fronting caused by a lost i in an ending (man/men, foot/feet), and the German two dots marking it; laut is related to [[same-root:loud]].
Middle English noumpere; through [[see:rebracketing]] the N moved to the article, so a noumpere became an umpire.
Originally 'a numpire'; the N moved to the article, an example of [[see:rebracketing]].
A rebracketing example discussed in an earlier episode.
McWhorter predicts it may settle in as one more word for dead, with its own shade of meaning, even after algorithms stop mattering.
ITU maritime word for one, combining two ways of saying the number, like [[see:nadazero]].
A 20-letter word that you might realistically use.
A French word for extended family, reflecting the Norman nobility's interest in lineage.
U in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]].
An example of 1800s fictional characters who became emblematic of groups, like [[see:Baron von Roorback]].
Wartime personification of the US that took over from [[see:Columbia]].
Harriet Beecher Stowe's abolitionist novel, the best-selling American novel of the 19th century, which tied [[see:sell down the river]] to the Mississippi.
Freud's interest, meaning things you don't know you're thinking; often confused with [[see:subconscious]], with which it has merged.
A French mishearing of [[from:découvrir le pot aux roses]] that Rob jokes sounds like a filthy euphemism.
Means to uncover a secret; the rose pot held ladies' perfumes; often misheard as [[gave:découvrir le pot rose]].
A phrase German businesses tack onto names, along with 24, when they can't think of a brand name.
Originally related to inter, meaning among, which explains [[gave:understand]].
Hungarian for a bad situation, mood or quality: a frog's backside is already near the ground, so beneath it is lower still, like [[equivalent:hit rock bottom]].
The next level of intensity after [[see:under the gun]]: actively dodging problems as they come your way.
Roof standing for the whole house, an example of [[see:synecdoche]].
A phrase similar to [[see:under the gun]], meaning under pressure or at risk of punishment.
Under intense pressure; popularised by poker, where the player who acts first in each betting round, with no information, sits under the gun.
A prefixed verb English still uses, though it means something different from go under.
Old English for receiving something from someone, literally taking between two people.
Literally 'under pantaloons' ([[from:pantaloons]]), and shortened to give British [[gave:pants]] and [[gave:undies]].
Jess compares it with [[see:subtle]]: something subtle underpins something else.
Old English for to examine or closely investigate, literally to seek among things.
An Old English compound meaning to stand among something, since [[from:under]] is related to inter; you are immersed within the subject.
Old English for to think critically or consider carefully, literally to think between or among.
Invented as the opposite of the figurative sense of [[from:overwhelm]], which makes little sense given that [[see:whelm]] means to turn over; Rob covered it recently.
Coined later as a playful twist and opposite of [[see:overwhelmed]], though underwhelming a boat would also sound like drowning it.
A word for underwear, short for [[from:underpants]].
Swedish counterpart of [[same-root:wonder]].
Danish counterpart of [[same-root:wonder]].
Jess's favourite example of [[see:tmesis]].
Mentioned alongside [[see:ghosted]] as a Shakespearean example of [[see:verbing]].
One theory for [[see:absurd]], since Latin surdus meant both unable to hear and unheard; Rob notes it applies a modern English expression.
The latest replacement for [[see:homeless]] on the [[see:euphemism treadmill]].
The other meaning of [[see:monoceros]]; Rob jokes that a one-horned rhino is a heavy unicorn.
Taken from non-Germanic languages; contrasted with [[same-root:one horn]] and German [[equivalent:Einhorn]] to show the C to H shift.
Means one horn, a Latin translation of Greek [[from:monoceros]]; compare German [[equivalent:Einhorn]] and French [[equivalent:licorne]].
Current U in the NATO alphabet, previously [[see:Union]].
A hieroglyph representing one consonant sound, alongside the [[see:biliteral sign]] and the [[see:triliteral sign]].
Former U, which became [[see:Uniform]].
The name pedants insist on for the [[see:Union Jack]] when it isn't flown from a boat.
The common name for the UK's flag; pedants prefer [[see:Union flag]], since a [[see:jack]] is flown from a boat, but Rob sees it as a proper name now.
Suffix for football teams formed when several teams merged into one, as with [[see:Manchester United]].

term: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

mentions.note: The UK's full official name, a mouthful. It was the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland until Ireland seceded.

term: United States and major outlying territories

mentions.note: Unofficial collective name for the US that Jess compares with the long [[see:United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland]].
Shortened to [[see:America]] because the founding fathers committed to that name, an example of branding in country names.
Huge map that went with the [[see:Cosmographiae Introductio]] and also labelled the new continent [[see:America]].
Literally turned into one, the verse part meaning one turn; source of the element [[gave:-verse]].
Made of Latin elements meaning turned into one; source of the back-formation [[gave:-verse]].
Like [[see:murder of crows]], reflects ravens' folkloric association with death.
A euphemism, discussed in an earlier episode, used for both the private parts and the underwear that covers them.
A word rarely found without its prefix or suffix, such as [[see:disgusted]], whose base form should exist under English word-building rules but doesn't.
Words like [[see:exuberant]] and [[see:ineffable]] that lack a counterpart; also called [[see:lost positive]] or [[see:orphaned negative]], discussed before.
The hosts observe that unravel and [[see:ravel]] are contronyms, which makes the show's own title one.
Means the same as [[see:raveled]]; the word is on Rob's merch shirt.
The hosts decided the podcast's name should have two L's, as in [[see:traveller]] and revelled, to avoid a long-E reading.
In Æthelred the Unready it means badly advised, a pun on [[see:Æthelred]], meaning well advised.
An Old English word used for a wrongdoing before English took [[see:crime]] from French.
Still in common use, unlike its lost positive [[see:seemly]].
Another online euphemism for [[see:suicide]], heard alongside [[see:self-unaliving]].
German for to support, literally being underneath something, compared with [[see:understand]].
Comes from [[from:till]], with Old Norse [[from:und]], as far as or up to, even though till is often treated as its shortening.
Old English for bad weather, where un- means bad. This is odd because the root of [[see:weather]] means wind.
German for bad weather, the counterpart of Old English [[equivalent:unweder]].
Meant powerless in the 14th century; by the 16th it meant clumsy, and now difficult to handle because of size, like a heavy sword.
Rob's British way of saying he is keen, where Jess says [[equivalent:down for it]].
Used jokingly near the end of the episode as one more expression built on [[see:shit]].
Means to be in jail; it refers to [[see:Sing Sing]] prison, which is up the Hudson River from New York City.
[[see:Tesco]]'s cop-out replacement for [[see:10 items or less]], which Rob says actually means nine.
From boxing, where fighters came up to a line drawn on the ground, ready to fight; [[see:Charles Dickens]] wrote come up to the scratch in an 1843 letter.
Capital letters were stored in the upper type case, so strictly it applies only to printed text, not handwriting.
Senior professional rogues in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy.
Named after the planet Uranus.
Has two pronunciations, one the butt of jokes; once called [[see:Georgium Sidus]], it is the only planet named after a Greek god, son and husband of [[see:Gaia]].
A French-derived adjective used for the Anglo-Saxon noun town.
A word for a hedgehog in the 1300s, which is why a [[see:sea urchin]] is a sea hedgehog.
Sea urchins are named after land urchins, or [[see:hedgehog]]s; street urchins are compared to little scurrying creatures.
Original name for the [[see:hedgehog]], which gave us [[gave:sea urchin]].
Originally a hedgehog, which gave [[gave:sea urchin]]; calling a Victorian child an urchin likens them to a lost little spiky animal.
Formerly [[see:Spice]]; named after the sycophantic David Copperfield villain in Dickens's centenary year; debut album referenced his 'very 'umble' line.
Jess is surprised by Rob's British pronunciation; stress shifts depending on suffixes, as with [[see:urinary]] and [[see:urine]].
Grose's name for Ireland, because it rains so much.
Compared with [[see:urinal]] to show stress shifting with what follows.
Rob claims nostalgia for an older pronunciation, while [[see:urinal]] keeps the stress pattern.
Commonly called the [[see:Big Dipper]], or in England the [[see:Plough]]; always visible in the northern polar sky, hence [[see:Arctic]].
The constellation called the Plough in Britain and the Big Dipper elsewhere, referred to by [[see:septentriones]].
Commonly called the [[see:Little Dipper]].
Rob's favourite elegant if stretched [[see:backronym]], though he objects to the A in USA standing for America.
One of the world's fastest people, an [[see:aptronym]].
Online discussion groups where the first [[see:spam]] is often said to have appeared, and the source of [[see:troll]].
Sanskrit for the dawn, related to [[same-root:east]].
Used much more widely in Latin America than in Spain and is the safest second-person pronoun there, where [[see:tú]] can seem over-informal.
The plural you that Latin America uses instead of [[see:vosotros]].
Related to [[same-root:rape]], from the idea of snatching.
The first syllable of Guido's scale, from the start of [[from:Ut queant laxis]]; it later became do and forms the second part of [[gave:gamut]].
A Latin hymn for St John the Baptist's day whose line-opening syllables gave the hexachord notes; the hosts translate it.
Cited as one source for Jurassic Park's hybrid [[see:Velociraptor]].
Jess routinely edits it out of corporate writing, replacing it with use, which works perfectly well.
Given as an example of a Germanic word with the superlative ending, like [[see:most]].
The ancient forked letter with its stalk shortened; originally the same letter as [[same-root:U]].
A language like the Scandinavian ones where the verb always comes second, though not necessarily in subordinate clauses.
To vacation somewhere is an American verb from a noun, matched in British English by to [[equivalent:holiday]] somewhere.
Someone you only get involved with on holiday.
One of the cow-related words connected to [[same-root:buckaroo]].
A hidden cow: [[see:Edward Jenner]] protected people against smallpox with cowpox, so to vaccinate is literally to cow-ify.
Means from cows, as smallpox was prevented with a small dose of [[from:cowpox]]; credited to [[see:Edward Jenner]], though [[see:Benjamin Jesty]] and others tried it earlier.
Related to vaquero, the source of [[same-root:buckaroo]].
Polari for looking.
Dutch for father, making [[see:Darth Vader]] a spoiler for Germanic speakers.
Literally a wanderer, from Latin [[from:vagari]], to wander around.
A borrowed Latin euphemism, originally a word for any pod or sheath, now a technical term; the source of [[gave:vanilla]].
In Latin a euphemism meaning pod or sheath, a place to park your sword, borrowed as the medical term; it gave [[gave:vanilla]].
Means a sword sheath, framing the body part by its use to men, as discussed in a past episode.
Literally the sheath you put a [[see:sword]] in.
Seen at different times as romantic or criminal, like [[see:vagabond]].
Pronounced differently in the US and in British high society, showing that neither side consistently sticks closer to French.
Has the same -able ending as [[see:vegetable]].
Forearm armour, from French avant-bras, forearm.
Older American frontier term from the 1830s, from Spanish [[from:vamos]], let's go; less about running away than [[see:skedaddle]].
A Slavonic word, perhaps Russian, that came to English through French and German writing after a 1720s Serbian vampire craze; first seen in a manuscript [[see:Samuel Johnson]] edited.
Rob tries the Dutch pronunciation and wonders whether a name meaning from Gogh suits him, suggesting just Vincent.
A [[see:Dracula]] character whose English swings between fluent and awkward as the plot needs, one of the novel's inconsistencies.
Named after one of the many names for [[from:Freya]].

Named in 1886 after [[see:George Vancouver]], a Dutch-origin name, 'from [[from:Coevorden]]'; formerly [[see:Gastown]] and [[see:Granville]]; its Squamish name K'emk'emelày means place of many maple trees.
A people who were literally wanderers, related to [[same-root:wander]] and to [[same-root:wandel]], a word for crime.
Named after [[from:Cornelius Vanderbilt]], an example of an [[see:eponym]].
The phrase [[from:avant-garde]] after it went through English processing.
Means little [[from:vagina]], in its sense of a pod, via Spanish [[from:vainilla]], little pod.
From Latin [[from:vagina]], so it means little vagina, i.e. little pod; covered in an earlier food episode.
Another word for smallpox, meaning speckled or spotted; gave [[gave:variolation]].
Scratching material from smallpox sores into the arm, risky as it could cause a bad case; from [[from:variola]].
Means drinking glass in Spanish, while Portuguese [[same-root:vaso]] can mean vase or toilet bowl.
Related to the Nordic [[same-root:fat (Swedish)]], a plate or barrel.
William Beckford's orientalist novel, first written in French, whose translation brought [[see:ghoul]] into English.
The killing of a prophet, one of the unusual [[see:-cide]] words.
The author of the [[see:Kama Sutra]], written around the first century.
Perhaps from French [[from?:chanson du vaudevire]], song of the Vire valley, linked with [[see:Olivier Basselin]], or from [[from?:vauder]] and [[from?:virer]]; -ville wrongly replaced -vire.
Has no scientific definition; originally an adjective meaning capable of life or growing, from Latin [[from:vegetare]], to animate, so technically humans are vegetables too.
Recalled from the previous episode as basically any living thing, in contrast with [[see:animal]], which also breathes.
Perhaps not yet a victim of [[see:trademark death]], the hosts suggest.
Open grassland, a word from [[from:Afrikaans]].
Pedal-driven bicycles; the name means roughly speed feet.
A dinosaur whose name means speedy thief, from [[from:raptor]].
Means fast thief; [[see:Michael Crichton]] gave this name to Jurassic Park's raptors, really modelled on [[see:Deinonychus]], because it sounded scarier. Real ones were turkey-sized.
Ultimately shares its origin with [[same-root:velvet]].
From Latin [[from:villus]], shaggy hair, ultimately the same origin as [[same-root:velour]].
A fuzzy, bright red wingless wasp that looks like an ant; Jess once mistook one for an ant queen and handled it.
Older than you'd think: [[see:Hero of Alexandria]] designed a coin-operated device that dispensed a fixed amount of holy water in temples.
Shares a root with [[same-root:Venus]].
Rob recalls this term when finding the sexual sense of [[see:venery]].
The sport of hunting, from Latin [[from:venari]], to chase or pursue; since the 15th century also a double entendre for sexual pursuits.
Related to [[same-root:Venus]], as touched on in the collective nouns episode.
Shares a root with [[same-root:Venus]].
Little Venice: [[see:Amerigo Vespucci]] thought the stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo looked like [[from:Venice]], giving Veneziola and then Venezuela.
Shares a root with [[same-root:Venus]].
The French-derived word for [[see:deer]] meat.
Once meant medicine, drug or ointment as well as something harmful; now it is injected under the skin, unlike [[see:poison]].
Shares the wind root of [[same-root:weather]].
A Latin-derived coinage from [[from:ventus]], wind, recorded from the 14th to 19th centuries, meaning either flatulence or being a windbag; often used by [[see:Washington Irving]].
Literally belly talking; it first described demonic possession with rumbling internal speech, then entertainers whose mouths you can't see moving.
Named after the goddess of beauty and love, like [[see:Aphrodite]]; related to [[same-root:venery]]; in Old English called the [[see:morgensteorra]] or [[see:Lucifer]].
Previously discussed; means what is desired, sharing roots with [[same-root:venery]], [[same-root:venerate]], [[same-root:win]] and [[same-root:wish]].
Includes [[see:sarcasm]] and ironic similes like [[see:as clear as mud]], but needn't be self-aware, like angrily yelling that you're not angry.
Distorting a word's meaning through misuse until it's meaningless, which misinformation and disinformation do a lot today.
Turning nouns into verbs and vice versa, a long English tradition that Shakespeare used with [[see:ghosted]], [[see:portcullis]] and [[see:dog]].
A portmanteau of [[from:verdant]] and Ana, the name of the designer's daughter.
Literally means green, used as a pun on the words that share a root with [[see:green]].
Literally true said, from Latin; its dict is the same as in [[same-root:dictation]].
Freud's German word, later rendered with Latin elements as [[gave:repression]].
German original of [[gave:forget-me-not]]; folklore says a knight picking flowers for his lover drowned in a river, crying 'forget me not'.
A long-standing form of French back slang that swaps the sounds of words, as in [[see:Stromae]], [[see:meuf]] and [[see:cimer]].
French slang swapping syllables, as in [[see:Stromae]]; similar to [[see:back slang]].
A Germanized word for [[from:wormwood]], used traditionally to aromatize it, as in [[see:absinthe]].
Shares a Latin root beginning with V with [[same-root:Baroque]], the idea being something warty, lumpy and irregular.
Pulled from [[from:universe]], where it meant turn, it now means world or realm, as in [[see:Buffyverse]] and [[see:metaverse]].
Kids also use the bare verb, as in 'I verse him', alongside [[see:versing]].
Back-formation from [[from:universe]], literally turn, now meaning world or realm; first used this way in [[see:Enderverse]], though [[see:multiverse]] is older; often a rebracketing.
A kids' verb from 'versus', recorded since at least the 1980s, probably from gaming; it fills a gap, as in 'our school is versing them in a spelling bee'.
Rob notes that some Americans prefer to say 'verse' rather than 'versus', and that the episode is really a comparison anyway.
Business and journalism jargon for a segment or section serving one sector or topic, imagined as lines off a [[see:horizontal]].
Latin for wasp, cognate with [[same-root:wasp]] and [[same-root:guêpe]].
Latin for evening, related to [[same-root:west]].
The American word for what Britons call a [[equivalent:waistcoat]].
From Latin [[from:vestigium]], footprint or trace; first used of where a building once stood, hence something no longer present, as in [[see:vestigial]].
As in vestigial organs, an example of the sense of [[same-root:vestige]] as something no longer active.
Turn-of-the-century abbreviation for 'very highly commended', like something on a school report.
One of Jess's favourite roots, meaning way or road, found in [[gave:deviant]], [[gave:obvious]] and [[gave:impervious]].
Latin for way, road, path or course, hidden in English words like [[gave:obvious]], [[gave:impervious]], [[gave:trivia]] and [[gave:invoice]].
The French for meat, from the Latin for a living thing, which Rob links to the meaning of [[see:ambrosia]].
Millennial slang, though 'that's such a vibe' feels more Gen Z; now used differently grammatically.
Related to [[same-root:vicarious]] as someone who stands as a representative.
Mostly in living vicariously but spreading; meaning taking another's place, first used of Jesus dying for humanity; related to [[same-root:vicar]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with [[same-root:week]].
Psychology concept where Rob first met [[see:vicarious]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with [[same-root:week]].
V in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]].
Contains the Latin root for looking also behind [[same-root:envy]].
Old Norse for regular old killing, less heinous than [[see:morð]].
The word for base-20 counting; its start relates to French [[from:vingt]], twenty, and it is formed like [[see:decimal]].
Base-20 counting, found in Danish, Celtic languages and French [[see:four twenties]]; Jess finds the word endlessly funny. The word is missing from the captions.
Related to [[same-root:surveillance]] through Latin [[from:vigilare]], to watch.
Related to [[same-root:surveillance]] through Latin [[from:vigilare]], to watch.
Old Norse word for a creek or bay, possibly the source of [[gave?:Viking]], and found in [[gave:Reykjavik]] and probably [[gave:Wick]].
Old Icelandic for a distance travelled at sea, possibly before changing rowers, supporting the change-of-duty theory of [[same-root:week]].
From Old Norse [[from:víkingr]], pirate or sea rover, probably from [[from?:vík]]; little used in English until revived in the early 1800s; a job description, not an ethnic identity.
Vik- means bay or camp and [[see:-ing (noun suffix)]] means the people of; also discussed in an earlier episode.
Ends the string of insults in a [[see:William Shakespeare]] history-play rant quoted by Jess.
In Latin a farm rather than a house, compared with the weil of [[same-root:Rottweiler]].
Named after [[from:Greenwich Village]]; made for the gay disco market, with members modelled on macho archetypes ('must dance and have a mustache').
Once just a peasant or poor farmer, it came to mean the bad guy through use as an insult, like [[see:white trash]].
Like [[see:vulgar]], once meant something ordinary before turning negative.
Like [[see:clown]], it originally meant a person from the countryside or a peasant farmer, before taking on moral overtones.
Name French colonists gave [[see:Montreal]] in 1642, city of Mary, honouring the Virgin Mary.
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:wine]], with V and W switching between languages.
Means sour wine, so it is related to [[same-root:oxygen]] via French [[from:aigre]].
Means sour or sharp wine, related to [[same-root:wine]]; discussed in an earlier episode.
Shares its root with [[same-root:wine]] and [[same-root:vine]]: a thing that comes from the vine.
A six-string instrument invented around the same time as the [[see:violin]], and a predecessor of the [[see:double bass]].
Basically every string instrument is a viola; the family comes from a Latin verb meaning to exalt or be joyful, related to the Roman goddess [[see:Vitula]].
An old [[see:flat adverb]] use that shows they used to be more common.
Means little [[from:viola]]; the smallest of the family, and the subject of jokes about how it differs from a [[see:fiddle]].
Means big [[from:viol]]; an early version of the [[see:double bass]].
Possibly ultimately related to [[same-root?:wyvern]].
Virginity is a social construct, and English has no single noun for someone who is not a virgin, a [[see:lexical gap]].
Non-alcoholic [[see:Bloody Mary]]; not the original 'virgin' drink, since virgin [[see:daiquiri]]s came first.
An orchid with what looks like a tiny carving of a Catholic Madonna inside.
An old name, like [[see:bastard potato]], for white potatoes grown in North America.
A long forward-slash mark that shrank into the modern [[see:comma]]; French and Italian speakers recognise it as their word for comma.
Its plural viruses, like [[see:campus]]es, is a Latin -us word with an English ending, which supports octopuses as a plural of [[see:octopus]].
Has a Latin plural that English never adopted; we only say viruses.
The French word for face, built on the verb to look, so basically the thing you can look at; compare [[equivalent:face]].
A Romance word with [[see:-able]], unlike hybrids such as [[see:watchable]].
A Roman glass with a blue or green tint; [[see:Julius Caesar]] wrote that Britons dyed their skin with it, and it was sometimes translated as [[see:woad]].
The song quoted to show how [[see:Las Vegas]] is commonly pronounced.
French general whom a code group in the [[see:Great Cipher]] suggests was the [[see:man in the iron mask]].
One of Santa's reindeer named in [[see:A Visit from St Nicholas]]; a self-explanatory name.
Father of [[see:Vlad the Impaler]], possibly called 'dragon' after joining the [[see:Order of the Dragon]].
The real Wallachian prince, called Vlad Dracula, who impaled victims and supposedly dipped bread in their blood; [[see:Dracula]] was named after him.
Another ruler known by a memorable epithet.
The case used to address a person directly, as in poetic 'O Jess'; English lacks one, but Gaelic uses it, giving [[see:Hamish]].
The grammatical form used to address someone directly; an overheard vocative of [[see:Seamus]] gave [[see:Hamish]].

The geologist who first described [[see:Megalosaurus]].

England's first printer, trained in Bruges, who added the Flemish H to [[see:ghost]].
Produced the first English-language books and set up Britain's first printing works in London, bringing in continental printers to run his presses.
In an article, possibly from 1807, he told of using herring to draw dogs off a hare's trail, attacking the London press's false Napoleon reports ([[see:red herring]]).
Identified [[see:Uranus]] as a planet in the late 1700s.
Senior officer commanding US forces in Texas, after whom [[gave:Fort Worth]] is named.
Philosopher who coined [[see:Multiverse]] in the 1890s, predating [[see:Orson Scott Card]]'s use of [[see:-verse]].
Philosopher who coined [[see:multiverse]] in the 1890s.
Second Viscount Melbourne, named after [[see:Melbourne (England)]], and after whom [[see:Melbourne (Australia)]] was named.
Owner of the New York Journal, Pulitzer's rival in the circulation wars behind [[see:yellow journalism]].
Son of [[see:William the Conqueror]], called Rufus, red, for his red beard or hair.
The king of the old-fashioned insult, whose ability to coin them is one of his great gifts; Rob reads several from a mug his dad gave him.
Never used the [[see:ellipsis]], though it had been invented by his time.
The first to use [[see:employer]] for a person who employs another, as Rob found while making a video about him.
Coined [[see:one fell swoop]], used [[see:scandal]] and [[see:havoc]]; the hosts note how many crimes happen in his plays.
Born in 1564 and died on his birthday, 23 April, in 1616; wrote about 40 plays and 154 sonnets, and is credited with about 1,700 words.
In one of his plays he calls [[see:Z]] a useless letter.
Often credited with coining [[see:grovel]] in Henry VI, though he actually back-formed it from groveling.
An Oxbridge-educated candidate in the [[see:Shakespeare authorship question]], from Derby, where Rob is recording.
The most famous [[see:bastard]], [[see:William the Conqueror]], was known by this name first; it's unclear whether friends or enemies gave it.
Had a huge impact on English; before this name he was known as [[see:Guillaume le Bâtard]].
Also called William the Bastard, the Duke of Normandy who became king in 1066 and replaced the Anglo-Saxon nobles and bishops with Normans.
The most famous English monarch with a moniker, also known as William the Bastard before his conquests.
Known as [[see:Guillaume]] in French, though Rob thinks in Norman French his name sounded more like Wilhelm.
Brought the Germanic-influenced French of the [[see:Normans]] to England in 1066.
A descendant of the Vikings, so the [[see:Battle of Hastings]] was more of a Germanic face-off than people think.
A classic [[see:aptronym]].
Popularised [[see:cooch]] with his 1954 song [[see:Hoochie Coochie Man]].
From the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:Venus]].
Corporate jargon that has made it into everyday usage.
A barely changed Old English weather word that shares its root with [[same-root:weather]] and [[same-root:vent]].
The older, more common name for the [[equivalent:dead cat]], avoiding images of a fallen feline.
Originally a trademark, now generic.
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
Listed by Jess as a genericized trademark.
Another dialect word for the kestrel, probably derived from [[from?:windfucker]].
Another name for the land [[see:anemone]].
An old name for the kestrel, probably referring to it striking the wind or moving rapidly; related dialect names include [[see:windsucker]] and [[see:windcuffer]].
Old name for the [[see:kestrel]], from the rapid beating of its wings, since [[from:fuck]] meant to beat.
Taken from a Danish word meaning wind eye, and it replaced the Old English [[see:eyethurl]].
Old Norse, literally wind eye; it replaced an Old English word meaning eyehole, and the hosts have discussed it before.
British word; it seems odd to Jess, since to her a [[see:screen]] is wire mesh.
The US word for a [[see:windscreen]], which Rob admits makes more sense.
A modern dialect word for the kestrel, probably derived from [[from?:windfucker]].
Nickname for [[see:Chicago]] that began in sports and civic rivalries with Cincinnati, describing boastful windbags rather than the weather.
Taken from Latin into Germanic before English existed, via Roman contact; it means vine and is basically the same word as [[same-root:vine]].
Taken from the Romans by the Germanic dialects before English existed, so English has always had the word.
From Latin [[from:vinum]], a very early borrowing into Germanic straight from the Romans, like [[see:cheese]].
Homer's description of the sea, cited as a sign the Greeks had no word for [[see:blue]], evoking brightness rather than blueness.
Used to mean sleep long before the phrase [[see:40 winks]].
A [[see:hybrid word]] putting Latin [[see:-able]] on a Germanic stem.
Rob dislikes it, seen of a jockey in NPR, sounding like [[see:embiggen]]; Jess grew up hearing it of [[see:Pat Summitt]].
A superlative Rob dislikes; Jess notes that '-ing' participles like [[see:excitingest]] rarely take the [[see:-est]] ending.
Animation pioneer and newspaper cartoonist who led people to call early animated films [[see:cartoon]]s; made [[see:Little Nemo]] and [[see:Gertie the Dinosaur]].
Attracts many misattributed quotes, listed by the International Churchill Society; he was a Conservative by 15.
Said he preferred short Anglo-Saxon words; his [[see:We Shall Fight on the Beaches]] speech relies heavily on them.
A variety of [[see:rapeseed]] gardeners might grow, which sounds worse than it is.
Contrasted with [[see:wipe up]] as an example of [[see:phrasal verbs]].
Means something very different from [[see:wipe out]], showing how [[see:phrasal verbs]] puzzle learners.
Jess likes it because wombats seem wise and ponderous.
Someone using supernatural powers for good, rather than witchcraft, was simply called wise, reflecting a link between knowledge and magic.
Related to the first element of [[same-root:wiseacre]].
From Dutch [[from:wijsseggher]], soothsayer, folk-etymologised into acre; once a respected prophet, now a know-all; physician [[see:Richard Whitlock]] mocked doctors as wisacres.
From the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:Venus]].
A Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:desire]].
The modern word for what Johnson called a [[see:merrythought]].
An archaic term meaning to know, existing in a different form in Old English.
An archaic word meaning to know, from Old English [[from:witan]] of the same meaning.
Named after [[from:Caspar Wistar]].
Built on [[from:wist]]; it came to mean bittersweet melancholy or nostalgia through [[from:had-I-wist]].
Paired with archaic [[see:wist]]; came to suggest bittersweet melancholy or nostalgia through the term [[see:had I wist]].
Appears to blend the old word [[from:whist]], be quiet, with [[from:wishfulness]], making it more pensive than plain silence.
Originally meant understanding or knowledge rather than cleverness; related to [[same-root:wiseacre]] and [[same-root:wise]].
From Old English wicce, feminine of [[from:wicca]]; originally not gendered, it became associated with women around the 1600s.
Its origin was discussed in an earlier episode.
Old English had five or six words for kinds of witch, discussed in a spooky words episode; now there is essentially one word.
From Old English wicce, feminine of [[from:wicca]], a male sorcerer; the gender-neutral term for practitioners until around the 1600s.
Preserves the old sense of [[see:craft]] as power.
The older English word for magic practice, originally not tied to either gender.
A name for the [[see:foxglove]], given because it is extremely toxic.
A former name for the [[see:dandelion]] meaning an evil [[see:marigold]], since gowan is a word for marigold.
A purist replacement proposed by opponents of [[see:inkhorn terms]] for knowledge; Rob later uses it himself.
An [[see:inkhorn]]-era native alternative, first said to replace [[see:knowledge]] but actually used for [[see:logic]], closer to the original meaning of wit.
Another Old English word that meant a crime.
Old English for prophet, seer or wise man, a close relative of [[same-root:wiseacre]].
Given as a very similar phrase to [[see:with the greatest respect]].
An Old English way of saying [[equivalent:pregnant]].
In a YouGov survey most Brits heard it as 'I think you're an idiot', while half of Americans took it as 'I am listening to you'.

term: with the skin of my teeth

mentions.note: The Book of Job phrase in the King James and Geneva Bibles, referring to the gums, which gave [[gave:by the skin of your teeth]].
Gold-mining region with an apparently Afrikaans name, whose ending gave the [[gave:rand]].
Long ridge of gold-bearing rock near [[see:Johannesburg]]; its rand [[gave:rand]] the currency its name.
Literally someone very wise; not an insult but shows the same intensifying [[see:-ard]] ending.
An example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] suffix.
Simply a very wise person, with the intensifying [[see:-ard]]; effectively a doublet of [[same-root:wiseacre]], used from the 15th century.
A remedy made of alcohol, sassafras, clove and camphor and sold in America until the 1920s; an example of dubious [[see:apothecary]] medicine.
Not really a colour name: a yellow-flowered European plant fermented into indigo-blue dye, a staple by the 1400s; the blue-skinned Celts idea rests on [[see:vitrum]].
Anglo-Saxon equivalent of [[see:Odin]], behind [[gave:Wednesday]].
The Anglo-Saxon name for Odin, behind [[see:Wednesday]].
From Middle English [[from:begon]], surrounded or overwhelmed, so beset by woe; Jess associates it with [[see:A Prairie Home Companion]].
An example of [[see:collocation]].
Coined to encourage social awareness but taken up by others as an insult, a parallel to weaponised [[see:therapy speak]].
The Old English word for cloud, related to German and Dutch [[same-root:Wolken]]; the hosts think it should be our word for cloud. It gave [[gave:welkin]].
A very old word, from when wolves troubled the Anglo-Saxons; its plural keeps the Old English f-to-v shift between vowels, as in [[see:knife]].
Its plural wolves shows the same F-to-V change as [[see:leaf]].
German name for tungsten, behind the symbol W; perhaps an old mining nickname meaning wolf's cream, or more plausibly wolf's soot or dirt.
Former English name for [[see:tungsten]].
German for clouds, a cognate of Old English [[same-root:wolcen]].
A language of Senegal with strong French influence; outsiders could pick out its prestige varieties, perhaps by recognising the French.
Said to be the only city in England named after a woman, as discussed in an earlier episode.
The only English city named after a woman, probably [[from:Wulfrun]]; originally Wulfrun's high town, its -hampton differs from the usual [[see:-ham]] plus town.
Developed from Old English [[from:wifman]].
In Danny's English its plural women changes only the vowel around three fixed consonants, like Semitic [[see:triradical roots]]; for one British Columbian, both sound identical.
A fairly literal word for the vulva from the 1200s.
Currency of both Koreas, meaning round coin like the [[see:yen]] and [[see:yuan]].
Common to Germanic languages, originally meaning miracle, but its origin before that is unknown; the state of having witnessed a wonder.
From the Romani [[from:wongar]], meaning money or coal, which says something about the historical value of coal.
The old go-to word for irrational behaviour, spelled w-o-d, replaced by [[see:mad]]; wood dogs were rabid dogs.
Old English word meaning a tree, a grove, a forest or the material; it could also mean wild, and was used for mad animals before 'mad'.
The Germanic equivalent of Romance [[see:forest]].
The French for someone who cut bits of wood, another kind of tailleur besides the [[see:tailor]].
Unlike a [[see:forest]], by definition has trees; woodland words had a whole episode in an earlier season.
Actually won the election the [[see:New York World]] hedged on.
Rob believes it isn't actually a worm, an example of the broad sense of [[see:worm]].
From a Monty Python sketch: words that sound satisfying, like gorse, caribou and wasp, set against [[see:tiny words]].
An example of a hard-to-pronounce name whose -cester is [[from:-chester]].
A strong dislike of a particular word, such as [[see:moist]], which reportedly about 20% of people share.
Widespread hatred of words like [[see:moist]], [[see:panties]] and [[see:crud]], which is driven partly by their meaning and perhaps by their sounds.
A word, often funny, made up for an unnamed concept; coined by [[see:Barbara Wallraff]] of the Atlantic Monthly because they are wanted words.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement, alongside word building, for etymology; Rob loves it.
Rob starts with [[see:stare]], experts suggest [[see:tales]] or [[see:slates]], and Jess notes the name's [[see:-le]] ending, which suggests something done repeatedly.
Another Old English word with the same liar element as [[see:warlock]].
A slightly pretentious self-description, like [[see:wordwright]], that deliberately borrows the hands-on image of a [[see:smith]]; Rob calls Jess one.
How [[see:Ben Jonson]] mockingly saw himself when he coined [[see:playwright]].
From the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:wright]], [[same-root:wrought]], [[same-root:energy]] and Greek [[same-root:ergon]].
Uses -holic rebracketed from [[see:alcoholic]].
A [[see:retronym]]: what was the Great War had to be renamed the First World War.
Another Old English compound for the sea, alongside [[see:hwælweg]].
A phrase that preserves the 17th-century use of [[see:profession]] as a euphemism for prostitution.
Rob and Jess note that worm was once used for dragon, which makes the pebble-worm reading of [[see:crocodile]] less unflattering.
In the sense of vermin, it needn't mean a wriggly worm and can mean an insect, as in [[see:bookworm]] and [[see:woodworm]].
From Old English [[from:wermod]], unrelated to worm or wood, perhaps man plus courage; possibly influenced by its use repelling larvae, insects and hawks' mites.
A folk etymology of an Old English Germanic compound, perhaps courage-man; the worm story says it protected clothes from moths; also a hawk mite remedy.
Every sense comes from killing or injuring by biting and shaking the throat, so sheep worrying means killing sheep.
From Old English [[from:wyrt]], sharing a root with [[same-root:root]] and unrelated to [[unrelated:wart]]; it recurs in plant names.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for botany.
A British greeting, used around London, East Anglia and the Home Counties, from [[from:what cheer]]; said by [[see:Nymphadora Tonks]] in the Harry Potter films.
Has a grammatically justified L from [[from:will]], which printers copied into [[see:could]].

term: wouldn't touch someone with a ten-foot pole

mentions.note: In the mid-1800s it was a 40-foot pole, alongside the [[equivalent:barge pole]] version; the Grinch needs a 39-and-a-half-foot pole.

term: wouldn't touch with a 10 ft pole

mentions.note: Originally a [[from:40 ft pole]], then a [[see:barge pole]]; earliest pole references date to the mid-1800s; see also the Grinch's 39½-foot pole.
Related to [[same-root:wrong]].
Same word as [[same-root:wroth]]; the Old English form had one or two thorns, and the doubled consonant changed the vowel, yielding the two forms.
Related to [[same-root:wrong]]; intense fury and the sin of rage, and the usual Old English word for what we now call [[see:anger]].
From Old English for drive out or avenge; extended to mean inflict in the 1800s, notably by [[see:Percy Bysshe Shelley]], who paired it with ruin.
Wreak means to cause or inflict, from an Old English word meaning to avenge or drive out, surviving mainly here and in wreaking revenge.
Uses the semi-fossil [[see:wreak]], which took on the sense of inflicting in the 1800s, with [[see:havoc]].
An eggcorn for [[from:wreak havoc]], arising because wreak is rarely used now.
Mistake for 'wreak havoc', given as an example of an [[see:eggcorn]].
A common British term for drunk from the linguists' list.
An Anglo-Saxon name with [[from:-ham]], meaning Wryhtel's settlement; its football club is owned by Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.
A word for a maker found in many old job titles, often used figuratively, as in poemwright; related to [[same-root:wrought]].
From Old English [[from:wyrhta]], worker; in Anglo-Saxon times nearly everyone seemed to be a wright or a [[see:smith]], and it survives as a surname.
Connected with [[same-root:write]] through the idea of fashioning something.
An old word for a liar, someone who adds figurative wrinkles to the truth.
Coined by [[see:Alexander Pope]] to match [[see:talkative]]; Johnson called it 'a word of Pope's, not to be imitated'.
Unlike other Germanic languages' scribe-type words, it relates to fashioning things, like [[same-root:wright]].
English is the only Germanic language to keep this word, originally 'scratch' and linked to runes; the others use words related to [[see:scribe]].
From Old Norse [[from:vrangr]], crooked, from a root meaning curved; it moved from bent to unjust, a fitting opposite of [[see:right]].
Once the common word for anger, largely replaced by [[see:mad]]; etymologically the same as [[same-root:wrath]], once written with two thorns.
Cited as related to [[same-root:wright]].
Comes from the same root as [[same-root:work]].
Related to [[same-root:wrong]].
A psycholinguistic test where children shown a made-up creature called a wug supply the plural wugs, showing they internalise morphology young.
An Anglo-Saxon name meaning wolf ruler, with the -ric ending meaning ruler.
A woman granted land by [[see:Æthelred the Unready]], thought to be the namesake of [[gave:Wolverhampton]]; the hosts think her name should come back.
The only Anglo-Saxon bishop that [[see:William the Conqueror]] did not sack.
An Anglo-Saxon name meaning wolf stone, borne by an English Benedictine monk.
German counterpart of [[same-root:wonder]].
Rob calls this German slang for sex the most German one by far.
A rune for the W sound that looked too much like a P, confusing readers of [[see:Beowulf]], and was replaced by double U.
Old English word for a dragon or serpent, used by Tolkien for [[see:Smaug]]; amusingly reduced to the tiny [[see:earthworm]].
Two-legged winged dragon of heraldry, from Old French [[from:guivre]], snake, also javelin; possibly related to [[same-root?:viper]].
X in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]] and the NATO one, where it replaced [[see:Extra]].
The first X in the place-based alphabet, though it is Socrates's wife; unhelpful because it does not even start with the X sound.
The stranger gas, related to [[same-root:xenophobia]]; strange because it is unusually reactive for one of the [[see:noble gases]] and was discovered late.
Fear of the strange or foreign, related to [[same-root:xenon]].
Like [[see:homophobia]], more a bias than a fear, but rooted in the notion of fear, from psychology terminology entering public discourse.
With [[see:Plato]], one of the writers through whom [[see:Socrates]] is known.
The older word for photocopying, with xero- from Greek for dry, since it uses dry powder melted by heat rather than wet ink; it gave [[gave:Xerox]].
A trademark at risk of [[see:trademark death]], so the company ran ads against using it as a verb; from [[from:xerography]], and the Russian word for photocopy.
The company fought generic use of its name for photocopiers, with slogans like 'when you use Xerox the way you use aspirin, we get a headache'.
Along with [[see:za]], a short word that players complain has ruined [[see:Scrabble]] now that everyone knows it.
The woody part of a plant, coined alongside [[see:phloem]] in the late 1800s from Greek for wood, which also gave [[same-root:xylophone]].
Shares the xylo- element meaning wood with [[same-root:xylophone]].
From the Greek for wood, like [[same-root:xylem]]: a way to remember it's the wooden one, unlike the [[see:glockenspiel]].
Means wood sound, sharing its xylo- with [[same-root:xylem]]; mentioned in a previous episode, and contrasted with [[see:glockenspiel]].
Closest in shape to the ancient forked letter; it represents the Greek use of it and is called a 'Greek I' in some languages.
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
Supposedly popularised by [[see:Seinfeld]]; sounds Yiddish but isn't, with versions from 1825 apparently from a northern English dialect.
A form of [[same-root:James]].
Current Y in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]], replacing [[see:Yorker]].
The ditty in which a feather is called [[see:macaroni]] and Yankee Doodle is a [[see:dandy]]; it gave us [[gave:dude]].
Shares a Germanic element with [[same-root:hangar]].
One of the [[see:Kama Sutra]] sex positions in English translation.
The plural of you, or just a shortened you, at the end of early spellings of [[see:goodbye]].
Appears for 'the' because printers without a [[see:thorn]] used the similar-looking Y instead.
Old idiom meaning to hit the bullseye, the [[see:prick]] being the point of the target.
A very old native word going back to Proto-Indo-European, probably related to [[same-root?:ὥρα]]; its root means both year and season.
Means to froth or bubble, like the root of [[see:bread]].
Older meme slang, imitative of something being thrown through the air.

Its Old English predecessor covered light things, including green, grey, white, light blue and daytime skies; from Germanic [[from:*gelwaz]], like German [[same-root:gelb]]; American slang for cowardly.
Comes from the same place as [[same-root:gold]], both tracing back to an h sound.
Shares the Proto-Indo-European shine root with [[same-root:glad]].
American term for cowardly; the hosts can't explain where it comes from and ask viewers to say in the comments.
In that era meant a street mutt, another negative association of yellow; gave [[gave:yellow dog Democrat]].
A 19th-century Southern Democrat who would vote for a [[from:yellow dog]] before a Republican.

Sensationalist news, coined in the 1890s circulation wars of [[see:Joseph Pulitzer]] and [[see:William Randolph Hearst]], named after [[from:The Yellow Kid]]; perhaps reinforced by yellow meaning cowardice.
The Old English way of naming [[see:orange]].
Old English name for the colour before [[see:orange]] stuck.
An earlier American way of calling someone cowardly; nobody has worked out what the streak refers to.
Another name for [[equivalent:butter and eggs]].
Japan's currency, meaning round coin like the [[see:won]] and [[see:yuan]]; a Portuguese rendering turned the original W sound of the Japanese word into a Y.
Back slang for penny.
From a Sherpa compound variously translated as rocky place plus yellow bear, so roughly rock bear; also called the [[see:abominable snowman]].
Has always been called something like yew, and named a [[see:rune]].
A Yolŋu Matha name for the [[equivalent:didgeridoo]], and one the hosts suggest using more widely.
A West Germanic language close enough to German to be partly understood; many seemingly German English words, like [[gave:mensch]], came via Yiddish and New York slang.
Language of the Ashkenazi Jews, many in New York, a form of High German through which English probably got [[see:shvitz]] and [[see:mensch]].
Mandarin name for England, meaning brave land, chosen because ying sounds a little like England.
Newly discovered pigment that inspired [[see:Bluetiful]].
[[see:Village People]] song once considered by the Navy; a founding member recently denied it is a gay anthem.
[[from:yogurt]] turned into a sentence, creating the character Gert behind [[gave:gerting]].
British word for a hoodlum, [[see:back slang]] for boy.
[[see:back slang]] for boy.
The Hebrew source of [[gave:John]] and its European variants, thought to mean God is gracious.
Used among London Jews for a gentile, [[from:goy]] reversed.
Prefix for 10^-24, the small counterpart of [[see:yotta]].
A very quick y sound before a vowel, which fuses with a preceding H into a palatal sound, as in [[see:human]].
Dropping the y sound, as Jess does in [[see:news]]; it varies across English, and East Anglia takes it to an extreme, as in [[see:bootiful]].
Possibly from a Hebrew word, though the character was originally Minch Yoda; [[see:George Lucas]] wanted an eastern-sounding name for a Dalai Lama-like figure.
Reanalysed as [[see:yo, Gert]], the starting point of [[gave:gerting]].
Y in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]].
Rob's joke extension of [[see:outlaws]] for in-laws you've never even met.
Someone from Michigan's Upper Peninsula.
Literally means of years, from an Old English word for formerly or in former times.
Developed from Roman [[from:Eboracum]] through Anglo-Saxon [[from:Eoforwic]] and Viking [[from:Jorvik]], then worn down by Norman accents and centuries of use.
Rob has talked about how it became Jorvik because people thought it meant place of the boar, though it didn't.
A cricket reference used for Y in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet, now [[see:Yankee]].
Looney Tunes character Jess associates with what in [[see:tarnation]], letting him swear on children's TV.
Prefix for 10^24 accepted in the 1990s, a deliberate distortion of Latin [[from:octo]].
A thousand [[see:zettabyte]]s, using the prefix [[from:yotta]].

term: you do not sue the devil when the court is in hell

mentions.note: A [[see:Cornish]] devil idiom about situations where authority should solve the problem.
Most Brits see it as mere politeness rather than an invitation; Americans were split between politeness and a genuine invitation to come.
Suggested by Jess as a possible equivalent of [[equivalent?:raise crows and they will peck out your eyes]].
English equivalent of [[equivalent:a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current]].
Age comes before origin under [[see:OSASCOMP]], so 'American young singer' sounds wrong.
An ego-fluffing [[see:LinkedIn]] message that actually means a customer satisfaction survey.
A [[see:LinkedIn]] message that just means some people visited your profile.

term: you've shat in the blue cupboard

mentions.note: Swedish for making a blunder; blue cupboards were fancier because [[see:Berlin blue]] paint arrived in the 1800s. Compare [[equivalent:shit the bed]].
One of four elements named directly after [[from:Ytterby]].
Element named after [[from:Ytterby]].
Small village on Sweden's Baltic coast with the most elements named after it; a Stockholm barista taught Rob its Germanic Y pronunciation.
Swedish village near Stockholm with more elements named after it than any other place: [[gave:yttrium]], [[gave:ytterbium]], [[gave:terbium]] and [[gave:erbium]].
One of four elements named directly after [[from:Ytterby]].
Element named, not very creatively, after [[from:Ytterby]].
Chinese currency, meaning round coin like the [[see:yen]] and [[see:won]].

Old English name for the midwinter festival, still with us; its Nordic relatives include [[equivalent:jul]], [[equivalent:jólin]] and Finnish [[equivalent:joulu]], and it is cognate with [[same-root:jolly]].
Related to [[same-root:jolly]]; similar words still mean Christmas in the Scandinavian languages.
Yule plus [[from:tide]], an old word related to time.
The Romans dropped it, then reluctantly restored it at the end of the alphabet to spell Greek words; its name, [[see:zed]] or [[see:zee]], is disputed.
Along with [[see:xi]], a short word that players complain has ruined [[see:Scrabble]] now that everyone knows it.
In a Polish tale, a man who smuggled soap underwater and watched it dissolve, giving [[gave:end up like Zabłocki did with his soap]].
Rob's joke philosophy named after Jess, a counterpart to [[see:Robism]] that Rob says he could subscribe to.
Jess's own surname is a portmanteau, blending her maiden name Farris with her Greek husband's surname Zafiris.
Jess's married surname, made by mashing two surnames together rather than hyphenating them, as an example of [[see:portmanteauization]].
German word for number, directly related to [[same-root:tally]].
An arch servant character of commedia dell'arte, prone to playing tricks, whose name gave English [[gave:zany]].
A recurring commedia dell'arte servant clown, a Venetian form of [[from:Gianni]], pet form of [[from:Giovanni]]; it gave [[gave:zany]].
From [[from:Zanni]]: someone was first called a zany, a tricky servant type, before the word came to mean a quirky character.
From [[from:Zanni]], the servant clown of commedia dell'arte; a noun before it was an adjective.
Not used for zapping until [[see:Buck Rogers in the 25th Century]] illustrated it as onomatopoeia; popularised as a ray-gun sound in sci-fi comics, now a verb.
Typeface named after [[see:Hermann Zapf]]'s typographical ornaments, called [[from:dingbat]]s.
The [[see:verlan]] form of bizarre.
Z in the RAF and [[see:Able Baker alphabet]]s, replaced by [[see:Zulu]] because it is pronounced differently in different places.
Honours etymology, coming from Greek [[from:zeta]] through French; Danny says both zed and [[see:zee]] are correct and the rivalry is very modern.
Rhymes with other letter names and suits the alphabet song; Roman letter-naming logic for a [[see:fricative]] would instead favour "ez", matching "ess".
